points: Complete the interactive check on Microsoft Learn.

lessons.title: Summary
points: Use regions and zones for physical placement and resilience, and the management hierarchy for organization, access and governance.

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Azure Policy evaluates resource configurations against governance rules and applies the configured effects.
An initiative groups policy definitions into a single assignment and compliance view for a shared governance goal.

lessons.title: Cloud Adoption Framework for Azure
points: Cloud governance is an ongoing process: build a governance team, assess risks, document policies, enforce them and monitor results.
Translate business risks and tolerance into clear rules and processes for identifying violations.
Governance policies cover regulatory compliance, security, operations, costs, data and resource management.
Azure Policy can restrict regions or VM sizes, require tags, assess existing configurations and support remediation.
Use the compliance dashboard to investigate both overall compliance and specific resource or policy results.
Balance governance controls with operational needs and test new policies before they affect important workloads.

sections.title: Turn risks into operating rules
paragraphs: Governance begins with understanding the risks of the organization’s cloud usage. A governance team assesses areas such as security, compliance, operations, costs and data handling, then documents acceptable behavior and the processes used to monitor it. A policy should therefore have a reason that people can explain, not simply a technical restriction copied from another environment. For example, a data-location requirement can become a rule limiting regional deployment, while a need for consistent cost reporting can become a tagging requirement. The rule, the business tolerance and the response to violations should remain connected.

sections.title: Use automation alongside ongoing review
paragraphs: Azure Policy turns suitable configuration rules into repeatable evaluations and effects. It can identify existing noncompliance, block some future noncompliant requests and support remediation with suitable effects. Use the compliance dashboard to move from an overall percentage to the particular resource and policy responsible for a result. Governance remains an ongoing process: the team must review what controls achieve and update them as risks or workloads change. Test new policies against representative workloads before broad enforcement, because a technically valid restriction can still interrupt a legitimate operational process. Balance the guardrails needed for control with a deployment process that teams can use predictably.

lessons.title: Azure Policy design principles
points: Choose assignment scope carefully: management groups cover many subscriptions, while resource-group or resource scope narrows the impact.
Resource Manager handles control-plane operations such as creating and configuring resources; service data-plane operations access data directly.
Resource Manager authenticates and authorizes a control-plane request before passing it to the appropriate resource provider.
Azure Policy is integrated with Resource Manager; certain services also support specialized data-plane policy modes.
For a new or updated resource, policy evaluates the intended resource state during the request.
For existing resources, a newly assigned policy evaluates compliance through scans. A deny policy does not delete existing noncompliant resources.
Use management groups and subscriptions to organize governance rather than repeatedly configuring every resource separately.

sections.title: Understand where a request is evaluated
paragraphs: Azure Resource Manager receives control-plane requests such as creating a storage account or changing a VM configuration. It authenticates and authorizes the request before passing it through the relevant evaluation and resource-provider processing. Data-plane requests, such as downloading a stored object or reading a secret, go to the service’s data endpoint instead. Azure Policy is integrated with Resource Manager, and particular services also implement specialized policy modes for supported data-plane scenarios. Do not assume that a generic resource policy evaluates every individual data read simply because it governs the resource that contains the data.

sections.title: Design for new and existing resources
paragraphs: A policy applied before deployment can evaluate a new or updated resource request against the desired target configuration. Assigning a policy after resources already exist also triggers compliance evaluation, but the effect on existing resources depends on the policy. For example, a new allowed-location deny rule can mark an existing out-of-region VM noncompliant without deleting or moving it. The same rule can block a later noncompliant request. Choose the assignment scope to match the intended governance boundary: a management group covers many subscriptions, whereas a resource-group assignment has a narrower reach. This makes staged testing and investigation easier than starting with an unnecessarily broad impact.

lessons.title: Azure Policy resources
points: A definition describes the condition to test and the effect to apply; an initiative groups definitions for a shared purpose.
The definition’s location, at management-group or subscription level, limits where it can be assigned.
An assignment applies a definition or initiative at a scope and can supply parameters, exclusions, selectors and noncompliance messages.
An exemption records an accepted exception: Mitigated means the policy intent is met another way, while Waiver accepts noncompliance.
Manual policy effects use attestations to record the compliance state.
Remediation tasks can bring existing noncompliant resources into compliance for modify or deployIfNotExists assignments.
Remediation for deployIfNotExists or modify requires a managed identity on the assignment with the necessary Azure RBAC permissions.

sections.title: Definition, initiative and assignment
paragraphs: A definition contains the condition and effect of one policy. An initiative combines definitions for a shared objective, while an assignment selects the scope where a definition or initiative applies and supplies its parameter values. A custom definition’s storage location constrains where it can be assigned: a subscription definition is not a convenient way to govern unrelated subscriptions. Assignment settings can narrow evaluation through exclusions or resource selectors and can supply explanatory noncompliance messages. For example, a shared initiative can express the organization’s tagging rules while separate assignments provide the values and scopes appropriate to different environments.

sections.title: Exceptions, evidence and remediation
paragraphs: An exemption records an accepted exception after assignment. Mitigated means the intent is achieved another way; Waiver means the noncompliance is accepted. Manual policies use attestations to record their compliance state rather than relying on an automated resource-property test alone. Remediation tasks serve a different purpose: they apply modify operations or deployIfNotExists deployments to existing noncompliant resources. That work requires the assignment’s managed identity and the Azure RBAC permissions needed for the change. The identity is used to perform remediation, not to turn evaluation into an unrestricted administrative operation. Configure and verify those permissions when planning the assignment.

lessons.title: Azure Policy definitions
points: A policy definition is JSON containing a policy rule and optional parameters, with metadata and mode controlling its interpretation.
The if block identifies matching resources; the then block specifies an effect.
Combine conditions with allOf, anyOf and not, and use field, value or count expressions to inspect resource properties or arrays.
Deny blocks a noncompliant resource request; audit reports a warning without blocking it.
Modify changes supported properties or tags; deployIfNotExists can deploy a related resource when its conditions are met.
AuditIfNotExists checks a related resource, denyAction can block supported deletion actions, and manual allows compliance attestation.
Disabled turns off evaluation for the assignment’s effect. When policies are layered, each is evaluated independently and the combined restrictions apply.

sections.title: Build a rule that tests the right resources
paragraphs: A policy definition separates its condition in the if block from the effect in the then block. Combine conditions with allOf when every condition must hold, anyOf when one matching condition is enough and not to invert a condition. Field expressions inspect properties through supported aliases, while value and count expressions handle calculated values or array membership. Parameters let one definition serve several assignments without rewriting its logic. For example, a location rule can accept an array of permitted regions, then test the resource’s location against that input rather than embedding a different region list in every copied policy.

sections.title: Choose an effect for the intended outcome
paragraphs: Deny blocks a matching noncompliant request, whereas audit records the issue without blocking it. Modify can add, change or remove supported properties; deployIfNotExists can deploy a related resource when its conditions are met. Their remediation behavior should not be confused with deny deleting an existing resource. AuditIfNotExists checks for a related resource, manual allows attested compliance, and denyAction can block supported deletion actions. Disabled stops evaluation for that effect. When several assignments apply, a permissive assignment does not cancel another assignment’s restriction; each rule is evaluated and the combined applicable restrictions matter. Select the resource mode as deliberately as the condition and effect.

sections.title: Mode controls which resource types are evaluated
paragraphs: Resource Manager modes affect the applicability of a definition. The all mode can evaluate resource groups, subscriptions and all resource types. The indexed mode evaluates resource types that support tags and location, which avoids labeling unsupported types noncompliant in a typical tagging or location policy. A rule targeting tags or location on resource groups or subscriptions should use all and deliberately target those types. Mode is therefore part of the policy design, not just metadata for its display: a sound condition cannot assess a resource that the selected mode excludes.

lessons.title: Evaluation of resources through Azure Policy
points: Policy evaluations are triggered by assignments or updates, resource changes, exemptions, subscription changes and scheduled or on-demand scans.
The standard full compliance evaluation runs every 24 hours; use az policy state trigger-scan for an on-demand evaluation when appropriate.
Compliance evaluation can take time depending on scope, policy complexity and system load; do not assume results update immediately.
Investigate noncompliant, conflicting or error states rather than relying only on the overall compliance percentage.
Set assignment enforcementMode to DoNotEnforce to evaluate compliance without enforcing policy effects; this differs from the disabled effect, which prevents evaluation.
Start new deny or modify policies without enforcement, check compliance and application health, then enable them through progressively larger deployment rings.
Azure Policy state-change events can be routed through Event Grid to handlers such as Functions, Logic Apps or a webhook.

sections.title: Interpret compliance as an evaluated state
paragraphs: Compliance can change when an assignment or resource changes, an exemption is updated, a subscription moves or a scan runs. The standard full evaluation cycle runs every 24 hours, and an on-demand scan can refresh a chosen scope when needed. Results are not necessarily instantaneous: scope size, definition complexity and system load influence processing. Investigate individual noncompliant, conflicting or error results instead of treating one overall percentage as a complete diagnosis. A policy with contradictory assignments or an evaluation error needs a different response from a resource that simply has a missing required property.

sections.title: Roll out enforcement in stages
paragraphs: Use enforcementMode DoNotEnforce to retain compliance evaluation while suppressing the policy effect during resource requests. This differs from a disabled effect, which prevents evaluation. Start with representative nonproduction resources, check the policy results and application health, and then progressively enable enforcement in larger deployment rings. Manual remediation can still be relevant to deployIfNotExists assignments even when automatic enforcement is disabled, so do not mistake that setting for a universal prohibition on remediation work. Policy state-change events can be sent through Event Grid to a Function, Logic App or webhook, allowing an operational process to respond without continually polling every resource.

lessons.title: Check your knowledge
points: Complete the interactive check on Microsoft Learn.

lessons.title: Summary
points: Design policy scope and effects carefully, evaluate before enforcing, and expand deployment only after compliance and application-health checks.

modules.title: Secure your Azure resources with Azure role-based access control (Azure RBAC)

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Azure role-based access control specifies who can access Azure resources, which operations they can perform and where that access applies.

lessons.title: What is Azure RBAC?
points: A role assignment combines a security principal, a role definition and a scope: who, what and where.
Principals include users, groups and applications. A role definition lists permitted operations.
Scopes include management group, subscription, resource group and individual resource; child scopes inherit parent assignments.
Owner manages resources and access. Contributor manages resources but cannot grant access. Reader views resources. User Access Administrator manages access.
Assign the least privilege needed, using a narrow scope and a suitable built-in or custom role.
Azure RBAC permissions are additive across assignments. NotActions subtract operations from one role’s Actions but do not prevent another role from granting them.
Use Access control, also called IAM, to inspect assignments, grant access or remove role assignments.

sections.title: Combine who, what and where
paragraphs: An Azure role assignment binds a security principal to a role definition at a scope. The principal identifies who receives access, the role lists the permitted operations and the scope identifies where those permissions apply. A suitable role at the wrong scope can still give too much access. For example, Virtual Machine Contributor on one project resource group can support that team’s VM work without making the assignment apply to unrelated groups. Owner and User Access Administrator can manage access, whereas Contributor manages resources without granting Azure role assignments. Choose both the role and scope according to the actual task.

sections.title: Evaluate the combined grants
paragraphs: A principal can receive access through several assignments, including group membership and parent scopes. Azure RBAC is additive: a narrow Reader assignment does not reduce a broader Contributor assignment already inherited from the subscription. NotActions subtracts operations from one role’s Actions; it is not a global deny that cancels permissions allowed by another role. Deny assignments and other applicable access restrictions still matter during authorization. When diagnosing access, inspect the effective set of grants instead of focusing on the last role added. Also distinguish management operations from service data operations: role definitions can contain separate management and data permissions.

lessons.title: Knowledge check - What is Azure RBAC?
points: Complete the interactive check on Microsoft Learn.

lessons.title: Exercise - List access using Azure RBAC and the Azure portal
points: Use My permissions in the Azure portal to review your own role assignments and their scopes.
Open a resource group’s Access control, IAM, and Role assignments tab to see who has access.
Distinguish assignments made at the current scope from permissions inherited from a parent scope.
Use the Roles tab to inspect built-in and custom role definitions and their assignments.

sections.title: Start with the effective scope
paragraphs: The My permissions view helps an administrator see their own role assignments and where they apply. To investigate a particular resource group, open its Access control (IAM) and inspect Role assignments. Look at both assignments made at the current scope and those inherited from a parent. For example, a user who appears to have only Reader directly on a resource group might also inherit Contributor from the subscription. The local entry is therefore not a complete description of that user’s effective access. Identify the principal, role and assignment origin before deciding why a resource operation is allowed.

sections.title: Inspect roles before changing them
paragraphs: The Roles tab shows built-in and custom definitions, letting you investigate what a role permits rather than deciding from its name alone. Open the relevant definition and its assignment details when comparing access against the requested task. This is especially useful for custom roles whose names do not describe every included operation. An inherited assignment must be addressed where it was originally made; adding a more limited local role does not erase a broader parent grant. Use the inspection exercise to distinguish viewing current access, defining a role and creating an assignment, which are separate administrative operations with different purposes.

lessons.title: Exercise - Grant access using Azure RBAC and the Azure portal
points: Use an account with role-assignment permissions, such as Owner or User Access Administrator at the intended scope.
Open the resource group’s Access control, IAM, and choose Add role assignment.
Select Virtual Machine Contributor, select the intended user, then review the role, member and scope before assigning.
The assignment lets the user manage virtual machines within that resource group; its scope does not cover unrelated groups.
Remove the specific role assignment to revoke that grant, and check whether other assignments still provide access.

sections.title: Choose the narrowest useful grant
paragraphs: Before opening Add role assignment, state the user’s task and the resources it should cover. The exercise gives a user VM-management permissions in one resource group using Virtual Machine Contributor. A subscription-wide Owner assignment would add both a broader scope and access-management authority that the task does not require. The administrator performing the assignment must also have role-assignment permissions at the intended scope, such as through Owner or User Access Administrator. Selecting a principal in the portal does not bypass that authorization requirement; the add action is unavailable without the necessary permission.

sections.title: Review the assignment and its removal
paragraphs: In the resource group’s IAM pane, choose the role, select the intended user and review the role, member and scope before completing the grant. Verify the new assignment at the resource group after processing. When the task ends, remove that particular assignment to revoke its grant. Then check whether the user still receives the same or broader permissions through group membership or an inherited assignment. For example, deleting the direct Lab-group grant will not remove an independent subscription-level grant. Access removal is therefore a review of the relevant assignment paths, not simply a check that one visible row disappeared from the portal.

lessons.title: Exercise - View activity logs for Azure RBAC changes
points: Open Azure Activity Log and choose the timespan for the access-change investigation.
Filter operations for role-assignment creation or deletion and custom-role definition creation, updates or deletion.
Open an event to review its details and identify the change.
Download the filtered activity log as CSV when a report is needed.

sections.title: Use history to explain a change
paragraphs: The current Role assignments view answers who has an assignment now. The Azure Activity Log answers a different question about recorded management changes, including role-assignment creation or deletion and custom-role definition changes. For an investigation, choose the relevant timespan before filtering by operation. Include the operation categories that fit the question: investigating a deleted assignment is different from investigating a custom role whose permissions were updated. For example, a report about last month’s access administration should consider both assignments and role definitions if either could explain the change under investigation.

sections.title: Inspect details before exporting a report
paragraphs: After applying the filters, open an event and inspect its details to understand the recorded operation and identify the change. Use the filtered results as evidence for the investigation rather than assuming that every access issue comes from a new role assignment. A CSV download can capture the selected activity records for a report. Keep its interpretation tied to the chosen timespan and operation filters: it is a report of those recorded changes, not a full export of every principal’s current effective permissions. If the question is who currently has access, return to IAM and inspect direct and inherited assignments alongside the historical evidence.

modules.title: Allow users to reset their password with Microsoft Entra self-service password reset

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Self-service password reset lets eligible users recover access without waiting for an administrator to reset their password.

lessons.title: What is self-service password reset in Microsoft Entra ID?
points: Changing a known password while signed in differs from resetting a forgotten or expired password through SSPR.
The reset process identifies the user, verifies identity using configured methods, accepts a new password and can send configured notifications.
Require users to register the minimum number of permitted authentication methods before they rely on SSPR.
Administrator accounts have stronger reset requirements: two authentication methods and no security questions.
Enable user notifications to reveal unexpected resets, and enable administrator notifications so Global Administrators are alerted when another administrator resets a password.

Cloud-only password reset requires an eligible Microsoft 365 or Entra premium license. On-premises password writeback requires Entra ID P1/P2 or Microsoft 365 Business Premium plus supported synchronization configuration.
For synchronized users, password writeback sends cloud password changes back to the on-premises directory through a supported Connect or Cloud Sync deployment.

sections.title: Reset requires proof of identity
paragraphs: Changing a known password while already signed in is different from recovering access after forgetting it. SSPR first identifies the account, then verifies the required authentication information before accepting a replacement password. Users must have registered enough permitted methods to satisfy the configured requirement. A method available in the policy but missing from the user’s account cannot help them recover access. Microsoft Authenticator notification and code are two uses of the app, not two independent methods for meeting a two-method requirement. Administrator accounts follow a stronger reset policy that requires two authentication gates and excludes security questions.

sections.title: Plan notifications and hybrid writeback
paragraphs: User reset notifications are configurable and help the user spot an unexpected password change. When administrator-reset notifications are enabled, Global Administrators receive notice that another administrator reset a password. Licensing must match the deployment: eligible Microsoft 365 or Entra premium licenses support cloud-only reset, while on-premises writeback needs P1/P2 or Microsoft 365 Business Premium and supported synchronization. For a synchronized user, writeback returns the cloud password change to on-premises AD through the configured Connect or Cloud Sync deployment. Enabling a cloud reset interface alone is not proof that the on-premises password will also be updated.

lessons.title: Implement Microsoft Entra self-service password reset
points: For the pilot described here, prepare an eligible licensed tenant, an Authentication Policy Administrator, a non-administrator test user and a security group.
Choose None to disable user SSPR, Selected to pilot with a security group, or All for tenant-wide user rollout.
Set the required number of methods in Password reset. Manage allowed methods in the Authentication methods policy; security questions remain in the SSPR policy.
Require registration at sign-in if appropriate and decide how often users should reconfirm their authentication information.
Configure user and administrator reset notifications and a custom helpdesk email address or URL.
Test with a non-administrator account because administrator reset requirements differ from ordinary users.

sections.title: Use a pilot with representative users
paragraphs: Prepare a licensed tenant, an Authentication Policy Administrator and a non-administrator test account in a security group. Selected limits the user rollout to the chosen group, while All enables the user rollout tenant-wide and None disables that ordinary-user rollout. Administrator reset policy is separate, so testing only with an administrator can produce a result that does not represent the pilot users. Choose accounts whose authentication registration and password source reflect the intended deployment. For example, a cloud-only pilot does not on its own validate the writeback path needed by synchronized production users.

sections.title: Configure methods in the current policy
paragraphs: Set the required number of reset methods in Password reset, but manage the allowed methods through the Authentication methods policy. Legacy MFA and SSPR method-management controls were deprecated from September 30, 2025; security questions remain a documented exception managed through the SSPR policy. Plan registration at sign-in and reconfirmation so users maintain usable recovery information. Configure user and administrator notifications, plus the helpdesk contact for users who cannot complete self-service recovery. Before widening the pilot, verify that a non-administrator can register permitted information, satisfy the configured method count and successfully complete the intended reset or writeback flow.

lessons.title: Exercise - Set up self-service password reset
points: Create an assigned security group for pilot users and add a non-administrator test account.
Set password reset to Selected, choose the pilot group and save the configuration.
Review the required method count, registration and notifications in Password reset, enable Email OTP for the pilot users in the Authentication methods policy, and configure the helpdesk contact.
Sign in as the test user at the official registration portal and register the email method used by this exercise.
Use the official reset portal to verify identity, receive the verification code, set a new password and confirm the reset works.
Use a separate private browser session if an existing administrator session interferes with the test.

sections.title: Build an isolated pilot configuration
paragraphs: Use a clearly named assigned security group and add a non-administrator test user. Under Password reset, enable Selected for that group and save the scope. Review the required method count, registration behavior and reset notifications. For the email-based exercise, enable Email OTP for those users in the current Authentication methods policy, then set the helpdesk contact. This separates the user rollout scope from the policy controlling permitted authentication methods. Do not infer that a method is usable simply because the user has an email address: the user must be in scope and the method must be enabled and registered.

sections.title: Verify registration and then recovery
paragraphs: Open the official registration portal as the test user, using a separate private browser session when an existing administrator session would select the wrong account. Add the email sign-in method and verify the address with the received code. Then open the official reset portal, enter the test user’s identifier, complete the identity checks and use the registered method to set a new password. These are distinct stages: registration prepares recovery information; the later reset proves that the information and policy work together. Confirm the result using the test identity and keep the configuration separate from production before cleaning up the temporary account and group.

lessons.title: Exercise - Customize directory branding
points: Use an eligible licensed tenant and an Organizational Branding Administrator, then prepare background and logo files to the current branding image requirements.
In the intended Entra tenant, open Company branding and configure the favicon, background image and background color.
Review and save the branding, then sign in as the test user in a new browser window to check the result.
Verify that branding also appears when the user selects the forgotten-password flow.

sections.title: Prepare the branding and permissions
paragraphs: Company branding gives organizational sign-in experiences a consistent visual identity through elements such as a favicon, background image, color and layout. It does not replace authentication or decide which users are authorized. Use an eligible licensed tenant and the Organizational Branding Administrator role, then prepare the images according to the current requirements shown for each branding element. A small favicon and a large background image serve different purposes and have different requirements. Verify the tenant before saving so a lab customization does not accidentally alter another organization’s sign-in experience.

sections.title: Test the experience seen by the user
paragraphs: Open Company branding, configure the chosen elements, review the result and save. Then test in a new browser window as the intended user rather than relying only on the administration preview. Check the ordinary sign-in experience and the forgotten-password flow used by the exercise. Branding depends on the account and sign-in context; it does not carry over to personal Microsoft accounts simply because a guest visits the organization’s application. Default elements remain where a custom element was not specified. For example, adding a logo without a background still leaves the appropriate default background rather than requiring every branding element to be customized.

lessons.title: Summary
points: After a lab, remove its test user and group and turn off the pilot SSPR setting if it is no longer needed.
Keep production password-reset settings separate from temporary exercise configuration.

paths.title: AZ-104: Configure and manage virtual networks for Azure administrators

lessons.title: Introduction
points: A virtual network gives Azure resources a private network and can connect them to on-premises networks.

lessons.title: Plan virtual networks
points: Plan a virtual network as a logically isolated network with its own CIDR address space.
Choose nonoverlapping address ranges before connecting Azure networks to each other or to on-premises networks.
Control DNS settings and divide the address space into subnets suited to your workloads.
Use a cloud-only network when no on-premises connection is needed; use a site-to-site IPsec VPN for a secure hybrid connection.

sections.title: Start with the communication map
paragraphs: Treat the address plan as part of the application design. Identify which resources communicate only inside Azure, which accept internet traffic, and which need existing on-premises systems. A virtual network provides an isolated address space for Azure resources, but isolation does not by itself define every allowed connection. Subnets, security rules and routing turn that address space into the communication pattern your application needs.

sections.title: Plan ranges before connections
paragraphs: Consider a reporting application with a web tier and a data-processing tier. Reserve separate, nonoverlapping subnet ranges inside the application VNet. If its office network already uses 10.20.0.0/16, choose a different VNet range before designing ordinary peering or a hybrid connection. Otherwise, the same destination address can refer to different places. Leave room for dedicated service subnets and later growth rather than allocating every address immediately.

sections.title: Choose the connection deliberately
paragraphs: A cloud-only application can communicate between its Azure resources without extending an office network. For a hybrid application, a site-to-site VPN creates an IPsec connection between the on-premises gateway and Azure. DNS settings also belong in the plan: decide whether Azure-provided resolution is sufficient or a custom name-resolution design is needed. Review the network ranges and intended traffic paths together before creating resources.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: virtual network peering overview

lessons.title: Create subnets
points: Each subnet must use a unique, nonoverlapping CIDR range contained within the virtual network address space.
In each IPv4 subnet, Azure reserves the first four addresses and the final address; allow for these when sizing the subnet.
Leave address space for services that need dedicated subnets, such as VPN Gateway.
Azure routes between subnets by default; use custom routes when traffic must pass through a network virtual appliance.
A subnet can have at most one network security group. Its rules filter traffic to and from subnet resources.
Private Link provides private connectivity to supported services without exposing the connection to the public internet.

sections.title: Size the usable address space
paragraphs: A subnet is a CIDR range inside its VNet, and its range cannot overlap another subnet in that VNet. Count usable IPv4 addresses rather than only the total range size. For example, a /27 contains 32 addresses, but Azure reserves the first four and the final address, leaving 27 assignable addresses. Include planned resource addresses and services that require their own subnets when deciding whether that size is sufficient.

sections.title: Segmentation and routing solve different problems
paragraphs: Putting web and database resources into separate subnets gives you separate places to apply network controls. It does not automatically prevent communication: Azure creates system routes between subnets in the VNet. If an appliance must inspect traffic between the tiers, define the required custom routes and forwarding configuration. An NSG supplies allow/deny filtering, while a route determines the next hop. Each subnet can have one associated NSG.

sections.title: Allocate space for services
paragraphs: A VPN gateway needs a dedicated gateway subnet, so reserve its space while planning the VNet. Private Link addresses a different need: private connectivity from a VNet to supported services. For a worked layout, assign distinct ranges to the web tier, data tier and required infrastructure subnet. Check the service-specific subnet requirements before deployment, then test that both allowed traffic and intended blocked traffic behave as designed.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: virtual networks udr overview
Microsoft Learn: network security groups overview

lessons.title: Create virtual networks
points: Create a virtual network with a subscription, resource group, name, region and planned IP address space.
Define at least one subnet inside that address space and avoid overlap with other subnet ranges.
Check current networking resource limits in Microsoft documentation before deploying a large design.

sections.title: Prepare the resource details
paragraphs: Choose the subscription and resource group that will contain the network, a clear name, the deployment region and the planned address space. These choices identify and place the resource; the CIDR ranges determine which private addresses can be allocated inside it. Use a range that fits the organization’s connected-network plan, especially if the VNet will later peer with another network or connect to on-premises systems.

sections.title: Translate the plan into subnets
paragraphs: In a worked design, a VNet with 10.44.0.0/16 could contain a web subnet at 10.44.1.0/24 and an application subnet at 10.44.2.0/24. Both ranges are inside the VNet and do not overlap. Keep the rest of the range available for future requirements rather than assuming every subnet must be created immediately. For the portal workflow in this lesson, define the initial subnet while creating the network.

sections.title: Review before and after creation
paragraphs: Validate the settings as one design, not as unrelated form fields. After creation, inspect the address space and subnet list before placing dependent resources in the network. Current networking limits matter for large designs, so consult Microsoft’s limits rather than memorizing a number from an older tutorial. A successfully created network is the starting point; the later addressing, connectivity and security configuration still need to match the workload.
steps: Confirm the intended subscription, resource group and region.
Check that each subnet is contained in the VNet and nonoverlapping.
Review the created network before adding dependent resources.

lessons.title: Plan IP addressing
points: Private IP addresses support communication inside a virtual network and over private hybrid connections such as VPN or ExpressRoute.
Public IP addresses support internet-facing communication.
Choose a static address when DNS records, firewall rules, IP-based security or server roles require a predictable address.
Use dynamic private-IP assignment when the resource does not require a fixed address; Standard public IPs use static allocation.

sections.title: Identify the direction of communication
paragraphs: Private addresses identify resources inside the virtual network and across suitably configured VPN or ExpressRoute connectivity. Public addresses support internet-facing communication. These are different access paths: adding a public address does not replace the private address used between application tiers. For example, an internet-facing web service may need a public frontend while its database communication continues over private addresses.

sections.title: Choose predictability where it matters
paragraphs: A static private address is useful when a DNS record, IP-based access rule or server role depends on a predictable destination. Dynamic private assignment is appropriate when the resource does not need a selected fixed address. Azure chooses an available, unreserved subnet address for dynamic allocation. With static allocation, choose an available address from the deployed subnet; do not assign a reserved address or one belonging to a different subnet.

sections.title: Separate private allocation from public SKU behavior
paragraphs: Do not carry the private dynamic/static choice over to every public IP design. Current Standard public IP resources use static allocation; Basic public IPs retired on 30 September 2025. A static public IP is allocated when its resource is created and remains allocated until that public IP resource is deleted. Document which address your firewall or DNS entry depends on so the configuration uses the intended private or public resource.

lessons.title: Create public IP addressing
points: For new public IPs, select a supported Standard SKU, IP version and tier; Standard public IP allocation is static. Basic public IPs retired on 30 September 2025.
The public IP SKU and tier must match the load balancer that uses it.
A static public IP is allocated when its resource is created and released when that resource is deleted.

sections.title: Choose a supported public IP configuration
paragraphs: Create a public IP resource for an internet-facing frontend rather than treating a public address as an arbitrary subnet address you can select. Specify the supported IP version, SKU, tier and region for the consuming resource. For current deployments, Standard allocation is static. Basic public IP resources retired on 30 September 2025, so an older tutorial offering Basic dynamic allocation should not guide a new design.

sections.title: Match the frontend resource
paragraphs: When the public IP will serve a load balancer, its SKU and tier must match the supported load-balancer configuration. A regional frontend and a cross-region frontend are different configurations. Standard v2 public IP support is also resource-specific, so do not assume that every Standard variant can be attached to every service. Read the consuming service’s support requirements before selecting the resource, not after an association fails.

sections.title: Understand the address lifecycle
paragraphs: Azure assigns the static public address when the public IP resource is created; you do not choose a particular address from Azure’s public pool. The allocation belongs to that public IP resource and ends when the resource is deleted. For a worked deployment, record the created public IP resource and attach it to the intended frontend. Verify the association and required traffic controls separately: owning an allocated address is not proof that the application is reachable.

lessons.title: Associate public IP addresses
points: Associate a VM public IP through its network interface configuration.
Load Balancer, Application Gateway and Azure Firewall use public IPs in their front-end configurations; gateways use gateway IP configurations.
Standard public IP addresses use static allocation and a secure-by-default model, with zonal and zone-redundant options where supported.

sections.title: Find the configuration that owns the association
paragraphs: The public IP resource is separate from the service using it. For a VM, the association is made through a network-interface IP configuration. A public load balancer uses a frontend configuration, while a virtual network gateway uses its gateway IP configuration. Start by identifying the receiving resource and the correct configuration location; attaching an address to the wrong resource will not expose the intended application.

sections.title: Apply the Standard security model
paragraphs: Standard public IPs use static allocation and are secure by default. For a VM NIC with a Standard public IP, an applicable NSG allow rule is needed for the intended inbound traffic. Avoid interpreting the existence of the address as permission for every port. In a worked VM setup, allow the application port from the required sources, then confirm the guest and application are also listening. Network permission and application readiness are separate checks.

sections.title: Consider availability before allocation
paragraphs: Where availability zones are supported, Standard public IPs offer zonal and zone-redundant configurations according to the SKU and consuming resource. A zonal address is associated with one zone; a zone-redundant configuration supports resilience across zones. Check the supported configuration before creating the resource because its zone characteristics affect the design. After association, verify the frontend references the intended public IP and test the expected service endpoint.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: network security groups overview

lessons.title: Allocate or assign private IP addresses
points: A private IP comes from the subnet in which the resource is deployed.
Dynamic assignment is the default: Azure selects an available address that is neither assigned nor reserved.
Static assignment lets you select an unused, unreserved address in the subnet range.
VMs use NIC IP configurations; internal load balancers and application gateways use front-end configurations.

sections.title: Allocate from the deployed subnet
paragraphs: A private address must come from the subnet containing the resource. Dynamic allocation asks Azure to select an available, unreserved address; static allocation lets you select one yourself. For example, if a subnet is 10.44.2.0/24, a private address in 10.44.3.0/24 is not valid for a NIC deployed in that subnet. The first four IPv4 addresses and final address in the subnet remain reserved.

sections.title: Put the setting on the Azure resource
paragraphs: For a VM, private addressing is part of its NIC IP configuration. Internal load balancers and application gateways use frontend configurations for their private frontend addresses. This distinction matters when troubleshooting: changing the application’s DNS name does not allocate an address, and a public IP resource does not define the VM’s private subnet address. Inspect the actual resource configuration that owns the private IP.

sections.title: Use a fixed address for a fixed dependency
paragraphs: Suppose a firewall policy identifies an internal server by its private IP. Select an available address in that server’s subnet and configure static allocation on the relevant Azure IP configuration. If no external setting depends on a particular address, dynamic allocation is simpler. Whichever method is chosen, check the assigned address and connectivity after configuration. A valid private allocation does not by itself provide peering, hybrid routing or an NSG allow rule.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: network security groups overview

lessons.title: Exercise: Create and configure virtual networks
points: Plan an application virtual network with separate front-end and back-end subnets, plus a hub network with a firewall subnet.
Create both networks in the same region and configure private peering between them.
The official hands-on exercise needs an Azure subscription; read its steps before choosing to deploy resources.

sections.title: Build the network plan before the lab
paragraphs: The exercise models an application VNet with separate frontend and backend subnets and a hub VNet with a firewall subnet. Give the two VNets distinct, nonoverlapping address spaces, then place each subnet inside its parent range. Both networks are in the same region in this lab. The layout is a starting point for a hub-and-spoke design, not evidence that traffic is automatically inspected by a firewall.

sections.title: Carry out and inspect each stage
paragraphs: Read the official instructions before creating resources in your subscription. Record the intended names, ranges and region, create the VNets and subnets, and inspect their resulting configuration. The peering task establishes private communication between the networks; successful peering should be Connected on both sides. Keep network creation separate from later security and routing decisions so a failure can be traced to a particular stage.
steps: Create the application VNet with the frontend and backend subnets.
Create the hub VNet and the required firewall subnet.
If completing peering, configure both relationships and inspect their status.

sections.title: Explain what the result proves
paragraphs: After the lab, you should be able to identify which subnet hosts each application tier and how the networks are connected. Peering uses the Microsoft backbone and does not merge the VNets into one resource. It also does not automatically force application traffic through a hub firewall; an inspection design needs appropriate routing. The exercise requires your own subscription if deployed, so treat reading the steps and creating resources as different activities.

points: Complete the interactive check on Microsoft Learn.

lessons.title: Summary and resources
points: Size nonoverlapping networks and subnets, then choose private or public addressing for each resource.
Use segmentation and connectivity controls together to support secure communication.

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Network security groups filter inbound and outbound traffic using allow and deny rules.

lessons.title: Implement network security groups
points: Associate an NSG with a subnet or a network interface to filter traffic at that scope.
One NSG can be reused across multiple associations, but each subnet or NIC can have at most one NSG.
Subnet rules affect the resources in that subnet; NIC rules affect traffic through that interface.
Inspect a VM overview to find its associated NSGs, subnets, interfaces and rules.

sections.title: Choose where filtering applies
paragraphs: Associate an NSG with a subnet when you want that filtering scope to cover resources in the subnet. Associate one with a NIC when the interface needs an additional resource-level filter. Each subnet or NIC can have at most one associated NSG, but the same NSG can be reused across multiple associations. Reuse can simplify consistent policy, while a shared rule change affects every resource using that group.

sections.title: Understand the combined result
paragraphs: A subnet NSG and NIC NSG are independent filters. If both apply, traffic must be permitted at both scopes; an allow rule in one does not cancel a deny in the other. For inbound traffic, Azure evaluates subnet filtering before NIC filtering. Outbound evaluation uses the reverse order. This is why checking just one visible allow rule can miss the reason a connection is blocked. Azure Virtual Network Manager security admin rules are evaluated first: Deny and Always allow end evaluation, while an ordinary admin Allow continues to the NSGs. The two-scope rule applies to traffic that reaches NSG evaluation.

sections.title: Inspect a worked deployment
paragraphs: Consider a web subnet with a shared NSG and one VM with a more restrictive NIC NSG. The subnet may permit HTTPS while the NIC denies it, so the VM remains unreachable through that flow. Use the VM’s network information to identify both associations before changing rules. An NSG is packet filtering, not a device that creates routes or supplies application availability; verify each part of the connection separately.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: network security groups overview

lessons.title: Determine network security group rules
points: An NSG includes default inbound and outbound rules. You cannot delete them, but a higher-priority custom rule can override their effect.
Define source, destination, port ranges, protocol and an allow or deny action.
Custom priorities range from 100 to 4096. A lower number is evaluated first.
Default inbound rules permit VirtualNetwork service-tag traffic and AzureLoadBalancer health probes, then deny other inbound traffic.
Default outbound rules permit virtual-network and internet traffic, then deny other outbound traffic.

sections.title: Describe the flow precisely
paragraphs: A custom rule identifies source and destination, source and destination ports, protocol, direction and an allow or deny action. State the traffic requirement before choosing those fields. For example, an HTTPS application rule might permit TCP destination port 443 from a defined client range. Making the source Any is a broader policy than selecting a client range, even when both rules use the same application port.

sections.title: Use priority to control the first match
paragraphs: Custom priorities range from 100 to 4096, and a smaller number is evaluated earlier. Once a matching rule decides the flow, a later rule does not overturn that decision. Place a narrow permitted exception before a broader deny. For example, an allow at 240 can precede a matching deny at 300. Leave numbering gaps so later changes can be inserted without renumbering every rule.

sections.title: Read the defaults as policy too
paragraphs: Every NSG includes default inbound and outbound rules, which cannot be removed. Default inbound filtering permits VirtualNetwork traffic and AzureLoadBalancer probe traffic before denying other inbound traffic. The probe allowance is not a general permission for all load-balanced client traffic. Default outbound rules permit virtual-network and internet traffic before their final deny. Override an unwanted default effect with a matching custom rule at higher priority; also remember that filtering permission alone does not supply routing or outbound connectivity.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: network security groups overview

lessons.title: Determine network security group effective rules
points: Inbound traffic is evaluated at the subnet NSG before the NIC NSG; outbound traffic is evaluated at the NIC before the subnet.
If both scopes have NSGs, traffic must be permitted by both. An allow rule at one scope cannot cancel a deny at the other.
Subnet NSGs can also affect communication between VMs in the same subnet.
Leave gaps between priority numbers so later rules can be inserted without renumbering existing rules.
Use Effective security rules to inspect the rules applying to a NIC. Network Watcher IP flow verify can identify the rule allowing or denying a proposed flow.

sections.title: Evaluate every applicable scope
paragraphs: For traffic that reaches NSG evaluation after any security admin rules, for an inbound connection, start with the subnet NSG and then inspect the NIC NSG. Outbound filtering proceeds from NIC to subnet. A permitting rule at one scope is insufficient if the other scope denies the traffic. Rule priority is local to its own NSG: a priority-100 allow in one group does not outrank a priority-300 deny in another. This distinction prevents misleading comparisons between separate rule lists.

sections.title: Include traffic within a subnet
paragraphs: A subnet NSG can affect communication between VMs in that same subnet, not just traffic arriving from outside it. In a worked case, a custom deny of the required application flow can stop two neighboring VMs communicating even though their IP addresses belong to the same range. Inspect source, destination, protocol and ports for the actual flow instead of assuming that sharing a subnet means every connection is allowed.

sections.title: Use diagnostic evidence
paragraphs: Effective security rules shows the rules applying to a NIC. IP flow verify evaluates a proposed VM flow and identifies the allowing or denying rule; it is useful before blaming the guest application. Supply the relevant IPs, ports, protocol and direction accurately. NSGs are stateful, so changing a rule affects new connections and may not terminate an existing allowed flow. Test with a new connection when validating a policy change.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: network security groups overview

lessons.title: Create network security group rules
points: Create inbound or outbound rules with the required source, destination, protocol, ports, action and priority.
Predefined services such as HTTPS, SSH or RDP help populate protocol and destination-port settings.
Augmented rules can combine multiple IP ranges and port ranges to reduce separate rule definitions.
Assign lower priority numbers to rules that must be evaluated before broader rules.

sections.title: Convert the requirement into a narrow rule
paragraphs: Decide whether the rule controls traffic entering or leaving the resource, then define the source, destination, protocol and required ports. A predefined service such as HTTPS, SSH or RDP can populate useful protocol and destination-port values, but review them rather than assuming the service name captures the entire policy. The allowed source range and the priority still need to match your requirement.

sections.title: Use augmented rules deliberately
paragraphs: Augmented rules combine multiple IP addresses or ranges and multiple ports in a single rule. For example, one rule can permit a small list of application ports from approved client ranges instead of creating a separate rule for every combination. This reduces rule count while keeping the intended traffic visible. An augmented rule does not let you list several service tags in one selector. Choose supported IP, service-tag or ASG selectors for each side of the rule and inspect the resulting source and destination values.

sections.title: Validate ordering and behavior
paragraphs: Place a specific exception before a broader rule that would otherwise match it. Give the new rule a valid, unused priority and a meaningful name so its purpose remains clear during troubleshooting. After saving, inspect the effective rules and test a new matching connection plus a connection that should remain blocked. Existing flows can continue after a rule change because NSGs are stateful; a fresh test checks the new policy.
steps: Select the direction and traffic selectors.
Review action and priority before saving.
Check effective rules and validate fresh allowed and blocked flows.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: network security groups overview

lessons.title: Implement application security groups
points: An application security group groups VM network interfaces by application role, such as web servers or database servers.
Use an ASG as a source or destination in NSG rules instead of maintaining a list of individual VM IP addresses.
Assign each server NIC to the appropriate ASG, then define traffic allowed between application tiers.
For example, allow web traffic to the web tier, allow database traffic from that tier to the application tier, and explicitly deny other database sources before the default VirtualNetwork allow rule.
ASGs group your VMs; service tags represent Microsoft-managed IP prefixes for Azure services.

sections.title: Make application membership the selector
paragraphs: An ASG is a logical grouping of VM network interfaces, such as the web tier or application tier. Refer to that group in NSG source or destination fields rather than maintaining every member IP in a rule. When server membership changes, assign the new NICs to the appropriate ASG. This expresses what the machines do, while the NSG continues to define which traffic is allowed.

sections.title: Enforce exclusivity rather than just adding an allow
paragraphs: Suppose only the web ASG should reach the application ASG on its database port. Add the required web-to-application allow, then a broader deny for other sources to that destination and port, ordered before the default VirtualNetwork allow. An allow for one source does not implicitly deny every other source. Without the explicit restrictive rule, the default policy may still permit other VNet resources to connect.

sections.title: Respect the grouping boundary
paragraphs: ASGs are not the same as service tags. Service tags represent Microsoft-managed address prefixes for Azure services; ASGs represent your VM interfaces. The ASG membership and source/destination combinations must satisfy the documented VNet restrictions: interfaces in an ASG belong to the same VNet, and ASGs used together in a rule must share that VNet. Logical grouping can simplify policy without requiring one subnet per role, but it does not establish cross-network routing.

lessons.title: Exercise - Implement virtual networking
points: Create virtual networks and subnets, then configure ASGs and NSGs to allow required communication and deny unwanted access.
Test the resulting VM connectivity rather than relying only on the rule definitions.
The official exercise requires an Azure subscription and includes optional public and private DNS configuration.

sections.title: State the traffic policy before creating groups
paragraphs: The lab asks you to restrict VM access with NSGs and application security groups. Write down the roles of the VMs, the connections each role requires and the unwanted connections that should fail. Creating an NSG or ASG alone does not enforce the whole policy: the NIC memberships, associations and rule selectors must describe the intended workloads. The official exercise uses your own Azure subscription if you deploy it.

sections.title: Configure and check the associations
paragraphs: Create the network and subnets, assign the participating VM interfaces to the required ASGs, and associate the NSG at the specified scope. Compare the effective policy with your requirement. For traffic evaluated by both subnet and NIC NSGs, each must permit the desired flow; a terminating security admin Deny or Always allow is handled before NSG evaluation. If only one tier should reach another, account for the default VirtualNetwork allowance instead of assuming a specific allow automatically excludes every other source.
steps: Map VM interfaces to their application roles.
Create and order the required allow and deny rules.
Inspect both subnet and NIC associations before testing.

sections.title: Demonstrate the intended result
paragraphs: Test a connection that should work and one that should be denied, using the actual protocol and ports. A successful unrelated connection is not proof that the required application flow is allowed. Use effective rules or IP flow verify to explain a failure before changing the configuration blindly. Public and private DNS tasks are optional extensions in this exercise; resolving a name and permitting its traffic are separate checks.

modules.title: Host your domain on Azure DNS

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Azure DNS hosts domain records using Azure infrastructure; domain registration remains with a registrar.

lessons.title: What is Azure DNS?
points: DNS translates domain names into IP addresses using authoritative records and cached lookup results.
Azure DNS hosts and manages zones with Azure credentials, tools, RBAC, activity logs and resource locks; it does not register domain names.
A records map names to IPv4 addresses, CNAME records map names to other names, MX records identify mail servers, and TXT records carry text such as ownership verification.
A record set groups records with the same name and type. SOA and CNAME record sets each contain only one record.
Azure creates NS and SOA records when you create a DNS zone.
Private DNS zones provide name resolution for linked virtual networks without publishing those records to the internet.
Alias record sets can reference supported Azure resources and use A, AAAA or CNAME record types.

sections.title: Separate registration, hosting and resolution
paragraphs: A registrar records ownership of a domain, while Azure DNS hosts its authoritative DNS records. A resolver answers client lookups using authoritative information and cached results. Moving a zone to Azure DNS does not register the domain or move the web application itself. Azure DNS can host records for Azure and external services, using familiar Azure management tools, RBAC, activity logs and resource locks.

sections.title: Choose records by the answer needed
paragraphs: Use an A record for an IPv4 address, AAAA for IPv6, CNAME for another host name, MX for mail-exchange information and TXT for text such as domain verification. A record set contains records with the same name and type. For example, one www A record set can contain two IPv4 addresses. CNAME and SOA sets contain one record; adding several targets to those types is not the same as a multi-address A set.

sections.title: Public and private zones have different audiences
paragraphs: A public zone serves publicly delegated names. A private zone provides internal resolution for linked VNets without publishing those records to the internet. Links determine which networks use the private zone, and optional registration can maintain VM host records. Azure also provides alias record sets that reference supported Azure resources, reducing manual address maintenance. Choose the zone audience and record type independently: a private name can still use an A record.

lessons.title: Configure Azure DNS to host your domain
points: Create a public DNS zone using the registered domain name, subscription and resource group.
Retrieve its Azure DNS name servers and update domain delegation at the registrar to use all four.
Verify delegation by querying the domain SOA record with a tool such as nslookup. Allow time for DNS changes to propagate.
Create host records with the appropriate type, target and TTL; TTL determines how long a resolver may cache the record.
For private names, create a private DNS zone and add a virtual network link for each network that needs to resolve its records.

sections.title: Delegate ownership of DNS answers
paragraphs: Create the public zone with the registered domain name in the intended subscription and resource group. Azure assigns four authoritative name servers. Update the domain’s registrar delegation to use all four, so ordinary internet resolution discovers the Azure-hosted zone. Creating the zone alone does not change that delegation. Allow time for existing DNS caches to expire after the registrar change.

sections.title: Publish and verify the records
paragraphs: Add records that describe the actual service endpoints. For example, create a www A record for an IPv4 web frontend or a CNAME for a supported target hostname. TTL determines how long answers may remain cached; a changed authoritative value does not instantly replace every cached answer. Query the SOA record to help verify delegation, and check that the answer reflects the intended Azure zone. DNS verification is separate from testing whether the web service responds.

sections.title: Link private namespaces instead of delegating them
paragraphs: For internal naming, create a private DNS zone and link each VNet that needs to resolve its records. A private zone does not require public registrar delegation. In a two-VNet design, explicitly link both networks rather than expecting peering to publish the zone automatically. If your design uses custom DNS servers, include the necessary DNS forwarding or resolution configuration rather than assuming Azure-provided resolution will handle every query.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: virtual network peering overview

lessons.title: Exercise - Create a DNS zone and an A record by using Azure DNS
points: Create a public DNS zone, inspect its automatically created NS and SOA records, then add a www A record pointing to the example IP address.
Query the assigned Azure DNS name server to verify the A record even if the example domain has not been registered or delegated.
This exercise is optional and requires your own Azure subscription if you deploy it.

sections.title: Create a zone and a host answer
paragraphs: The exercise creates a public zone and then a www A record pointing to a sample IPv4 address. Azure creates the zone’s NS and SOA sets automatically. Inspect those before adding the host record: the NS set identifies the authoritative servers assigned to this zone, while the SOA describes its authority information. The sample address demonstrates DNS data; it is not evidence that a web server is listening there.

sections.title: Query the authoritative server directly
paragraphs: You can verify the A record even if the example domain is unregistered or undelegated by querying an assigned Azure DNS server explicitly. An ordinary recursive lookup will not automatically discover an undelegated zone. Use the host’s full name and one actual name server from the zone, then compare the returned address with the record you configured. This isolates the zone answer from registrar delegation and recursive caching.
steps: Create the www A record with the example IPv4 value.
Copy one name-server name assigned to the zone.
Query the full www name against that specific server.
Compare the returned address with the configured record.

sections.title: Know what the test demonstrates
paragraphs: A correct answer from the assigned server proves that server is serving the configured host record. It does not prove ordinary internet clients will resolve the domain, because that requires correct delegation. It also does not prove application connectivity to the returned address. If you choose to deploy this optional lab, read the official resource instructions first and use your own subscription; reading the exercise does not create a DNS zone.

lessons.title: Dynamically resolve resource name by using alias record
points: The zone apex is the root domain, often represented by the at sign in DNS records. A conventional CNAME cannot be placed there.
Use an Azure alias record to connect a supported A or AAAA record at the apex to an Azure resource rather than hard-coding its IP address.
Supported targets include public IP resources and supported Traffic Manager, CDN and Front Door resources.
Alias records track the target resource lifecycle and changes, reducing stale or dangling references.

sections.title: Understand the apex restriction
paragraphs: The zone apex is the root name, such as example.org rather than www.example.org. Its NS and SOA records already occupy that name. A conventional CNAME cannot coexist there with the other required records, so it is not a valid way to point the root name to another hostname. Azure alias record sets solve supported apex scenarios while retaining an A or AAAA record type instead of a conventional apex CNAME.

sections.title: Reference a resource rather than a copied address
paragraphs: For a load balancer frontend using a supported Standard public IP resource, create an apex A alias that references that public IP resource. The DNS answer is coupled to the referenced resource instead of a manually copied address. Alias support also includes documented Traffic Manager, CDN and Front Door targets, with supported record types depending on the target. Choose a supported combination rather than assuming every Azure resource is an alias target.

sections.title: Account for the resource lifecycle
paragraphs: If a referenced public IP changes, the alias can track the underlying resource. If the target is deleted, the alias becomes an empty record set instead of retaining a dangling address reference. In a worked service change, inspect both the DNS alias and frontend resource before and after the change. Alias lifecycle handling reduces stale configuration, but cached DNS answers still obey TTL and an alias does not create the application or its network access rules.

lessons.title: Exercise - Create alias records for Azure DNS
points: The official setup creates two VMs and a load balancer, then connects them to a public IP resource.
Create an apex A record, enable Alias record set, choose Azure resource and select the load balancer public IP resource.
Verify the test site responds through the load balancer. Registered-domain resolution also requires correct DNS delegation.
Read the optional exercise before deploying; it creates resources in your own Azure subscription.

sections.title: Identify the actual DNS target
paragraphs: The optional setup builds a test environment with two VMs, NICs, a VNet and a load balancer using a public IP resource. The alias references that public IP resource, not one of the backend VM addresses. That distinction keeps the public domain attached to the frontend that distributes requests. Inspect the setup instructions before running them because the exercise creates resources in your own subscription.

sections.title: Create the apex alias
paragraphs: In the public DNS zone, create an A record at the apex, enable the alias setting and choose the supported Azure public IP resource used by the load balancer. A blank record name represents the apex in this portal workflow. Verify the selected resource carefully: an ordinary A record containing a copied IP is different from an alias linked to the resource lifecycle.
steps: Check the load balancer’s public IP resource.
Create an apex A alias record in the intended zone.
Select the frontend public IP resource as its target.
Inspect the resulting alias record configuration.

sections.title: Test DNS and the application separately
paragraphs: Browsing the frontend public IP can confirm the test web service responds through the load balancer. It cannot prove the domain’s DNS alias resolves correctly. Query the zone’s assigned authoritative server to check the apex answer, and use a normally resolving registered domain only after correct delegation is in place. A successful backend web page and a correct DNS answer are complementary results, not interchangeable evidence.

lessons.title: Summary
points: Delegate a registered domain to Azure DNS, then use suitable record sets and aliases to resolve its services.
Remove resources created by the optional exercises when finished to avoid continuing charges.

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Virtual network peering provides private communication between Azure networks in the same or different regions.

lessons.title: Determine Azure Virtual Network peering uses
points: Regional peering connects networks in the same region; global peering connects networks in different regions.
Traffic stays on the Microsoft backbone rather than traversing the public internet. Peering does not require a VPN gateway for direct network-to-network communication.
Peered virtual networks remain separately managed resources and may belong to different subscriptions or tenants.
Peered address spaces must not overlap.
Azure-provided name resolution does not automatically span peered networks; use linked private DNS zones or custom DNS for cross-network names.
Check cloud-specific and resource-specific peering support before designing connections across regions.

sections.title: Use private connectivity without merging resources
paragraphs: Regional peering connects VNets in one region; global peering connects supported VNets in different regions. Communication uses the Microsoft backbone rather than a public-internet path, and direct peering does not require a VPN gateway. The VNets remain separately managed Azure resources, including their subscriptions and policies. Resources can communicate across the connection only when the relevant peering and traffic settings permit it.

sections.title: Check addresses and name resolution independently
paragraphs: Ordinary peering requires nonoverlapping VNet address spaces. In a worked design, app-vnet at 10.44.0.0/16 can peer with services-vnet at 10.55.0.0/16, while two VNets using the same /16 cannot use that ordinary peering configuration. Private-IP reachability and name resolution are different concerns: Azure-provided VM name resolution does not automatically cross the peering. Link an appropriate private DNS zone or provide custom DNS.

sections.title: Plan support and later changes
paragraphs: Check support for the cloud, region combination and consuming resource rather than assuming that every global connection is identical. When you change an address space on a peered VNet, current peering supports synchronization of the changed space; deleting and recreating the peering is not inherently required. Inspect peer status and updated address information after the change, then validate the actual workload connection and security rules.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: virtual network peering overview

lessons.title: Determine gateway transit and connectivity
points: Gateway transit lets a peered network use a VPN gateway in another network, commonly a hub.
Configure the hub to allow gateway transit and the spoke to use the remote gateway. A spoke using a remote gateway cannot also have its own gateway.
Peering settings also control traffic to the remote network and acceptance of traffic forwarded from that network.
A virtual network can have only one VPN gateway; gateway transit avoids deploying a separate gateway in each spoke.
Gateway transit supports regional and global peering and can extend connectivity to site-to-site, point-to-site or other network connections.
NSG rules still control which traffic is permitted between the networks.

sections.title: Share the external connection through a hub
paragraphs: Gateway transit lets a spoke use a supported VPN gateway in a peered hub. The gateway can provide access to on-premises systems or other connections supported by the design, avoiding a separate gateway in every spoke. Think of peering as the private VNet connection and transit as permission to use the remote gateway; creating peering alone does not configure gateway sharing.

sections.title: Configure the two sides correctly
paragraphs: The hub allows gateway transit and the spoke uses the remote gateway. The spoke cannot select a remote gateway while also having its own gateway. Current gateway-transit support includes regional and global peering for supported gateway configurations; the Basic VPN gateway SKU is not supported for gateway transit. Check the gateway configuration and peering permissions before changing the flags. Forwarded-traffic settings are separate controls and may also matter for the intended traffic path.

sections.title: Verify the full path
paragraphs: In a worked layout, the hub has the gateway connection to an office network and the application spoke has no gateway. After enabling transit, inspect the peering and effective routing, then test a destination across the hybrid connection. NSG rules still control applicable traffic; transit does not bypass filtering. A failed test can therefore reflect gateway connectivity, missing routes, peering settings or a security rule, so inspect those separately.
