lessons.title: Create virtual network peering
points: Prepare two virtual networks and an account with Network Contributor or equivalent peering permissions.
Create the peering relationships and select the required traffic and gateway settings in the portal, CLI or PowerShell.
Verify that the peering status is Connected on both networks. An Initiated status on only one side is not a completed connection.

sections.title: Prepare access on both networks
paragraphs: You need two existing VNets with compatible, nonoverlapping address spaces and permissions to create their peering relationships. Network Contributor or an equivalent custom role can provide the required actions. Across subscriptions or tenants, confirm access to the appropriate resources on both sides rather than assuming rights in one subscription extend to the other. Gather the VNet identities and desired traffic/gateway settings before opening the creation workflow.

sections.title: Create reciprocal relationships
paragraphs: A normal peering is represented by a relationship in each direction. The portal can create both when you have the necessary access; CLI and PowerShell workflows must also result in both relationships. Choose the remote VNet and the settings needed for direct traffic, forwarded traffic or gateway transit. Do not enable remote gateway use casually: that choice has gateway prerequisites and changes the intended connectivity design.

sections.title: Read status as a configuration checkpoint
paragraphs: An initial one-sided relationship can show Initiated. The connection is established when both VNets show Connected. That is the first verification step, not the entire application test: security rules, routes and name resolution still matter. For a worked check, confirm both statuses, test a remote private IP, then test the hostname separately. If the IP succeeds but the name fails, inspect DNS rather than repeatedly recreating the peering.
steps: Confirm permissions and nonoverlapping ranges.
Create the relationships with the required settings.
Verify Connected on both sides before testing workloads.

lessons.title: Extend peering with user-defined routes and service chaining
points: Peering is not transitive: peering A to B and B to C does not automatically connect A to C.
A hub-and-spoke design centralizes shared NVAs or gateways in the hub.
Use user-defined routes to send traffic to an NVA or VPN gateway in a peered network for service chaining; an ExpressRoute gateway cannot be a UDR next hop.
Azure Virtual Network Manager can centrally manage hub-and-spoke or mesh connectivity at scale.

sections.title: Do not assume a transitive path
paragraphs: If spoke A peers with hub B and hub B peers with spoke C, the two outer VNets do not automatically gain A-to-C connectivity. Ordinary peering is nontransitive. A hub-and-spoke diagram therefore needs an explicit traffic design, not only connecting lines. Decide which shared services the hub hosts and whether spoke-to-spoke traffic should be permitted, inspected or kept separate.

sections.title: Direct traffic through the intended appliance
paragraphs: Service chaining uses custom routing to send traffic to an NVA in a peered VNet. For example, a spoke route can use the private IP of a hub firewall appliance as a Virtual appliance next hop. Configure the appliance to forward the traffic and account for the return path as well. A VPN gateway can be a supported gateway next hop, but an ExpressRoute gateway cannot be directly selected as a UDR next hop.

sections.title: Combine routing with connectivity policy
paragraphs: A UDR supplies a path; it does not override NSG denies or configure appliance forwarding automatically. Relevant peering forwarded-traffic settings must also allow the design’s forwarded packets. Azure Virtual Network Manager can centrally manage supported hub-and-spoke or mesh connectivity at scale, reducing manual relationship management. That is a different management approach from assuming ordinary peering itself has become transitive. Validate the resulting effective routes and actual flows.

lessons.title: Exercise - Implement Intersite Connectivity
points: Deploy test VMs into separate networks and verify the initial connectivity using Network Watcher or PowerShell.
Configure network peerings, then test connectivity again; the exercise also offers an optional custom route.
The official hands-on lab requires your own Azure subscription.

sections.title: Establish a useful before-and-after test
paragraphs: The exercise places test VMs in separate networks, representing segmented parts of an organization. Inspect their private IPs and the intended ranges before testing communication. Test the initial path with the official Network Watcher or PowerShell instructions, then record the result. The purpose is to demonstrate what connectivity changes when the peering is configured, rather than assume that creating another VNet alone establishes communication.

sections.title: Configure and verify peering
paragraphs: Create the required relationships between the networks and check that both report Connected. Keep the address spaces nonoverlapping, and inspect the traffic settings chosen for each direction. Retest the same destination and protocol used for the baseline so the comparison is meaningful. If it still fails, inspect the applicable NSGs and route information instead of treating a Connected status as proof that every application port is allowed.
steps: Record VM addresses and the baseline connectivity result.
Create both peering relationships.
Confirm Connected status on both networks.
Repeat the original test and inspect filtering if needed.

sections.title: Separate extensions from the basic result
paragraphs: The lab offers an optional custom-route task. Explain which traffic that route changes and which source subnet uses it; a route does not automatically configure the reverse path. Likewise, test a hostname separately from its private IP because built-in VM resolution does not automatically cross ordinary peerings. Read the lab first if you are not deploying: completing the hands-on resource steps requires your own Azure subscription.

modules.title: Manage and control traffic flow in your Azure deployment with routes

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Custom routes control traffic paths, including sending traffic through a network virtual appliance for inspection.

lessons.title: Identify routing capabilities of an Azure virtual network
points: Azure installs system routes for each subnet. You cannot delete these routes, but user-defined routes can override applicable defaults.
A route combines a destination address prefix with a next hop such as virtual network, internet, virtual appliance, VPN gateway or None; None drops matching traffic.
Use a route table and user-defined routes to direct traffic through a firewall or other network virtual appliance.
Service tags let Microsoft maintain the address prefixes for a supported Azure service instead of you tracking IP changes manually.
BGP exchanges routes between Azure gateways and on-premises networks over supported VPN or ExpressRoute connections.

Azure normally chooses the longest matching prefix, then prefers UDR, BGP and system routes for equal prefixes. Preferred system routes for VNets, peering and service endpoints override BGP; service-endpoint routes cannot be overridden by UDRs.
Do not create multiple user-defined routes with the same address prefix in one route table.

sections.title: Read a route as a forwarding decision
paragraphs: A route answers where a packet should go next, using its destination address. It does not decide whether the packet is authorized. For example, a route to a firewall can be correct while an NSG still denies the connection. Azure provides subnet system routes; a route table adds administrator-defined choices without deleting that underlying routing foundation.

sections.title: Work through specificity and exceptions
paragraphs: Suppose a workload has 10.64.0.0/16 through an appliance and 10.64.8.0/24 with next hop None. A packet to 10.64.8.20 selects the /24 and is dropped. For equal ordinary prefixes, a UDR precedes BGP and system routes. Preserve the important exception: preferred VNet, peering and service-endpoint system routes override BGP even when BGP is more specific; service-endpoint routes cannot be overridden by a UDR.

sections.title: Connect policy to the source subnet
paragraphs: The table must be associated with the subnet whose outgoing traffic needs the custom path. One table can serve several subnets, but a subnet can use only one table. BGP supplies learned hybrid routes; service tags reduce maintenance of service address prefixes. Inspect effective NIC routes to see the combined result rather than assuming the configured UDR table is the complete route list.
steps: Identify the destination prefix and required next hop.
Check the source subnet association and effective routes.
Test the selected path and its independent security permissions.

lessons.title: Exercise - Create custom routes
points: Create a route table and add a route for the private subnet with next-hop type Virtual appliance and the appliance private IP.
Create public, private and perimeter subnets, then associate the route table with the public subnet.
The example directs public-to-private traffic through an appliance that will be deployed in the perimeter subnet. The optional exercise requires an Azure subscription.

sections.title: Plan the three roles before creating resources
paragraphs: Treat this exercise as building a forwarding policy before building the device that will enforce it. In an original lab design, use a client subnet, a protected-server subnet and an appliance subnet. The route destination must describe the protected servers, while the next-hop IP must identify the appliance. Swapping those two values sends traffic toward the wrong destination or device.

sections.title: Understand what the association changes
paragraphs: A table stored in a resource group has no effect on an unassociated subnet. When you associate it with the client subnet, matching packets leaving that subnet take the chosen appliance path. The protected subnet does not automatically inherit this table. Creating the route first is valid, but it is not proof of working connectivity while the appliance and forwarding configuration are still absent.

sections.title: Review a complete configuration
paragraphs: For example, choose protected range 10.64.20.0/24 and appliance address 10.64.30.4. The custom route uses that /24 destination, Virtual appliance as next-hop type and 10.64.30.4 as next-hop address. Keep the appliance in a separate subnet to avoid routing loops. The optional lab uses your subscription; record the resource group so you can identify the resources afterward.
steps: Create the table and destination-specific appliance route.
Create valid, nonoverlapping client, protected and appliance subnets.
Associate the table with the client subnet and inspect the saved association.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: virtual networks udr overview

lessons.title: What is an NVA?
points: An NVA is a VM-based network function such as a firewall, router, proxy or intrusion detection appliance.
Place it in the traffic path with user-defined routes and enable IP forwarding on its network interface and inside its operating system.
Separate workloads into subnets when the appliance must inspect traffic flowing between them.
Each subnet can use one route table; a route table can be associated with multiple subnets.
An appliance in the traffic path becomes a dependency for connectivity, so design high availability rather than relying on a single failing instance.

sections.title: Separate routing from inspection
paragraphs: An NVA is software running on virtual machines that performs a network function. A routing appliance forwards traffic, while a firewall or intrusion-prevention appliance may inspect and reject it. Sending packets through a plain forwarding VM does not by itself provide threat detection. Choose the appliance function and configure its policy as well as the Azure route that sends traffic to it.

sections.title: Make transit possible at both layers
paragraphs: Azure NIC IP forwarding and operating-system forwarding address different parts of the path. The NIC must permit forwarded traffic, and the guest must actually relay it toward the destination. An appliance might have a management interface separate from traffic interfaces. Put workloads in their own subnets so user-defined routes can steer the intended traffic through the appliance without placing the appliance inside its own forwarding loop.

sections.title: Design for an appliance failure
paragraphs: Imagine two application tiers depending on one inspection VM. Even healthy application servers lose communication if that sole VM fails. Availability therefore includes the transit device, not just the workload VMs. Highly available NVA designs can use multiple appliances and an internal Standard Load Balancer with HA ports; the exact design must suit the appliance and traffic directions.
steps: Identify which subnet-to-subnet flows need inspection.
Confirm Azure and guest forwarding, appliance policy and return routes.
Include a supported high-availability design before making the device a production dependency.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: virtual networks udr overview

lessons.title: Exercise - Create an NVA and virtual machines
points: Deploy the example Ubuntu VM into the perimeter subnet to act as the network appliance.
Enable IP forwarding on the Azure NIC and in the guest operating system; both are needed for forwarded traffic to reach its destination.
Use the official optional instructions for the exact commands; deployment uses your own Azure subscription.

sections.title: Build a forwarding device deliberately
paragraphs: The Ubuntu VM in this exercise is a simple demonstration of forwarding, not a preconfigured production firewall. Its placement in the perimeter subnet makes it reachable as the next hop chosen earlier. Before changing settings, identify the VM and its NIC so you do not enable forwarding on a workload interface by mistake. The route must reference the appliance private IP, not its administration public IP.

sections.title: Understand the two forwarding switches
paragraphs: Enabling IP forwarding on the Azure NIC permits transit packets that are not addressed to that NIC itself. Inside Linux, the IPv4 forwarding setting makes the guest relay those packets. Either missing layer can leave traffic arriving at the appliance without reaching the protected server. The exercise sets the runtime guest value; avoid assuming that a one-time command is a complete persistent appliance configuration.

sections.title: Check the device before blaming the route
paragraphs: In the example design, packets for 10.64.20.0/24 are sent to 10.64.30.4. If tracing later stops there, inspect both forwarding layers and any guest filtering before changing the destination prefix. Keep the optional exercise confined to its known resource group and use its official instructions for deployment details. A successful VM deployment only establishes that the VM exists; forwarding behavior requires a traffic test.
steps: Deploy the appliance into the designated perimeter subnet.
Confirm its private address agrees with the route next hop.
Enable Azure NIC forwarding and guest IPv4 forwarding.
Test transit between separate workload VMs after they are ready.

lessons.title: Exercise - Route traffic through the NVA
points: Deploy public and private test VMs with traceroute available, then wait for deployment and package installation to complete.
Trace the public-to-private path: the first hop should be the NVA and the next hop the private VM.
Trace the return direction separately. In this example, the private subnet uses system routes and reaches the public VM directly.
This shows that a route table affects the associated source subnet; configuring one direction does not automatically configure the reverse path.

sections.title: Distinguish provisioning from readiness
paragraphs: A running VM is not necessarily ready for the test: the exercise installs traceroute through cloud-init, and package installation can finish after VM provisioning. If the command is missing, allow the setup to complete before interpreting that as a networking failure. Use the named private destination for the trace; the SSH administration address and the address being traced serve different purposes.

sections.title: Explain both traces
paragraphs: For an original example, a client at 10.64.10.4 sends toward server 10.64.20.4 through appliance 10.64.30.4. The forward trace should reveal the appliance before the server. If only the client subnet has the custom table, the server-to-client trace can go directly over system routes. This asymmetry follows the two source subnet configurations; a successful forward trace does not show that both directions are inspected.

sections.title: Use evidence to choose the next check
paragraphs: Write down the expected hops before testing, then compare the observed path with that prediction. If the appliance is never selected, check the source subnet association and effective route. If it is selected but transit fails, check NIC forwarding, guest forwarding and filtering. The lab demonstrates steering; deploying a VM called an NVA does not automatically establish a security policy or resilient firewall design.
steps: Wait for both VM provisioning and traceroute installation.
Trace client to server and record the appliance hop.
Trace server to client independently and explain the difference.

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Azure Load Balancer distributes network traffic across VMs or scale-set instances using rules and health probes.

lessons.title: What is Azure Load Balancer?
points: Use a public load balancer for internet-facing traffic and an internal load balancer for a private front end.
The public front end maps incoming IP and port combinations to private back-end addresses and ports.
Internal load balancing supports private application tiers and on-premises access over suitable hybrid connections.
Rules determine distribution; health probes prevent new traffic being directed to unhealthy back-end instances.

sections.title: Scale a service behind one entry point
paragraphs: A frontend address gives clients a stable entry point while several VM instances provide the service behind it. Load balancing spreads connection flows across eligible instances; it does not turn an application into a replicated system automatically. Health probes influence which instances receive new connections. You still need correctly configured application listeners and application behavior suitable for running on several servers.

sections.title: Choose public or private exposure
paragraphs: A public frontend receives internet-facing connections and maps the selected IP and port to backend private addresses and ports. An internal frontend uses a private address for a private tier. For example, internet-facing web VMs could call a calculation service through an internal frontend rather than giving each calculation VM a public endpoint. On-premises clients need an appropriate hybrid network path to reach that private address.

sections.title: Separate availability from access permissions
paragraphs: Consider a private TCP service on three VMs. Define its frontend, backend pool, traffic rule and probe; then verify that the caller can reach the frontend and the selected backend can accept the connection. Standard Load Balancer follows a secure-by-default model, so a frontend resource alone is not permission to enter every port. Network security and guest listeners must permit the intended traffic, including probe access.
steps: Decide whether clients need public or private access.
Identify the application port and meaningful health check.
Test normal service and the effect of one unhealthy backend.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: load balancer custom probe overview

lessons.title: How Azure Load Balancer works
points: Load Balancer operates at Layer 4 and makes decisions using IP addresses, TCP or UDP and ports, rather than HTTP host names or URL paths.
Configure a front-end IP, a back-end pool, load-balancing rules and health probes. A rule maps a front-end IP and port to back-end IPs and ports.
The default distribution hashes source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port and protocol. Client IP affinity uses fewer fields to keep related connections on a back-end instance.
TCP probes check connection establishment; HTTP and HTTPS probes expect a successful HTTP 200 response. A failed probe stops new connections to the affected instance.
Inbound NAT rules map front-end ports to individual back-end instances, for example for administration.
HA port rules on an internal Standard load balancer balance TCP and UDP flows across all ports, useful for highly available NVAs.
Outbound rules configure SNAT for back-end instances that need access to public endpoints.

sections.title: Follow a flow through the components
paragraphs: Suppose frontend TCP 443 maps to backend TCP 8443. The frontend identifies the address clients use, the rule maps the ports, and the pool lists eligible VM instances. The default five-tuple distribution includes both addresses, both ports and protocol, so separate connections can choose different backends. It does not inspect an HTTP path, and it does not promise equal application workload on every VM.

sections.title: Choose probes and affinity for a reason
paragraphs: A TCP probe proves that a listener accepts a connection. An HTTP or HTTPS probe can check an application readiness path and requires HTTP 200. If a server accepts TCP but returns 503 at that path, an HTTP probe excludes it from new-flow selection. Client-IP affinity uses fewer hash fields to keep related connections together; it is separate from HTTP cookie-based session affinity in Application Gateway.

sections.title: Do not confuse distribution with translation
paragraphs: An inbound NAT rule directs a frontend port to an individual instance, useful when the destination must be a particular VM. An outbound rule provides SNAT for backend-originated connections to public endpoints. HA ports on an internal Standard Load Balancer cover all TCP and UDP ports for scenarios such as redundant NVAs. Each serves a different purpose, so adding one is not a substitute for the ordinary application traffic rule.
steps: Check frontend and backend port mapping first.
Confirm the probe tests the intended listener or readiness path.
Inspect application distribution, affinity and translation requirements separately.

lessons.title: When to use Azure Load Balancer
points: Choose Load Balancer for high-performance TCP or UDP traffic and private or public VM application tiers.
Use Application Gateway when routing must inspect HTTP host names or URL paths, or needs regional web application firewall features.
Use Front Door for global Layer 7 delivery and acceleration across regions; Traffic Manager distributes traffic using DNS.
A single lightly used server may not need load balancing; choose the service from application and availability requirements.

sections.title: Choose from the information the service must inspect
paragraphs: Start with the protocol and routing decision. A private TCP processing service that only needs a common endpoint and healthy VM selection fits Layer 4 Load Balancer. A website requiring /orders and /images to reach different pools needs Layer 7 routing. The fact that an application uses HTTPS does not automatically choose Application Gateway; the decision depends on whether web-aware processing is required.

sections.title: Compare regional and global responsibilities
paragraphs: Application Gateway supplies regional web routing and TLS processing, with optional WAF. Front Door supplies global web delivery and acceleration across regions. Traffic Manager returns DNS answers that steer clients toward endpoints; cached DNS answers affect how quickly clients adopt a new target. Load Balancer operates on TCP or UDP traffic inside its supported network scope rather than choosing destinations by HTTP hostname or URL path.

sections.title: Apply the comparison to a deployment
paragraphs: Imagine an internal analytics tier with several VMs, plus two regional websites exposed to worldwide users. The private analytics endpoint can use an internal Load Balancer, while the global web requirement calls for evaluating Front Door or DNS-based Traffic Manager. These are different requirements rather than interchangeable names for one component. Before adding a pool, verify that demand or availability requirements justify multiple service instances.
steps: List protocols, client locations and required routing decisions.
Choose public or private frontend scope.
Identify regional versus global availability needs.
Check health-probe and session-persistence requirements against the chosen service.

points: Load Balancer combines Layer 4 rules, health probes and optional affinity to distribute traffic reliably.
Distinguish it from Layer 7 Application Gateway and Front Door, and DNS-based Traffic Manager.

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Application Gateway manages web requests with load balancing, TLS processing and optional web application firewall protection.

lessons.title: What is Azure Application Gateway?
points: Application Gateway routes HTTP traffic to pools containing VMs, scale sets, App Service apps or reachable on-premises servers.
It balances requests across healthy back ends; session stickiness can keep a client session on the same server.
It supports TLS termination and end-to-end encryption, plus optional WAF protection against common web attacks.
Standard_v2 and WAF_v2 support autoscaling as traffic changes; connection draining supports graceful removal of back-end servers.

sections.title: Place a web-aware gateway before the application
paragraphs: Application Gateway receives web requests and forwards them to healthy servers in a backend pool. Those servers can be Azure VMs, scale-set instances, App Service applications or reachable on-premises servers. The gateway is useful when the routing decision needs web information or when TLS processing and optional web application firewall protection belong at a shared entry point instead of on each frontend server.

sections.title: Separate encryption, session state and scaling
paragraphs: TLS termination ends the client encryption connection at the gateway; HTTPS backend settings establish another encrypted connection when the backend leg must also be protected. Cookie-based affinity can retain a session on one server, but it does not replicate that server’s session data. Standard_v2 and WAF_v2 support autoscaling; connection draining helps planned removal of pool members preserve existing work. These capabilities solve different problems.

sections.title: Work through a portal scenario
paragraphs: Suppose a regional customer portal needs HTTPS, a healthy pool of application servers and WAF checks for common web attacks. Use the gateway as the controlled web entry point, then choose whether backend traffic requires HTTPS too. Confirm health independently of the public certificate: a correctly encrypted listener cannot make an unhealthy backend ready. During updates, plan draining and backend validation rather than treating an instance-count change as an application release procedure.
steps: Identify backend targets and their network reachability.
Define listener TLS and backend encryption requirements separately.
Choose supported v2 scaling and WAF capabilities from the actual requirements.

lessons.title: How Azure Application Gateway works
points: A front-end IP receives traffic. A listener matches a protocol, port, host and IP combination, and a routing rule connects that listener to a back-end pool.
Layer 7 path-based routing sends different URL paths to different pools; multi-site listeners route using host names.
Back-end HTTP settings define protocol, timeout, session affinity, connection draining and probe behavior.
TLS termination decrypts incoming traffic at the gateway to offload back-end work. Configure HTTPS to the back end when traffic must be re-encrypted.
Optional WAF policies inspect requests for threats such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting before requests reach the application.
Health probes determine eligible back ends; HTTP responses from 200 through 399 are normally healthy for the probe described here.

Additional features include redirects, header rewrites, custom error pages, v2 autoscaling and WebSocket support. HTTP/2 is supported on client-to-gateway connections; back-end HTTP connections use HTTP/1.1.

sections.title: Connect listeners, rules and pools
paragraphs: The frontend receives a connection; the listener recognizes the relevant IP, port, protocol and, for multi-site listeners, hostname. A routing rule then selects a backend pool and its settings. A basic listener accepts requests without hostname-specific selection. Place site-specific rules ahead of broad basic or wildcard matches so the broad match does not capture requests intended for a particular site.

sections.title: Work through host and path routing
paragraphs: An original design hosts portal.example and help.example on one gateway. Separate multi-site listeners can direct those hostnames to different pools. Within the portal, a path-based rule can send /reports/* to report servers and other requests to the ordinary application pool. Backend settings must match the server protocol and port, and probes must check the appropriate endpoint; the ordinary probe healthy range is 200–399, unlike Load Balancer’s HTTP 200 requirement.

sections.title: Keep protocol legs and security controls distinct
paragraphs: Listener HTTPS protects the client leg, while backend HTTPS protects the gateway-to-server leg. HTTP/2 is a client-to-gateway capability on HTTPS listeners; backend HTTP connections use HTTP/1.1. WAF inspects web requests, whereas redirects and header rewrites change request handling. Validate these separately: hostname matching, route selection, backend health and encryption can each fail even when the other components are correct.
steps: Map each expected hostname and path to its listener and pool.
Check rule priorities and backend protocol settings.
Test probe health, redirects and the intended HTTPS behavior.

lessons.title: When to use Azure Application Gateway
points: Choose Application Gateway for regional HTTP routing, TLS offload, session affinity and optional WAF protection.
It can front reachable on-premises web servers as well as Azure-hosted web applications.
Choose Front Door for global web delivery, Traffic Manager for DNS-based distribution, or Load Balancer for Layer 4 TCP and UDP traffic.
Decide whether the application actually needs a pool and gateway before adding this service.

sections.title: Turn application requirements into selection criteria
paragraphs: Choose Application Gateway when a regional web application needs hostname or path routing, centralized TLS termination, session affinity or optional WAF. For example, a regional sales portal might route administrative and customer requests to separate pools while inspecting web attacks at the gateway. The requirement should explain which gateway feature is necessary; merely having a website does not establish that it needs this additional component.

sections.title: Check the backend reachability requirement
paragraphs: On-premises servers can be pool targets, but naming them in a pool does not build the network connection to the datacenter. The gateway must be able to reach the targets and probe them successfully. Affinity helps when an application retains session state locally, while healthy-pool selection avoids unavailable servers. HTTPS backend settings are a separate decision when encryption must continue beyond the gateway.

sections.title: Compare alternatives before deployment
paragraphs: A raw TCP or UDP service fits Load Balancer rather than HTTP path routing. A website needing global delivery and acceleration suggests Front Door. A requirement to steer clients among regional endpoints using DNS suggests Traffic Manager, with DNS caching affecting failover behavior. A small single-server site might need none of these distribution services. Compare the feature requirements and traffic geography before choosing a regional gateway simply because it is called a load balancer.
steps: Record the regional web-routing and security requirements.
Confirm backend reachability and meaningful probe responses.
Decide client and backend TLS independently.
Choose the service whose protocol and geographic scope match the application.

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Network Watcher provides monitoring and diagnostic tools for networking used by Azure IaaS resources.

lessons.title: What is Azure Network Watcher?
points: Use Topology to see resource relationships and Connection Monitor to track connectivity and latency over time.
IP flow verify identifies whether traffic is allowed or denied and which security rule applies. NSG diagnostics examines filtering for supported resources.
Next hop reports the route, next-hop type and IP used for a destination; Effective security rules combines applicable subnet and NIC rules.
Connection troubleshoot tests connectivity at a point in time rather than continuously monitoring it.
Packet capture records traffic for detailed analysis; VPN troubleshoot diagnoses virtual network gateways and their connections.
Virtual network flow logs record IP traffic in storage, and Traffic analytics visualizes it. New NSG flow logs cannot be created; existing NSG flow logs retire on 30 September 2027.
Network Watcher is primarily for IaaS networking, rather than general PaaS monitoring or website analytics.

sections.title: Choose the question before the diagnostic tool
paragraphs: Network Watcher groups tools for topology, connection monitoring, packet filtering, routing and detailed traffic investigation. A topology view explains resource relationships, not whether a TCP listener is healthy. IP flow verify answers a filtering question, while Next hop answers a routing question. Connection troubleshoot tests reachability now; Connection Monitor tracks it over time. Selecting the tool from the question prevents interpreting one successful check as proof of the whole path.

sections.title: Use several evidence types together
paragraphs: For an original example, a VM cannot reach an internal service. Start with the intended source, destination and port. Check the selected route and applicable security rules, then run a point-in-time connection test. If those results do not explain the failure, a filtered packet capture can expose what is actually sent and received. VPN troubleshoot supplies a different investigation path when the failing connection traverses a gateway.

sections.title: Use current traffic logging options
paragraphs: Flow records and Traffic analytics help investigate traffic patterns rather than application page views. Plan new logging around virtual network flow logs. New NSG flow logs cannot be created, and existing NSG flow logs retire on September 30, 2027. Network Watcher primarily targets Azure IaaS networking; use service-specific monitoring for PaaS behavior and web analytics.
steps: Identify whether the symptom concerns filtering, routing, connectivity or VPN health.
Collect the relevant test result before changing configuration.
Use historical monitoring or traffic records for recurring patterns.

lessons.title: How Azure Network Watcher works
points: Creating or updating a virtual network normally enables Network Watcher in that subscription and region. If automatic enablement was previously disabled, enable it manually; open the tool through portal search.
Topology shows resources and their Contains or Associated relationships so you can inspect the network layout.
Connection Monitor probes endpoints at intervals. Azure VM sources need the Network Watcher extension; on-premises sources need Azure Arc and Azure Monitor Agent.
For IP flow verify, provide the VM, NIC, local and remote IPs and ports, protocol and direction.
Next hop uses effective NIC routes to identify whether packets go to the intended network, gateway or appliance.
Packet capture uses the VM extension, accepts traffic filters and saves captured data to disk or blob storage.
Connection troubleshooting can identify DNS, guest firewall, NSG, route, CPU or memory issues; VPN diagnostics return health details and recommended actions.

sections.title: Establish the monitoring prerequisites
paragraphs: Creating or updating a VNet normally enables Network Watcher in its subscription and region, unless automatic enablement was previously opted out. The monitoring resource being available does not mean every guest has the required agent. Azure VM and scale-set Connection Monitor sources need the Network Watcher extension; on-premises sources need Azure Arc and Azure Monitor Agent. Destination endpoints do not all require those source agents.

sections.title: Describe an exact test instead of a vague failure
paragraphs: IP flow verify evaluates specified packet attributes: direction, protocol, local and remote addresses and ports, VM and NIC. Next hop reports the selected route for a destination using effective NIC routes. These inputs matter when a VM has multiple interfaces or the problem affects only one protocol or port. A check for one combination cannot establish that every flow to the same server is permitted.

sections.title: Build a small continuous monitoring example
paragraphs: Suppose two application VMs should reach a private API and an on-premises service. Define the source endpoints, destinations and test configurations, then combine them in a Connection Monitor test group. Repeated tests provide latency and failure history that a single connection test cannot show. Packet capture is another tool: its traffic filters limit recorded packets, and captures can be stored locally or in blob storage.
steps: Confirm regional Network Watcher availability and source agent prerequisites.
Specify the real failing addresses, protocol, port and direction.
Inspect monitoring history or capture relevant traffic when point-in-time results are insufficient.

lessons.title: When to use Azure Network Watcher
points: Use IP flow verify to investigate an NSG blocking communication, such as a required management port between VMs.
Use VPN troubleshoot for gateway and site-to-site connection health, then inspect its diagnostic logs and recommendations.
Measure endpoint latency across regions or hybrid connections before changing workload placement.
For PaaS service issues or website analytics, use the appropriate service-specific monitoring and health tools instead.

sections.title: Diagnose a blocked management connection
paragraphs: Imagine VM-A cannot open TCP 5986 to VM-B for HTTPS-based remote management. IP flow verify can test whether the relevant NSG rules allow that specific inbound or outbound packet and identify the matching rule. An allowed result only clears that filtering check; it does not prove that the guest firewall allows the port or that the remote service is listening. Follow with connection testing when necessary.

sections.title: Investigate hybrid failures and latency separately
paragraphs: If the failed path crosses a site-to-site VPN, inspect the gateway and connection with VPN troubleshoot and read its diagnostic details and recommended actions. If connectivity works but performance is poor, use repeated Connection Monitor tests to compare endpoint latency over time. For example, compare an Azure source and an on-premises source reaching the same service before deciding that moving a workload will improve its network path.

sections.title: Make a change that follows the evidence
paragraphs: A routing failure calls for route and next-hop inspection; a named NSG denial calls for checking the intended security policy; a DNS failure calls for name-resolution investigation. Change the control responsible for the observed result and rerun the same test to assess the effect. For PaaS application behavior or website analytics, use the appropriate service tools instead of treating Network Watcher as a general application monitor.
steps: Write the exact source, destination, port and symptom.
Run the tool that examines the suspected layer.
Inspect returned rule, route or gateway diagnostics.
After an authorized correction, repeat the same test and compare results.

points: Choose the Network Watcher tool that matches the problem: filtering, routing, continuous connectivity, packet details or VPN health.

paths.title: AZ-104: Implement and manage storage in Azure

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Choose storage services, performance and redundancy to fit your data and recovery requirements.

lessons.title: Implement Azure Storage
points: Azure Storage provides managed services for objects, file shares, messages and nonrelational structured data.
Use managed disks for VM block storage, Blob Storage for unstructured objects and suitable data services for application records.
Redundancy protects against hardware or wider failures; encryption and access controls protect data access.
Access services through supported APIs, SDKs, CLI, PowerShell, the portal or Storage Explorer.
Blob SFTP requires hierarchical namespace. Blob NFSv3 also requires hierarchical namespace and lets Linux clients mount containers.
The portal can default to Microsoft Entra authorization instead of Shared Key authorization.

sections.title: Start with the interface the application needs
paragraphs: Storage selection starts with how an application reads and writes, rather than with the extension of its files. A VM database needing a block device belongs on suitable managed disks. An application opening a shared directory needs Azure Files. An application retrieving objects by URL can use Blob Storage. These choices affect the client libraries, mount requirements and permissions you configure, so putting the same bytes in a different service can require application changes.

sections.title: Separate availability from protection
paragraphs: For an original example, imagine a document-processing service with uploaded PDFs, a worker VM and a shared configuration directory. Put uploaded objects in Blob Storage, the VM operating system on managed disks and the shared directory in Azure Files if the application expects file-system access. Then choose redundancy for each supported resource. Replication helps with infrastructure failures; it does not replace authorization or a recovery strategy for an accidental overwrite.

sections.title: Check protocol and identity prerequisites
paragraphs: The access protocol can narrow the account design. Blob SFTP and Blob NFSv3 require hierarchical namespace, so verify that prerequisite before planning a migration using those protocols. Hierarchical namespace also changes compatibility with features such as object replication. In the portal, defaulting to Microsoft Entra authorization changes the preferred authorization method, but you still need suitable data permissions. A setting that prefers identity authorization is not itself a grant of access.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: secure file transfer protocol support
Microsoft Learn: network file system protocol support

lessons.title: Explore Azure Storage services
points: Blob Storage stores large volumes of unstructured objects such as images, media, backups and archived data.
Azure Files provides managed file shares using SMB or NFS for applications that expect shared files.
Queue Storage holds messages for asynchronous processing, decoupling work such as image uploads from thumbnail generation.
A queue message can be up to 64 KB; queues can hold large backlogs of messages.
Table Storage is a schemaless key-and-attribute store for structured, nonrelational data.
Choose the service by the access pattern and data model rather than treating objects, file shares, queues and tables as interchangeable.

sections.title: Match the service to the data model
paragraphs: Objects, shared files, messages and table entities solve different problems. Blob Storage makes a named object accessible through object APIs. Azure Files exposes shared directories over the selected supported file protocol. Queue Storage holds messages describing work to perform. Table Storage holds structured key-and-attribute entities without imposing one relational schema. Table Storage should not be confused with the separate Azure Cosmos DB for Table offering and its additional distribution and indexing capabilities.

sections.title: Design a decoupled workflow
paragraphs: Consider an original invoice-processing example. Upload a scanned invoice as a blob, then place a small message describing the processing work in a queue. A worker can read the message and retrieve the corresponding object separately. The queue contains the work description rather than the entire large document: Queue Storage limits each message to 64 KB. This separation lets the receiving application and background processing capacity be considered independently when demand changes.

sections.title: Choose sharing deliberately
paragraphs: If several existing applications need the same mounted directory, Azure Files is usually a better interface match than replacing file operations with object API calls. If a new application simply downloads images by URL, Blob Storage avoids requiring a mounted file share. Record the expected readers, writers and client protocols before deploying. An Azure Files mount also needs a supported authentication and network path; file-sharing suitability does not mean every client automatically receives read/write permission.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: storage files active directory overview

lessons.title: Determine storage account types
points: Standard general-purpose v2 supports blobs, Data Lake Storage, queues, tables and Azure Files, and is suitable for most general storage scenarios.
Premium block blob accounts target high transaction rates and consistent low object-storage latency.
Premium FileStorage accounts provide high-performance file shares; premium page blob accounts provide page blobs for suitable I/O-intensive workloads.
Account types have different service and redundancy support: premium options are more specialized than general-purpose v2.
You cannot directly convert a Standard account into Premium or the reverse; create the desired type and move applicable data.
Legacy general-purpose v1 and BlobStorage accounts can be upgraded to general-purpose v2 to gain current capabilities.

sections.title: Account kind sets a capability boundary
paragraphs: An account kind determines which storage services and performance characteristics can be selected; it is more than a price label. General-purpose v2 is the normal starting point for mixed blobs, queues, tables and classic file shares. Premium block blob accounts serve object workloads requiring consistently low latency or high transaction rates. Premium page blob accounts serve specialized page-blob workloads. Check the service and redundancy support table before assuming a premium account can replace every service in a standard account.

sections.title: Use a workload-based comparison
paragraphs: Suppose one team stores large report archives while another reads small objects repeatedly with a strict latency requirement. The archive team should compare access tiers and retrieval needs in a suitable standard account. The latency-sensitive team can evaluate premium block blob storage against its measured workload. Paying for a specialized premium service does not automatically add geographic redundancy or archival tiering. Choose capacity, operations and failure protection together, checking regional support for the actual account type.

sections.title: Plan a change of account type
paragraphs: Standard-to-premium conversion is not an in-place account switch: create an appropriate destination and move applicable data. Before a move, check the destination's supported services and application endpoints, then verify that clients can access the copied data. Legacy general-purpose v1 and BlobStorage upgrades to general-purpose v2 are a different supported operation. Also keep Azure Files current: FileStorage is no longer synonymous only with SSD premium shares; StandardV2 SKUs support HDD provisioned v2 shares.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: create classic file share

lessons.title: Determine replication strategies
points: LRS keeps replicas within one datacenter and has the lowest cost, but a datacenter-wide disaster can affect every replica.
ZRS synchronously copies data across three availability zones in one region, maintaining access through a zone failure where supported.
GRS keeps local replicas in the primary region and asynchronously copies them to a secondary region. The secondary is not normally a read endpoint before failover.
RA-GRS adds read access to the secondary region without waiting for failover.
GZRS combines zone replication in the primary region with geographic replication to a secondary region; RA-GZRS adds secondary read access.
Compare the failure scope you must survive, required secondary access, region availability and supported account type before choosing redundancy.
Asynchronous cross-region replication means the secondary copy may lag the primary.

sections.title: Define the failure boundary first
paragraphs: Redundancy answers where additional copies live and which infrastructure failure they can withstand. LRS stays within one primary-region datacenter; ZRS synchronously spans primary-region availability zones. GRS starts with local primary copies and asynchronously transfers data to a secondary region. GZRS instead uses zone redundancy in the primary region before that geographic transfer. Region support and the chosen account or service limit which combinations you can actually configure.

sections.title: Read access is different from failover
paragraphs: The RA prefix adds a readable secondary endpoint for services that support it; it does not make the secondary a normal writable primary. Without read-access redundancy, the secondary is generally unavailable for ordinary reads before failover. Geographic replication is asynchronous, so a secondary reader can observe older data than a recent primary write. A recovery design therefore needs to consider lag and failover behavior rather than assuming regional copies are immediately identical.

sections.title: Work through a requirements example
paragraphs: Imagine a catalog that must remain accessible during one zone failure and also keep a geographic copy. GZRS addresses those two placement requirements where supported. If clients also need to read the secondary before failover, evaluate RA-GZRS and the service's secondary-read support. By contrast, a rebuildable temporary dataset might justify LRS. Neither decision solves accidental overwriting of valid data: retain an appropriate versioning, soft-delete or backup design alongside infrastructure redundancy.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: soft delete blob overview

lessons.title: Access storage
points: A storage account has separate service endpoints such as account-name.blob.core.windows.net and account-name.file.core.windows.net.
A blob URL adds the container and blob path to the Blob service endpoint.
Map a custom subdomain to a blob or static-website endpoint with a DNS CNAME. Direct mapping supports HTTP; use Azure Front Door or a supported CDN configuration for HTTPS on the custom domain.

sections.title: Build a resource URL from its parts
paragraphs: The service endpoint identifies both the account and the service. For a hypothetical account named reportstoreexample, a blob named june.pdf in a reports container has a resource path under reportstoreexample.blob.core.windows.net/reports/june.pdf. Queue and File service endpoints use different service names. Knowing the structure helps identify whether an application is calling the correct service before you investigate authorization; the address locates data but does not grant permission to read it.

sections.title: Understand what a custom domain changes
paragraphs: A custom subdomain can present a friendly name while DNS maps it to the blob or static-website endpoint. Direct CNAME mapping is an HTTP-only arrangement; creating the DNS record does not install a certificate for HTTPS on that name. Use the documented supported delivery configuration when HTTPS is required. This matters when secure transfer is enforced, because an HTTP-only custom-domain path does not meet the account's secure-transfer requirement.

sections.title: Plan and verify the mapping
paragraphs: Start by copying the actual endpoint hostname, then identify the subdomain you control and its intended CNAME target. Follow the custom-domain registration procedure and test access using that hostname. Microsoft documents both direct mapping and an intermediate verification approach to reduce interruption for an existing name. For an internal report site, also test an unauthorized client: a correct custom domain should not accidentally lead you to enable anonymous access for private documents.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: storage custom domain name

lessons.title: Secure storage endpoints
points: Storage firewall and virtual-network rules can restrict network access to permitted subnets or public IP ranges.
A service endpoint retains the service public endpoint while identifying permitted virtual-network traffic.

A private endpoint gives one storage service a private IP in your virtual network. Configure DNS to resolve that endpoint and separately restrict public access if private-only connectivity is required.
Test permitted and denied network paths after configuration to confirm access matches the intended restrictions.

sections.title: Network permission and data permission are separate
paragraphs: A storage firewall decides whether a request may reach the permitted public endpoint path. Authentication and authorization still decide whether that caller can perform the data operation. For example, admitting an office's public IP range does not grant everyone there permission to download private blobs. Likewise, assigning a data role does not bypass a blocked network path. Diagnose these two layers independently instead of treating either configuration as complete security.

sections.title: Compare the two virtual-network paths
paragraphs: A service endpoint leaves the storage service addressed through its public endpoint while the account rules identify allowed virtual-network subnets. A private endpoint creates a private-IP connection for a particular storage service, such as blob or file. Adding that endpoint alone does not disable the account's public endpoint. If the intended design is private-only, separately restrict public access and ensure clients resolve the service hostname to the correct private address.

sections.title: Trace a practical access test
paragraphs: For an original private-document scenario, choose the Blob subresource rather than assuming one endpoint covers every service in the account. Check name resolution from an allowed VM, then test a read with its authorized identity. Test a disallowed network separately and inspect the public-access configuration if it still succeeds. A Files workload requiring private connectivity needs its own private endpoint for the File subresource and a supported protocol path. Record DNS, network rules and data permissions together so a failed test can be traced to its actual layer.

lessons.title: Summary and resources
points: Select the data service and account type first, then choose redundancy and secure network access for the workload.
Storage availability, performance, security and cost depend on the configuration rather than one universal account choice.

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Blob Storage stores unstructured objects; access tiers and lifecycle rules help balance retrieval needs against storage cost.

lessons.title: Implement Azure Blob Storage
points: Blob Storage organizes text or binary objects inside containers within a storage account.
Use it for browser content, media streaming, distributed downloads, backup, archive and data analysis.
Plan container access, blob types, upload tools, access tiers, lifecycle rules and object replication as part of configuration.

sections.title: Think in objects and containers
paragraphs: Blob Storage gives applications an object interface: a named blob is retrieved through an API or URL, rather than through a required mounted file system. The account supplies the service boundary, containers organize collections and blobs hold the content. This arrangement suits independent documents, images and downloads. A blob name can include path-like segments for organization, but the application must still use the supported object or enabled protocol interface for the account.

sections.title: Translate a workload into settings
paragraphs: Suppose a training company publishes lesson videos and separately stores private attendance exports. It can organize these in different containers and make their access decisions independently, while remembering that account-level anonymous access and network settings also constrain the design. Frequently streamed videos and seldom downloaded exports might need different tiering decisions. The storage configuration should reflect how each dataset is used instead of treating every object as equally public, equally active or equally recoverable.

sections.title: Plan beyond the first upload
paragraphs: Before loading real data, record the chosen blob type, upload tool, permissions, redundancy and recovery protections. Decide whether a lifecycle rule is appropriate for older content and whether object replication is needed for additional regional consumers. These features have their own compatibility rules: for example, object replication requires supporting accounts without hierarchical namespace and does not replicate snapshots. Designing the requirements together prevents discovering after deployment that a chosen protocol or account feature conflicts with the distribution plan.

lessons.title: Create blob containers
points: Every blob belongs to a container, so create a container before uploading its blobs.
Container names must be unique within the account, 3 to 63 characters long and use lowercase letters, numbers or hyphens. Start and end with a letter or number; consecutive hyphens are not allowed.
Private access blocks anonymous reads. Blob access allows anonymous blob reads; Container access additionally allows anonymous listing.
Anonymous container settings only work when account-level anonymous blob access is enabled. Keep it disabled unless you need public content.

sections.title: Choose the container boundary
paragraphs: A container is both an organizational boundary and a place to configure access behavior. Name it for a stable collection, such as approved-brochures, rather than using a person's private details in a publicly visible path. Names must be unique within the account and follow the documented lowercase naming rules, including the prohibition on consecutive hyphens. Create the container before uploading data; a standalone blob without a container is not the storage model.

sections.title: Distinguish reading an object from listing a collection
paragraphs: The anonymous Blob setting permits readers who know an object's address to read it without allowing anonymous container listing. Container-level anonymous access additionally allows listing. Neither setting makes anonymous writes permissible. Both also depend on the account allowing anonymous blob access. A private container remains accessible to appropriately authorized callers; private means anonymous reads are blocked, not that only the account creator can ever use its data.

sections.title: Use a public-content example carefully
paragraphs: A public brochure collection may intentionally permit anonymous reads while an invoice collection should remain private. First determine whether public hosting is necessary, then enable only the required account/container settings in that dedicated scenario. Test a known brochure URL anonymously and, if listing must remain unavailable, test listing separately. Test the private invoice path without credentials as well. This checks the difference between object read permission, collection enumeration and authorized access rather than relying only on a portal label.

lessons.title: Assign blob access tiers
points: Hot storage suits frequent access: storage costs are higher and access costs lower than cooler tiers.
Cool suits infrequent access and Cold less frequent access; both remain online. In general-purpose v2 accounts, their minimum billable storage durations are 30 and 90 days respectively.
Archive is offline for block blobs that can tolerate hours of retrieval latency, with a 180-day minimum billable duration. It supports LRS, GRS and RA-GRS, not zone-redundant account configurations.
Deleting, overwriting or moving data before the tier minimum can incur prorated early-deletion charges; the duration is a billing rule, not a deletion prohibition.
Rehydrate archived blobs to an online tier by copying to a new blob or changing the tier in place. Standard and high-priority retrieval have different latency and costs.
Choose a tier using total storage, access and retrieval requirements rather than storage price alone.

sections.title: Compare total access cost and readiness
paragraphs: Hot, Cool and Cold keep data online, but exchange lower capacity cost for higher access and retrieval costs as data becomes less active. Archive is different: its content must be rehydrated before an ordinary read. A rarely accessed operational document that must open immediately therefore has a different requirement from a compliance copy that can wait hours. Account type, blob type and redundancy also constrain which tier choices are available.

sections.title: Treat minimum duration as a billing condition
paragraphs: For general-purpose v2 blob storage, Cool, Cold and Archive have minimum billable durations of 30, 90 and 180 days respectively. They do not prohibit an earlier deletion or tier change; eligible early operations can create prorated charges. An original example is a dataset expected to be deleted after ten days: moving it into a cooler tier simply because its daily capacity rate is lower can leave you paying an early-deletion charge as well.

sections.title: Plan retrieval before archiving
paragraphs: For an archived base blob, Set Blob Tier changes the tier in place, while copying to a new online blob preserves the archived original. Archived snapshots and previous versions require the copy approach. Retrieval priority changes latency and price, but a design should not promise an exact completion time. Archive supports LRS, GRS and RA-GRS rather than zone-redundant configurations. Confirm that these constraints fit the recovery requirement before applying a broad archive policy.

lessons.title: Add blob lifecycle management rules
points: Lifecycle management policies transition eligible blobs to cooler tiers or delete them when conditions are met.
Rules can apply to current versions, previous versions or snapshots, depending on the selected action.
Filter the affected data by container, name prefix or blob index tags rather than always acting on the entire account.
Configure an age or access-related condition and the resulting tier change or deletion action in an if-then rule.
Account and blob types determine which lifecycle features are supported; general-purpose v2 is recommended for new general-purpose deployments.
Consider minimum storage durations and retrieval needs before automatically moving data to colder storage.

sections.title: Turn a data policy into an if-then rule
paragraphs: A lifecycle policy applies actions to eligible data when its conditions are satisfied. Translate a business statement into a filter, a time condition and an action. For an original example, exported reports under reports/monthly/ may become less active after a defined age, while reports/live/ must remain readily available. A prefix filter can separate those collections so the policy does not unexpectedly tier all account content. Confirm which blob types and account features support the proposed actions.

sections.title: Account for versions and billing
paragraphs: Current blobs, previous versions and snapshots can have different retention needs, so review the relevant rule actions rather than assuming deleting a current object removes every retained copy. If the rule moves objects to Cool, Cold or Archive, compare their expected remaining lifetime with minimum billable durations. A rule that continually moves short-lived objects into a cooler tier may produce unnecessary charges. Review the whole policy because lifecycle policies are read and written in full, not through partial policy updates.

sections.title: Know what lifecycle will not do
paragraphs: Lifecycle management cannot rehydrate an archived blob to an online tier. Plan a separate retrieval operation when archived data is needed again, using a supported base-blob tier change or copy. Some features further restrict actions: an encryption scope prevents lifecycle archival, and immutable-container protection can prevent deletion. A useful review exercise is to trace one representative object through every applicable rule and confirm its planned tier, retrieval path and retention behavior before applying policy to production data.

lessons.title: Determine blob object replication
points: Object replication asynchronously copies selected block blobs between source and destination containers. It supports general-purpose v2 or premium block blob accounts without hierarchical namespace.
The replicated data includes blob content, metadata and versions; blob snapshots are not replicated.
Enable blob versioning on both accounts and change feed on the source account before configuring replication.
Policies identify source and destination accounts and contain rules selecting containers and blobs.
Source and destination blobs can use different online tiers. Moving either blob to Archive causes replication to fail; use replication for nearby reads or regional compute workloads.

sections.title: Object replication is selected asynchronous distribution
paragraphs: Object replication follows configured rules between source and destination containers instead of changing the account's own redundancy setting. It can distribute selected block blobs to a region where readers or compute need them. Because copying is asynchronous, a freshly updated source object may not yet be available in the destination. Replication includes content, metadata and versions, but not blob snapshots. Choose it for the selected-data distribution problem rather than assuming it provides a synchronous backup of every storage object.

sections.title: Prepare both accounts before the policy
paragraphs: Use supported general-purpose v2 or premium block blob accounts without hierarchical namespace. Enable change feed on the source and blob versioning on both accounts. Then define the source and destination containers and the rule filters selecting the desired blobs. These prerequisites are functional dependencies, not optional performance settings. They can also add storage or operation costs, so the estimate should include the supporting features rather than only the bytes copied into the destination.

sections.title: Walk through a regional processing example
paragraphs: Suppose a source container holds raw uploads and a results/ prefix holds completed analysis. A replication rule can distribute the selected results to another regional consumer without copying every raw input. Keep replicated source and destination blobs in supported online tiers while replication is required. Moving either side to Archive causes replication to fail; rehydration alone does not retrigger replication until the blob is updated again. Do not design continuous replication and automatic archival as if they were independent operations.

lessons.title: Manage blobs
points: Block blobs are the usual choice for files, images and other text or binary objects.
Append blobs optimize adding blocks and fit logging workloads; page blobs suit frequent indexed or random read-write operations.
A blob type cannot be changed after creation.
Use the portal for a few uploads, selecting blob type, access tier and encryption options as needed.
Use Storage Explorer for graphical management, AzCopy for command-line transfers, or Data Box Disk when a large offline transfer is more practical than uploading over the network.

sections.title: Select the blob type before creating it
paragraphs: Block blobs suit ordinary documents, images and binary objects. Append blobs are optimized for adding data to the end, which fits append-oriented logging. Page blobs support indexed or random reads and writes for suitable workloads. The type is fixed after creation, so choose it from the application's update pattern rather than deciding only from the file extension. A logging file uploaded as a block blob does not become an append blob merely because more log records arrive.

sections.title: Choose a transfer method for the workload
paragraphs: The portal is convenient for a few disposable files; Storage Explorer offers a graphical view across storage resources, while AzCopy suits scripted transfers. Data Box Disk is an alternative when a large offline transfer is more practical than the available network path. Tool choice does not replace permission and connectivity checks. Before a large migration, identify the target account, container, expected object names and access method so an incorrect destination is detected with a small sample first.

sections.title: Review a small upload end to end
paragraphs: For an original image-library exercise, create a private test container, upload one non-sensitive block blob and inspect its name, size and selected access tier. Retrieve it using the intended authorized client and verify the result before transferring the rest. Include encryption-scope choices if the workload requires them, and check compatibility with planned lifecycle actions. For a new VM workload, consider managed disks rather than treating this object-upload lesson as a recommendation to manually maintain page-blob operating-system disks.

lessons.title: Determine Blob Storage pricing
points: Estimate costs with the Azure pricing calculator using data volume, operations, redundancy and transfer needs.
Cooler tiers reduce capacity cost but increase access and retrieval charges.
Transactions, outbound bandwidth and geo-replication transfers can contribute to the bill.
Tier changes can incur operation or data-access charges, so include migration and expected access patterns in the estimate.

sections.title: Estimate operations as well as stored capacity
paragraphs: A useful estimate starts with more than total gigabytes. Record how much data remains stored, how often clients read and write it, the chosen tier and redundancy, and where data travels. Two equally sized containers can have different bills if one is read repeatedly and the other is retained without access. Include expected versions or other retained copies where those protections are enabled, because keeping recovery history can increase the amount of stored data.

sections.title: Compare a realistic lifecycle
paragraphs: Imagine reports that are read heavily for a week and then retained for a year. Compare an all-Hot design with a supported move to a cooler tier after active use. Include the tier-change operation, later retrievals and any expected early deletion, not just the cooler per-gigabyte capacity price. A report that must be restored quickly may justify an online tier even when Archive has a lower capacity rate. The lowest storage rate alone does not establish the lowest workload cost.

sections.title: Check location and supporting features
paragraphs: Geo-replication transfers and applicable outbound bandwidth can contribute to the total, alongside transaction and data-access charges. Object replication also introduces its own required supporting features and distribution costs. Use the pricing calculator with the actual region, tier and workload assumptions, and compare the assumptions with subsequent usage. These notes deliberately contain no fixed currency amounts: current service pricing and allowances must be checked for the deployment rather than inferred from a classroom example.

lessons.title: Exercise - Provide storage for the public website
points: Create a highly available storage account and a container for website documents.
For this public-content scenario, explicitly configure anonymous access and enable soft delete and blob versioning for recovery.
Use the official exercise for deployment instructions; it requires an Azure subscription.

sections.title: Define the lab's public-content boundary
paragraphs: This exercise concerns intentionally public website documents, not confidential business records. Its availability, access and recovery requirements are separate: redundancy addresses infrastructure failure, anonymous read settings address public delivery, and soft delete plus versioning address selected data-recovery scenarios. Before starting, identify which sample images or documents may be publicly visible and keep sensitive test data out of the container. Use your own authorized subscription and the full linked lab for the actual provisioning instructions.

sections.title: Verify behavior rather than only deployment
paragraphs: After creating the lab account and container, inspect both the account's anonymous-access setting and the container's chosen anonymous level. Test a known public document without authentication, and distinguish that read from permission to list the container. Then use a disposable document to inspect the effect of versioning after an overwrite and the available recovery behavior after deletion. The purpose is to demonstrate the requirements independently, rather than assuming a successfully created account proves all protections work.

sections.title: Interpret the results and finish safely
paragraphs: Public delivery does not give anonymous users write permission, and versions or soft-deleted data can add retained storage. Record which redundancy option you selected and what failure scope it covers; do not claim it guarantees worldwide low latency on its own. After the exercise, remove only the dedicated lab resources you created and no longer need. Inspect retained sample data and recovery copies before cleanup, and preserve any shared storage account or real data that was outside the exercise.

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Combine identity, restricted access, transport protection and encryption to secure stored data.

lessons.title: Review Azure Storage security strategies
points: Storage service encryption encrypts data at rest with AES-256; encryption and decryption are transparent to applications.
Require secure transfer and avoid deprecated TLS versions for connections to the account.
Prefer Microsoft Entra authorization with managed identities and scoped data-access roles when supported.
Shared Key authorization uses an account key; disabling Shared Key helps enforce identity-based authorization where the workload supports it.
A shared access signature delegates limited permissions for a limited time without handing the client the account key.
Keep anonymous access disabled for sensitive data and use logs to investigate access and usage.

sections.title: Apply independent layers of protection
paragraphs: Encryption, network restrictions and authorization address different threats. Encryption at rest protects persisted data, while secure transport protects supported requests on the network. Neither decides that a particular application may read a private container. Authorization assigns that right through an appropriate identity and data role or another supported credential. A secure design therefore checks both how a request reaches storage and what the authenticated caller is allowed to do once it arrives.

sections.title: Prefer identity where the workload supports it
paragraphs: Managed identities allow supported applications to use Microsoft Entra authorization without distributing a storage account key. Assign the relevant data-access role at an appropriate scope; a management role that shows an account is not automatically permission to read its objects. Shared Key remains a different authorization path with broad account credentials. Disabling it can help enforce supported identity-based access, but first verify clients and services are compatible with that change.

sections.title: Work through a private-upload design
paragraphs: For an original document-submission application, keep anonymous access disabled, require the supported secure-transfer configuration and authorize the application identity for only the required data operations. If browsers need temporary direct upload access, issue a narrowly scoped SAS rather than giving them the account key. Validate submitted content before trusting it. Add network controls where required and use logs to investigate failures. No single checkbox, including encryption at rest, substitutes for this combination of access and validation decisions.
