lessons.title: Create shared access signatures
points: A SAS delegates access to selected storage resources with defined permissions and validity times.

A user delegation SAS is signed with a key obtained using Microsoft Entra credentials. Current support includes Blob Storage, Data Lake Storage, queues, tables and Azure Files; service and account SAS are signed with an account key.
Stored access policies add server-side control for supported service SAS, including changing or revoking access without replacing an account key.
Distribute SAS URLs only over HTTPS, grant the minimum permissions and use short validity periods.
Account for clock skew: omit an immediate start time or allow an appropriate margin, and renew before expiry.
Validate data uploaded using a SAS before the application trusts or processes it.
For high-risk operations, a validating application service may provide more control than giving a client direct storage access.

sections.title: A SAS is a limited credential, not a public URL
paragraphs: A SAS adds signed access instructions to a resource URL. Anyone who obtains a usable token can exercise its permitted operations until it expires or is otherwise revoked. For an original export example, a consumer needing one download should receive read access to the relevant resource for a short period, not account-wide write or delete permission. Distribute the complete URL through HTTPS and treat it as a secret in logs, messages and application diagnostics.

sections.title: Choose the signing model and revocation plan
paragraphs: Current user delegation SAS support includes Blob Storage and Data Lake Storage, Queue Storage, Table Storage and Azure Files. It uses a delegation key obtained through Microsoft Entra credentials; service and account SAS use an account key. A stored access policy provides server-side control only for a supported service SAS, not user delegation or account SAS. Policy-linked service SAS can be revoked by changing or deleting its associated policy; deleting a client's copy of a token does not invalidate other copies.

sections.title: Design expiry and validation deliberately
paragraphs: An immediate start time can fail because client clocks differ, so follow the documented skew guidance and renew before expiry. A newly changed stored access policy can take up to 30 seconds to become active. When SAS permits uploads, authorization only proves that the request is allowed; it does not prove the uploaded document is safe or satisfies business rules. For high-risk operations, consider an application service that performs authentication, validation and auditing before writing to storage.

lessons.title: Identify URI and SAS parameters
points: A SAS URL consists of the storage resource URL followed by a signed query token.
The sv parameter identifies the storage service version; st and se specify start and expiry times in UTC.
The sp parameter lists permissions, and applicable resource or service parameters identify the permitted scope.
The sip parameter can restrict caller IP addresses; spr can restrict requests to HTTPS.
The sig parameter carries the signature that authenticates the token. Treat the complete SAS URL as a credential and avoid exposing it.

sections.title: Read the token as a set of constraints
paragraphs: Separate the resource address from the signed query token when examining a SAS URL. The address locates the account, service and resource. Parameters then describe access conditions: sv identifies the service version, sp the permissions, and st/se the validity interval where applicable. spr can restrict the permitted protocol to HTTPS, while sip can limit accepted source IPs. UTC times and URL encoding matter when troubleshooting a token that appears valid but is rejected.

sections.title: Use a coherent SAS type
paragraphs: Not every SAS type uses the same resource-scope fields. For a Blob service SAS, sr identifies the signed resource; account SAS instead includes account-level service and resource-type scope fields. Do not combine fragments from different token types and assume the result is meaningful. The signature is computed over the required signed fields, so editing the permission or expiry text in an existing URL is not a legitimate way to change access; generate an appropriately signed token or use its supported policy mechanism.

sections.title: Inspect an original read-only request
paragraphs: Suppose a consumer should read one report through HTTPS before its UTC expiry. Check the blob path, the relevant resource scope, read permission, expiry and protocol restriction as one coherent request. If there is an IP restriction, verify the source address seen by the service rather than assuming a client's local private address matches it. Keep the sig value and full token out of shared screenshots. A readable-looking parameter list is diagnostic information, not proof that the signature or authorization is valid.

lessons.title: Determine Azure Storage encryption
points: Azure Storage automatically encrypts data before persistence and decrypts it for authorized reads; encryption at rest cannot be disabled.
Microsoft-managed keys are managed by Azure; customer-managed keys give you control over the encryption key lifecycle.
Infrastructure encryption provides a second encryption layer with a separate key and algorithm when enabled.
Account access keys authorize Shared Key requests and signed SAS tokens; they are distinct from the keys used for storage encryption.
Store access keys securely and plan rotation so applications update their credentials without losing access.

sections.title: Encryption is automatic; authorization is separate
paragraphs: Storage encrypts persisted data and decrypts it for an authorized read. You do not gain read permission merely because data is encrypted, nor do clients normally need the at-rest encryption key to perform a permitted object read. Microsoft-managed encryption keys are the default model; supported customer-managed configurations allow organizational control of the key lifecycle. Infrastructure encryption adds a second layer using a different key and algorithm when configured, rather than replacing the service-level encryption.

sections.title: Keep access keys and encryption keys distinct
paragraphs: The two storage account access keys authorize Shared Key requests and account-key-signed SAS. They are not the customer-managed encryption key held in Key Vault or Managed HSM. Rotating an account access key therefore concerns callers using that credential, while encryption-key changes concern the storage encryption configuration. Treating these as the same operation can leave an application using an invalid credential or cause an administrator to change the wrong security control.

sections.title: Plan a credential rotation example
paragraphs: For a test application using one account access key, first identify every dependency using it and which alternate key is available. Move clients to the alternate valid credential before regenerating the old key, then verify their requests and update any dependent secrets. Repeat with care for other clients rather than regenerating both keys together. Account-key-signed SAS linked to a regenerated key can be invalidated too. Where supported, replacing key distribution with identity-based authorization reduces this credential-management burden.

lessons.title: Create customer-managed keys
points: Customer-managed encryption keys can be stored in a customer-owned Key Vault or Managed HSM.
You can generate a new key or use an existing key, and control its access, auditing, rotation and disabling.
Select the customer-managed vault and key or enter its URI. Enable vault soft delete and purge protection, and grant the storage managed identity the required key permissions.
Choose customer-managed keys when compliance or organizational policy requires control of the encryption key lifecycle.

sections.title: Define why the organization needs key control
paragraphs: Customer-managed keys are appropriate when policy requires ownership of key access, auditing, rotation or disabling. They change who manages the encryption key, not the fact that Storage already encrypts data at rest. The key can reside in customer-owned Key Vault or Managed HSM. Current product documentation allows the storage account and key service to be in different regions, subscriptions or tenants with the supported configuration, so an old training statement requiring the same region is not a universal rule.

sections.title: Prepare identity and key protection
paragraphs: Storage accesses the key through its configured managed identity, which needs the required get, wrapKey and unwrapKey permissions. The key service must meet the documented soft-delete and purge-protection prerequisites; use a supported key type and size. Distinguish permission to administer the storage account from permission to configure the vault and key. A technically valid key URI alone is not sufficient if the managed identity cannot access the key or the key service is unreachable.

sections.title: Work through a controlled setup
paragraphs: For an original compliance exercise, record whether you are using an existing approved key or generating a new one, identify the storage managed identity and review its required key access. Select the key through the supported storage encryption configuration or enter its URI, then verify the account's resulting settings. Plan rotation and loss-of-key-access handling before adopting the configuration: disabling or revoking access to the key can prevent storage data operations. Include the key-service cost and lifecycle responsibilities in the design.

lessons.title: Apply Azure Storage security best practices
points: Storage Insights provides a consolidated view of storage performance, capacity and availability using metrics and logs.
Track latency, throughput, transaction counts and usage trends, and use alerts to investigate anomalies.
Microsoft Defender for Storage provides threat detection, including supported malware scanning and suspicious-activity detection capabilities.
Use operational monitoring and threat protection together; viewing metrics alone does not replace access controls or active threat detection.

sections.title: Use monitoring to explain normal behavior
paragraphs: Storage Insights brings performance, capacity and availability views together so an administrator can compare accounts and investigate trends. Metrics such as latency, transactions and used capacity help identify operational changes. For an original example, an unexpected increase in transaction count might correspond to a new client release or a repeated retry pattern; the chart alone does not determine intent. Correlate appropriate metrics and diagnostic information before deciding whether the problem is performance, configuration or suspicious access.

sections.title: Add threat protection for a different purpose
paragraphs: Microsoft Defender for Storage supplies security detections and supported additional capabilities, including malware scanning and sensitive-data threat detection. These are different from merely viewing storage metrics. Check the selected Defender plan, supported resource types, settings and cost before assuming every account has every protection enabled. A malware-scanning result is also not a substitute for defining application upload rules and restricting who can read, write or delete data.

sections.title: Create an investigation workflow
paragraphs: Begin with the affected account and timeframe, inspect workload and capacity trends, then compare the relevant logs or security alerts. Identify the caller and operation where that evidence is available, and inspect the authorization and network configuration. For a new upload service, combine least-privilege permissions with validation and the required enabled threat-protection features. Monitoring should help verify and investigate the design; it does not itself create RBAC assignments, repair a broad SAS or make sensitive containers private.

lessons.title: Exercise: Manage Azure Storage
points: Create a storage account, secure blob containers and configure file shares using the official lab instructions.
Check how the chosen authorization and network settings protect both blob and file access.
The hands-on lab requires an Azure subscription; reading the steps does not deploy anything.

sections.title: Turn the storage lab into a security comparison
paragraphs: The lab includes both blobs and Azure Files, which makes it useful for examining service-specific access rather than applying one assumption to the entire account. Prepare an authorized subscription and non-sensitive sample data, then read the linked exercise before creating resources. Record whether you are testing object API access, a file-share mount or REST file access. Each can require a different client configuration even when the data resides under the same account.

sections.title: Verify credentials and network paths separately
paragraphs: Create the lab account and selected containers or shares using the full instructions, then inspect the intended authorization method. Keep private blob data private and test access with the designated identity or scoped credential. For an SMB share, check supported identity authentication, share-level access and file/directory permissions; a file SAS is for REST access and is not an SMB mount credential. If a request fails, inspect the network path as well instead of immediately broadening data permissions.

sections.title: Document what each test proves
paragraphs: Record a permitted test and a denied test for the chosen interface. A successful portal view proves neither that an external client can connect nor that another identity is denied. Keep account keys and SAS tokens out of observations and screenshots, and note any intentionally broad lab permission so it is not carried into production. Finish by removing only dedicated resources created for the exercise and no longer required, after checking retained sample data and any configured recovery protection.

points: Azure Files provides managed file shares, while Azure File Sync adds local Windows Server caching for hybrid access.

lessons.title: Compare storage for file shares and blob data
points: Choose Azure Files when applications expect shared directories and file-system access over SMB or NFS.
Use file shares for lift-and-shift applications, common tools, configuration files and shared diagnostic data.
Choose Blob Storage for object-oriented access to large amounts of unstructured data using REST APIs and client libraries.
Azure File Sync can centralize files in Azure while preserving local file-server access and caching.

sections.title: Choose the existing application's interface
paragraphs: A program opening a shared path has different expectations from a program fetching objects by URL. Azure Files preserves a shared-directory interface through the selected supported protocol, which can reduce changes for a file-share application. Blob Storage is designed for object access at scale and is a natural match for independent media or document objects. Do not infer that every Blob account has only a flat namespace: enabling hierarchical namespace changes supported namespace and protocol behavior.

sections.title: Work through two original migrations
paragraphs: A legacy reporting app that reads a shared configuration directory may fit an SMB Azure file share, provided its client identity and networking are supported. A redesigned service that downloads generated PDFs through object APIs may fit Blob Storage instead. Neither choice makes files freely accessible to every machine with internet connectivity. Confirm the access protocol, credentials, account restrictions and required network ports before expecting an existing client to work with a new storage address.

sections.title: Consider a local cache deliberately
paragraphs: Azure File Sync can retain Windows file-server access while centralizing a supported SMB Azure file share in Azure. Servers act as local caches, with cloud tiering available to reduce the locally retained content. That design differs from directly mounting Azure Files on every client and from accessing Blob objects through a REST SDK. Check server and workload compatibility, especially the SMB cloud-endpoint requirement, before assuming any protocol used locally is also supported as the Azure cloud endpoint.

lessons.title: Manage Azure file shares
points: Choose either SMB or NFS for a file share; a single share does not serve both protocols.
For classic shares, general-purpose v2 accounts provide HDD pay-as-you-go storage. FileStorage accounts support SSD provisioned shares and, with StandardV2 SKUs, HDD provisioned v2 shares.
HDD pay-as-you-go access tiers are Transaction optimized, Hot and Cool, with different capacity and transaction pricing. Provisioned shares use a separate billing model.
SMB identity authentication supports AD DS, Microsoft Entra Domain Services or Microsoft Entra Kerberos. Configure both share-level access and Windows file/directory permissions.
Account keys provide broad access and should not be shared casually. A file SAS is for REST API access rather than mounting an SMB share.
SMB uses port 445; blocked outbound port 445 is a common cause of failed mounts from on-premises networks.

sections.title: Select protocol, media and billing separately
paragraphs: A share uses SMB or NFS, not both simultaneously. For classic shares inside storage accounts, distinguish HDD pay-as-you-go shares in general-purpose v2 accounts from provisioned models. FileStorage supports SSD shares and, with StandardV2 SKUs, HDD provisioned v2. Provisioned v2 separates provisioned storage, IOPS and throughput, and you pay for what you provision rather than only current usage. Current guidance recommends provisioned v2 for new deployments; do not interpret premium as the only available provisioned model.

sections.title: Configure both identity and file permissions
paragraphs: For supported SMB identity access, choose the appropriate AD DS, Microsoft Entra Domain Services or Microsoft Entra Kerberos configuration. Then establish share-level access and Windows file/directory permissions. A successful identity sign-in does not mean both layers permit every operation. Account keys provide broad access and need careful protection. A file SAS serves REST API access rather than an SMB mounting password, even though current user delegation SAS support includes Azure Files.

sections.title: Troubleshoot a mount in the right order
paragraphs: For an original branch-office share, check whether the client can reach the endpoint over outbound TCP 445 before repeatedly changing permissions. Then check its supported identity setup, share-level role and the directory permissions for the requested path. Compare billing against expected usage: pay-as-you-go Transaction optimized, Hot and Cool optimize different usage patterns, while provisioned shares reserve capacity and performance differently. Protocol support, region availability and redundancy must still match the selected share offering.

lessons.title: Create file share snapshots
points: A share snapshot is an incremental, read-only point-in-time copy of an Azure file share.
Take snapshots before risky changes or on a schedule to recover from accidental edits, deletion or application corruption.
Restore individual files, folders or a share from the appropriate snapshot.
A share can have up to 200 snapshots; they use the share redundancy settings and remain until deleted.

Deleting a share removes its snapshots too, so snapshots alone do not protect the entire share. With share soft delete enabled, undeleting the share restores its contents and snapshots during retention.

sections.title: Understand the scope of a snapshot
paragraphs: A share snapshot preserves a read-only point-in-time view of the share. Although snapshots are incremental, recovery can select a snapshot without manually assembling a chain of earlier snapshots. Individual files can be retrieved when only one item was overwritten. The snapshot remains associated with the source share and follows its redundancy setting, so it is not an independent account or an automatic copy in an unrelated region.

sections.title: Use a change-protection example
paragraphs: Before an approved application upgrade modifies shared configuration files, take a snapshot and record its timestamp. If one configuration file becomes unusable, compare the appropriate earlier version and retrieve that file rather than replacing every current file unnecessarily. A full-share recovery is a different decision with a wider effect. Validate the recovered content before applications use it and ensure permissions and the chosen recovery interface match the share protocol and environment.

sections.title: Plan deletion and retained capacity
paragraphs: A share supports up to 200 snapshots, with retention supported for up to 10 years; delete obsolete snapshots deliberately. Their incremental storage still contributes to retained data, so define a lifecycle for obsolete restore points. Deleting the share also deletes its snapshots; snapshots alone therefore do not protect against removal of the whole share. With supported share soft delete enabled, undeleting the share within retention restores its contents and snapshots. Use snapshots, soft delete and backup according to the distinct loss scenarios being protected.

lessons.title: Implement soft delete for Azure Files
points: Enable soft delete at the storage account level to retain deleted classic file shares temporarily; this feature does not apply to standalone Microsoft.FileShares resources.
Choose a retention period from 1 to 365 days during which a deleted share can be recovered.
Soft delete protects share deletion; use snapshots or backup for point-in-time recovery of changed or deleted files within a share.

sections.title: Protect the share-deletion operation
paragraphs: Azure Files soft delete protects deletion of a supported classic file share as a whole. It does not rewind an overwritten file or undelete an individual item inside a share that still exists. Those item-level incidents require a suitable snapshot or backup recovery point. This distinction matters because the original lesson uses broad recovery language: enabling soft delete alone should not be described as complete protection against corruption, ransomware or every application upgrade failure.

sections.title: Set a retention window that fits operations
paragraphs: The setting is enabled at storage-account level for supported classic shares, with a configurable retention period from 1 to 365 days. While a deleted share remains recoverable, it continues to consume the applicable retained storage. The feature does not apply to standalone Microsoft.FileShares resources. Record who investigates accidental deletion and how quickly they must act so the chosen window provides a practical opportunity to notice and reverse the loss.

sections.title: Work through the two recovery paths
paragraphs: If an administrator deletes a whole test share, use the documented undelete operation within its retention period; its contents and snapshots are restored to their state before deletion. If an application instead overwrites one document while the share remains active, select a suitable snapshot or backup to recover the document. Test these cases with disposable data and describe the results separately. A successful share undelete proves the deletion-protection path, not a universal point-in-time recovery of every file change.

lessons.title: Use Azure Storage Explorer
points: Storage Explorer is a desktop tool for managing storage data across accounts and subscriptions on Windows, macOS and Linux.
Full access requires the appropriate management-plane and data-plane permissions; seeing an account does not automatically grant access to its data.
Connect through an Azure subscription, account credentials or a suitably scoped SAS, including selected services in another subscription.
An account has two access keys so clients can use one while you rotate the other; update dependent applications when credentials change.
Protect keys because they grant broad account access, and prefer appropriately scoped identity permissions where supported.

sections.title: Account visibility is not data access
paragraphs: Storage Explorer is a desktop client for inspecting and managing storage data across accounts and subscriptions. Its connection experience can expose a storage account while your identity still lacks permission to list or read its blobs. Full use may require both management-plane visibility and relevant data-plane permissions. Diagnose a missing container or access-denied operation by checking the required data role instead of assuming a subscription connection automatically grants every data operation.

sections.title: Choose the narrowest suitable connection
paragraphs: Signing in through a supported Azure identity, attaching an account with credentials and attaching a selected service with SAS are different connection models. For an original read-only review, a suitably scoped identity or service SAS can be more appropriate than handing the reviewer a broad account key. A successful connection only allows what its credential and network path permit. Store or distribute tokens and keys as secrets, and choose the actual endpoint for the service and Azure environment.

sections.title: Use two keys as a rotation mechanism
paragraphs: Two account access keys let dependent clients move to one valid key while the other is regenerated. Before rotation, identify every application using the old key and update its credential after a planned switch; otherwise a resource that appeared correctly connected can suddenly lose access. Do not regenerate both keys simultaneously as a shortcut. Shared-key-signed SAS can also be affected by key changes. Prefer scoped identity access where supported to reduce the number of long-lived account credentials that must be distributed.

lessons.title: Consider Azure File Sync
points: Azure File Sync centralizes file shares in Azure Files while Windows Servers act as local caches.
A Storage Sync Service manages sync groups; each sync group contains one cloud endpoint and participating server endpoints.
The cloud endpoint is an SMB Azure file share; a server endpoint identifies a local NTFS path on a registered Windows Server. Azure File Sync does not support NFS Azure file shares.
Install the Azure File Sync agent on each participating server to perform synchronization.
Cloud tiering keeps frequently accessed data local and recalls other files from Azure as needed.
Use the design for branch-office caching, hybrid application access and recovery scenarios while retaining familiar local file protocols.

sections.title: Map the synchronization relationship
paragraphs: A Storage Sync Service manages registered Windows Servers and sync groups. Each sync group has one cloud endpoint representing an SMB Azure file share and server endpoints identifying supported local NTFS paths. The agent on each participating server performs synchronization. An NFS Azure file share cannot serve as this cloud endpoint, even though a Windows Server may expose supported local protocols to its clients. Keep the Azure endpoint protocol separate from how branch users access their local server.

sections.title: Explain cloud tiering to users
paragraphs: Cloud tiering can leave less frequently used file content in Azure while local namespace information lets users see the files. Accessing a tiered file recalls its content when required, so remote connectivity and recall behavior matter to the user experience. An original branch-office design can keep frequently accessed working documents local while centralizing the full dataset in the cloud. Size the server and choose tiering policies for the actual file count and change rate rather than assuming minimal server requirements guarantee good performance.

sections.title: Review prerequisites and recovery expectations
paragraphs: Use supported Windows Server and agent versions, directly attached NTFS storage and an appropriate share and network design before registering endpoints. Not every workload is a good sync candidate: database and log files can get out of step, so File Sync is not a universal database replication solution. Synchronization also does not by itself supply retained point-in-time recovery. Pair the design with suitable Azure Files snapshots or backup and test how a replacement server obtains metadata and recalls the required data.

lessons.title: Knowledge check
points: Complete the interactive check on Microsoft Learn.

lessons.title: Summary and resources
points: Use file shares for native shared-file workloads and File Sync for hybrid caching.
Combine snapshots, share soft delete and appropriate backup with scoped access to protect and recover files.

paths.title: AZ-104: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Azure virtual machines provide on-demand compute with control over the guest operating system and installed software.
Plan the network, capacity, availability and backups before migrating a server.

lessons.title: Compile a checklist for creating an Azure Virtual Machine
points: Plan the virtual network, subnets and required traffic before creating the VM; connected networks must use nonoverlapping address ranges.
Azure reserves the first four and last IP addresses in each subnet. Network security groups filter traffic at subnet or network-interface level.
Inventory the operating system, CPU, memory, disk input/output and data-location requirements. Choose the region and VM size for those needs.
General-purpose sizes balance CPU and memory; compute-, memory- and storage-optimized sizes target different bottlenecks. GPU and high-performance-compute sizes serve specialized workloads.
Resizing a running VM restarts it. If a size is unavailable on its current cluster, stop and deallocate first to select another size available in the region.
Keep durable application data on data disks rather than temporary storage. VM size limits attached disks and network interfaces.
Deallocating stops compute charges, but retained disks still incur storage charges. Choose pay-as-you-go for variable use or reservations for predictable long-term use.

sections.title: Start with dependencies, not the size picker
paragraphs: A VM is one resource in a larger deployment. Its network interface connects to a subnet; disks hold the operating system and application data; security rules govern traffic. Before choosing a size, identify who must connect to the server and which other systems it calls. For example, a payroll server may need private database access and restricted administrator access rather than unrestricted inbound internet traffic. Plan address ranges before connecting networks: overlapping spaces create routing problems that cannot be solved by simply choosing a larger VM.

sections.title: Translate workload needs into a configuration
paragraphs: Inventory CPU, memory, disk throughput, operating-system compatibility and where the data is permitted to reside. These requirements narrow the region, VM family and disk choices. A memory-heavy analytics process and a CPU-heavy batch process can need different families even when they serve the same number of users. Region selection also affects which sizes exist and how much they cost. Put durable application data on persistent data disks; temporary storage is not a substitute for a database or document repository.

sections.title: Allow for change and separate costs
paragraphs: Size limits include the number of attached disks and network interfaces, not just CPU and RAM. Resizing a running VM normally restarts it. If the desired size is outside the current hardware cluster, deallocate before selecting another available regional size. Plan that interruption before changing a production server. Compute and storage are billed separately: deallocation stops compute charges, while retained disks remain chargeable. Reservations can reduce costs for predictable sustained use, whereas pay-as-you-go suits uncertain demand.

lessons.title: Exercise - Create a VM using the Azure portal
points: This optional exercise requires an Azure subscription and a resource group. You can study the instructions without deploying.
In the portal, create a virtual machine and choose its subscription, resource group, region, Ubuntu image and size.
Use SSH public-key authentication, supply an administrator username and generate or provide a key pair. The exercise enables SSH on port 22.
Review and validate the configuration, create the VM and securely download the private key when prompted.
After deployment, open the VM overview and use its public IP address with an SSH client.

sections.title: Prepare an isolated learning deployment
paragraphs: The optional exercise creates a Linux VM through the portal. You need an Azure subscription and a resource group where you can create resources. A dedicated lab resource group makes it easier to identify what belongs to the exercise when cleaning up. Choose the subscription and region deliberately: the account selected in the portal determines where charges and resources appear. You can learn the creation sequence without deploying anything; reading the instructions does not reserve compute or create a subscription.

sections.title: Understand the choices in the form
paragraphs: Select a supported Ubuntu image and a VM size available in the chosen region. For SSH public-key authentication, provide an administrator username and either an existing public key or a newly generated key pair. The exercise permits inbound SSH on port 22. That network rule and the SSH credentials have separate jobs: the rule allows the connection to reach the VM, while the key proves which user can sign in. If you generate a key, keep the downloaded private key secure rather than placing it in a shared repository.

sections.title: Validate, connect and inspect
paragraphs: Review the configuration before creating the VM, correcting any validation errors in the indicated tab. Deployment takes time, so wait for completion before using the VM overview and its public IP to connect with an SSH client. The overview also provides access to the related disks and network settings, helping you see the resources behind the VM. After studying the result, remove only your lab resources when finished so the demonstration does not become an unintended ongoing cost.
steps: Choose the subscription, lab resource group, region, image and size.
Configure SSH public-key authentication and the exercise’s inbound SSH rule.
Review and create; download a generated private key securely.
Wait for deployment, inspect the VM overview and connect using SSH.

lessons.title: Describe the options available to create and manage an Azure Virtual Machine
points: ARM templates declare resources in JSON and can parameterize names and settings for repeatable deployments. Exporting a resource template provides a starting point.
Azure CLI is cross-platform; az vm create creates a VM. Azure PowerShell provides cmdlets such as New-AzVM.
Terraform uses configuration files and a previewable execution plan to manage infrastructure.
REST APIs expose resource operations over HTTP; client SDKs wrap those APIs for application code.
VM extensions configure software after deployment. Automation can coordinate recurring management tasks.
Auto-shutdown schedules when a VM shuts down; configure the time and time zone to avoid unnecessary running time.

sections.title: Choose a tool that matches the operation
paragraphs: The portal is useful for learning and one-off configuration, but repeating a complex deployment by clicking through forms is hard to reproduce. ARM templates express infrastructure as JSON resources and parameters. An exported template is a starting point that you should inspect and adapt, not an assurance that it reproduces every runtime detail. Terraform offers another infrastructure-as-code workflow: define resources, preview its proposed changes and apply the reviewed plan. These approaches make environment-specific names and settings explicit.

sections.title: Separate scripting from application integration
paragraphs: Azure CLI and Azure PowerShell are appropriate for interactive commands and repeatable scripts. The CLI’s az vm create and PowerShell’s New-AzVM both create VMs, using different command conventions. REST APIs expose resource operations over HTTP; client SDKs package those APIs for application languages. A provisioning service with substantial business logic may benefit from an SDK, while a small administrative task may be clearer as a short script. All still require suitable Azure authorization and deployment settings.
This CLI example creates a VM using an existing lab resource group. Sign in first, choose the intended subscription and replace the example names for your lab.

code.text:
az vm create \
  --resource-group compute-lab \
  --name demo-linux-vm \
  --image Ubuntu2204 \
  --admin-username azureuser \
  --generate-ssh-keys

sections.title: Manage the machine after creation
paragraphs: Creation is only the beginning of administration. VM extensions can install or configure software after deployment, and Automation can coordinate repeated management tasks. Auto-shutdown schedules a daily shutdown in a chosen time zone, useful for a development machine that is not needed overnight. Treat it as an operational schedule, not an infrastructure template. For a team deploying test and production environments, one parameterized definition plus an explicit post-deployment configuration process is easier to reason about than two manually assembled servers.

lessons.title: Manage the availability of your Azure VMs
points: A physical-host failure can interrupt a VM while Azure moves it to a healthy host. Platform maintenance can also require a restart.
Deploy redundant application instances across availability zones to reduce exposure to a datacenter failure. Each zone has independent power, cooling and networking.
Scale sets manage groups of VMs and can change instance counts based on demand or a schedule. They can be deployed across zones.
A load balancer distributes requests across healthy instances; redundancy still requires multiple working application instances.
Choose storage replication based on regional failure protection, cost and whether secondary-region read access is needed.
Azure Site Recovery replicates workloads to another location and coordinates failover and failback. Test recovery plans before relying on them.

sections.title: Identify the failure you need to survive
paragraphs: Azure can move a VM away from a failed host, but that recovery can include an outage and reboot. Platform maintenance can also affect running instances. A single VM therefore remains a single running application instance. For a service that must survive a datacenter failure, deploy redundant instances across supported availability zones. Independent zone power, cooling and networking reduce shared failure exposure; the application must still be able to operate when an instance or zone is unavailable.

sections.title: Combine placement, capacity and traffic distribution
paragraphs: A scale set helps manage a group of VMs and can adjust the instance count to demand or a schedule. A load balancer distributes requests among working backends. These features solve different problems: placement spreads risk, scaling supplies capacity, and load balancing sends traffic to available instances. For example, placing three application instances across zones is useful only if requests can reach the surviving instances and the application’s data design can tolerate the failure. Merely putting a load balancer in front of one VM does not create redundancy.

sections.title: Plan recovery beyond the region
paragraphs: Storage replication choices determine whether copies exist only locally, across zones or in a secondary region, and whether the secondary is readable. Azure Site Recovery instead replicates workloads and coordinates failover and failback to another location. A recovery plan can include ordered actions and manual steps, so test it before relying on it. Regional recovery and historical backup are complementary: replication supports continuity, while backup recovery points help return to an earlier state after loss or corruption.

lessons.title: Back up your virtual machines
points: Azure Backup protects Azure VMs and selected on-premises workloads using components appropriate to the workload.
A Recovery Services vault manages backup data, recovery points and policies. Define when backups run and how long to retain them.
Application-consistent backups capture the information needed for application recovery, rather than relying only on a disk copy.
Backup storage is managed by the service; choose redundancy, encryption and retention to meet recovery requirements.

sections.title: Choose protection for the thing you must recover
paragraphs: A backup plan begins with a recovery need: an entire VM, selected files or an application workload. Azure Backup offers different components for different supported sources. Native Azure VM protection and on-premises protection do not use an identical setup. For Windows files, folders and system state, the MARS agent is an option; DPM or Azure Backup Server supports additional on-premises workloads. Check the appropriate workload support before treating one agent or vault setup as universal.

sections.title: Understand policy and consistency
paragraphs: A Recovery Services vault manages Azure VM recovery points and backup policies. The policy specifies when backup runs and how long recovery points remain available. Application consistency matters because an application may have pending writes or coordinated files that a simple disk image does not capture safely. Agent-based VM backups can coordinate application or filesystem consistency; supported agentless backups provide crash-consistent protection. On Linux, application-consistent backups require appropriate pre- and post-backup scripts. These are distinct recovery qualities, not interchangeable labels.

sections.title: Use recovery requirements to make tradeoffs
paragraphs: Consider a reporting VM whose documents must be retained for an audit. Frequent short-term points help operational recovery, while longer retention addresses historical retrieval. Choose storage redundancy and access controls appropriate to that requirement, and test restoring the expected data. Azure manages backup storage, but you still select policies and monitor results. Availability placement does not replace this work: a highly available VM can still lose useful data through an application error, and replicas can carry that error onward.

lessons.title: Summary
points: Select VM deployment tools for repeatability, then combine availability and backup services with the recovery needs of the application.

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Availability planning combines redundant VM placement with scaling rules that match changing demand.

lessons.title: Plan for maintenance and downtime
points: Plan for predicted hardware failure, unexpected host failure and scheduled platform maintenance.
Live migration can move a VM off failing hardware with a short pause; performance can still be affected.
Unexpected hardware failure can trigger a reboot on another host and loss of temporary-drive contents.
Azure maintains the physical platform; you remain responsible for updates to the guest operating system and application software.

sections.title: Different events produce different interruptions
paragraphs: Unplanned maintenance can begin before hardware fails, when Azure detects a component that is likely to become unreliable. Live migration moves a VM from that host while preserving its running state, with a short pause and possible performance impact. An unexpected hardware failure is different: the VM may need to restart on a healthy host, and temporary-drive contents can be lost. Scheduled platform maintenance addresses the underlying infrastructure. Avoid treating all three events as a planned reboot with an identical recovery time.

sections.title: Keep platform and guest responsibilities separate
paragraphs: Azure maintains the physical host and platform; you remain responsible for the VM’s guest operating system and application configuration. Redundant instances help only when the application can continue on an unaffected machine. For an internal ordering service, decide how users reach another instance, where durable data lives and which tasks can be retried after interruption. Keep temporary data disposable and protect important data separately. A maintenance plan should therefore connect VM placement to application recovery, rather than relying solely on Azure’s ability to repair its hosts. Test how the application behaves after an interrupted request instead of assuming a host recovery guarantees an uninterrupted user session.

lessons.title: Create availability sets
points: An availability set spreads related VMs across physical infrastructure to reduce shared hardware and maintenance failures.
Assign a VM to its availability set when creating the VM; changing that assignment requires recreation.
Use multiple VMs for redundancy and separate availability sets for different application tiers. Add load balancing to distribute traffic.
Availability sets do not protect against application or guest-operating-system failures; retain backup and recovery plans.

sections.title: Spread instances that perform the same role
paragraphs: An availability set groups related VMs so Azure distributes their infrastructure and maintenance exposure. Put redundant instances of one application tier together, with compatible software and responsibilities. For example, two web servers belong in the web-tier set, while redundant database servers belong in a separate set. Mixing every application tier into one group makes its purpose harder to reason about. Availability sets reduce shared host, rack and maintenance failures; availability zones provide broader datacenter separation where supported.

sections.title: Design the set before creating the VMs
paragraphs: Assign the availability set when you create each VM. Changing a VM’s availability-set assignment requires deleting and recreating the VM, so the choice belongs in deployment planning. Use at least two instances when you need redundancy, and provide traffic distribution such as a load balancer so users can reach the surviving application. An availability set does not repair a faulty application deployment or guest operating system. Retain backups and application recovery procedures, and use managed disks for the supported disk-placement behavior associated with the set. A set containing only one VM has no second application instance to keep serving requests when that VM becomes unavailable.

lessons.title: Review update domains and fault domains
points: An update domain groups VMs that can be restarted together during planned maintenance. Azure restarts only one update domain at a time.
Availability sets support 1 to 20 update domains, defaulting to five. The count cannot be changed after creation.
A fault domain groups VMs sharing infrastructure such as power or network switches. Distributing instances across fault domains reduces common hardware-failure exposure.
Each VM in an availability set belongs to one update domain and one fault domain.

sections.title: Update domains describe maintenance groups
paragraphs: An update domain groups VMs and associated hardware that can be restarted together during planned platform maintenance. Azure restarts one update domain at a time so every instance in the set is not deliberately restarted together. Availability sets support between one and twenty update domains, with five as the default. Choose the count during creation; it cannot be changed afterward. More domains do not make one VM redundant: the application still needs multiple working instances distributed across the groups.

sections.title: Fault domains describe shared infrastructure
paragraphs: A fault domain identifies VMs that share infrastructure such as a power source or network switch. Spreading redundant instances across fault domains reduces the chance that one hardware fault affects all of them. Each VM in an availability set belongs to both a fault domain and an update domain, because hardware failures and maintenance are different risks. Imagine two service instances: separating their fault exposure helps with a rack failure, while separating their update exposure helps during planned maintenance. Neither grouping protects the application from a software defect deployed to both instances. The supported number of fault domains varies by region, so verify the available values instead of assuming a universal count.

lessons.title: Review availability zones
points: An availability zone is a separate physical location within an Azure region with independent power, cooling and networking.
Enabled regions have at least three separate zones. Distribute application instances across zones to withstand a datacenter failure.
Zonal resources are pinned to a chosen zone; zone-redundant services replicate across zones automatically.
Managed disks and VMs can be zonal, while supported storage and database offerings can provide zone redundancy.

sections.title: A zone is a datacenter failure boundary
paragraphs: A supported Azure region contains at least three physically separate availability zones. Each has independent power, cooling and networking. Place redundant application instances across zones when your design must survive the loss of a datacenter group. A zone is inside a region, so cross-zone placement does not by itself cover a region-wide disaster. Consider the entire service: the application instances, storage and dependencies must all have a recovery design consistent with the failure you are trying to survive.

sections.title: Distinguish choosing a zone from using zone redundancy
paragraphs: A zonal resource is deployed into a particular zone, such as a VM or a zonal managed disk. You select its placement and design the redundancy around it. A zone-redundant service instead manages replication across zones for its supported configuration, such as appropriately configured Azure Storage. For example, one VM in zone one is still one application instance; zone-redundant storage does not automatically create another VM. Combine multiple instances, traffic distribution and the required data resilience. Verify region and service support before copying a zonal design between environments. For example, a replicated web tier still needs a supported traffic-distribution design and data access that works from the surviving zone.

lessons.title: Compare vertical and horizontal scaling
points: Vertical scaling changes a VM size, increasing or decreasing its CPU and memory capacity.
Horizontal scaling changes the number of VM instances serving the workload.
Vertical scaling is bounded by available hardware sizes and often requires a restart. Horizontal scaling provides more flexibility for distributing demand.
If scaling requires recreating a VM, plan how durable data is preserved and what interruption users experience.

sections.title: Change the machine or change the count
paragraphs: Vertical scaling makes an individual VM larger or smaller by changing its size. It is useful when one workload needs more memory or CPU, but the available sizes and regional hardware place limits on that approach. Resizing commonly requires a restart, so capacity changes can interrupt service. Horizontal scaling adds or removes VM instances instead. It suits applications that can distribute work across several machines, allowing capacity to grow without continually replacing one server with the largest available model.

sections.title: Match scaling to application behavior
paragraphs: Consider a document-processing service. If one process needs more memory to handle a document, a larger VM may help. If many independent documents arrive together, more worker instances may provide a better fit. Scaling in either direction still needs durable data planning. Reprovisioning removes an old VM and replaces it, so decide which information must move and which temporary state may be discarded. Removing an instance can also remove its local application state. Choose the strategy from the bottleneck and the application’s ability to distribute work, rather than treating all demand increases as a CPU-size problem. Increasing the instance count can be manual or automated; horizontal scaling describes the capacity change, not how the change is triggered.

lessons.title: Implement Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets
points: Virtual Machine Scale Sets deploy and centrally manage groups of VMs and can add or remove instances manually or through autoscale.
Uniform orchestration uses a shared base image and configuration. Flexible orchestration permits differing VM configurations within a scale set.
Choose the orchestration mode when creating the scale set.
Use Azure Load Balancer for layer-four traffic distribution or Application Gateway for layer-seven routing and TLS termination.
Multiple application instances help maintain service when one instance fails.

sections.title: Use a managed group for repeatable capacity
paragraphs: A Virtual Machine Scale Set groups VMs for deployment and ongoing management. Instance counts can be adjusted manually or by autoscale rules, reducing the need to create each new server individually. The application must be installed and configured appropriately on those instances; a scale set does not turn a single-machine application into a distributed service. For a service that processes independent requests, adding compatible instances can spread work and preserve service when one machine becomes unavailable.

sections.title: Choose the orchestration model deliberately
paragraphs: Uniform orchestration uses a common VM profile and manages instances through scale-set VM APIs. Flexible orchestration manages standard Azure VMs and supports identical or mixed VM configurations. Flexible is recommended for new deployments; requiring identical instances alone does not make Uniform mandatory. Compare the management APIs and feature support your workload needs before choosing. The mode is fixed when the scale set is created, so a change of orchestration model requires a deployment change rather than a routine configuration toggle.

sections.title: Add the correct traffic and availability design
paragraphs: Use Azure Load Balancer for Layer 4 TCP/UDP distribution or Application Gateway when HTTP routing and TLS termination are needed. A scale set can have multiple instances, but users benefit only when requests reach the working application instances. Choose placement across the supported zones or fault domains according to the failure scope. Scaling, traffic distribution and placement are complementary: one supplies capacity, one routes requests, and one reduces shared infrastructure exposure. None replaces backups for important data.

lessons.title: Create Virtual Machine Scale Sets
points: When creating a scale set, choose orchestration mode, image, architecture, size and instance count.
Flexible orchestration is recommended for new deployments and supports identical or mixed VMs. Choose Uniform when its scale-set VM model and feature set fit the workload.
Check application compatibility before selecting x64 or Arm64 architecture.
Maximum spreading places instances across as many available fault domains as possible; fixed spreading can fail when its required fault domains are unavailable.

sections.title: Select a compatible image and architecture
paragraphs: When creating the scale set, choose its orchestration mode, region, operating-system image, VM architecture, size and initial count. The image and architecture must support the application and its dependencies. An x64 application package is not automatically suitable for Arm64 simply because both options are offered. Size determines CPU, memory and other instance limits, while instance count determines how many machines initially run. For a new general deployment, start by evaluating Flexible orchestration and then check whether a required feature justifies another choice.

sections.title: Understand spreading before choosing a policy
paragraphs: Fault-domain spreading affects how instances are distributed within the deployment. Maximum spreading places instances across as many fault domains as Azure can use on a best-effort basis. Fixed spreading requires a particular fault-domain count; insufficient available domains can prevent allocation. The supported counts and available settings depend on orchestration mode and whether the deployment is regional or zonal. Do not copy a fixed count from a diagram into every scale set. Select a supported spreading configuration, then pair it with the required zone placement and application redundancy. Maximum spreading is a distribution strategy, not a promise that every deployment receives the same fixed number of infrastructure groups.

lessons.title: Implement autoscale
points: Autoscale changes instance counts as sustained workload demand changes.
Set scale-out rules to add capacity under increased load and scale-in rules to remove unneeded capacity when demand falls.
Use schedules for predictable demand changes such as working hours or regular events.
Match thresholds to acceptable application performance rather than reacting to every brief spike.

sections.title: Respond to sustained demand, not every spike
paragraphs: Autoscale changes the number of instances according to conditions that represent the workload. A scale-out rule adds capacity when demand remains high; a scale-in rule removes unneeded capacity after demand falls. Measurements over a time window help distinguish sustained pressure from a brief spike. For example, an order-processing service might tolerate a short burst while existing workers finish their requests, but need more instances when load stays elevated. Choose thresholds from acceptable application performance rather than an arbitrary percentage alone.

sections.title: Use predictable patterns and control the range
paragraphs: Schedules are useful when demand has a known pattern, such as a recurring working period or planned event. Scheduled profiles can apply capacity limits and rules at those times instead of waiting for the workload to become overloaded. Always define a useful minimum and a cost-conscious maximum. Combining scale-out and scale-in behavior lets the application recover capacity and later release unnecessary instances. Autoscale reduces repeated manual adjustments, but its rules still need to represent a workload that can actually use more instances and tolerate instances being removed. A scale-out trigger cannot grow capacity beyond the configured maximum, so limits need as much attention as the rule threshold.

lessons.title: Configure autoscale
points: Choose manual capacity for a fixed instance count, or autoscale for metric- or schedule-driven changes.
Set minimum, maximum and default instance counts so capacity remains within operating and cost limits.
Define scale-out and scale-in thresholds and the number of instances each action adds or removes.
Set the metric averaging period to allow readings to stabilize, and configure schedules where demand is predictable.
A scale-in policy determines which VM instances are removed.

sections.title: Capacity limits and fallback serve different purposes
paragraphs: Manual capacity holds the scale set at a configured count until you change it. Autoscale uses profiles with minimum, maximum and default counts. Minimum and maximum bound normal scaling; default is a safety fallback when metrics cannot be read. If current capacity is below the default, autoscale can scale out to it. It does not automatically scale in to the default when already above it. Select those counts using both service needs and the maximum cost you are prepared to support.

sections.title: Make rules and removals explicit
paragraphs: A metric rule describes what to measure, the aggregation and look-back window, the threshold and the scaling action. Define complementary scale-out and scale-in rules, allowing sufficient separation to avoid reacting to small fluctuations. A schedule chooses when a profile applies; its rules still need appropriate limits. The scale-in policy determines which instances are selected for removal. For a stateless web tier, that decision may be straightforward; for workers with local state, account for the application’s shutdown and data requirements before reducing capacity.

sections.title: Review an example before enabling it
paragraphs: Suppose a development service should use a small baseline but can add several instances during a regular testing period. Configure a bounded profile and examine which metric indicates its actual bottleneck. Use an averaging window that represents sustained load, then define both directions of scaling and the intended schedule. Confirm the settings as a coherent set: an unreachable maximum, a missing scale-in rule or an unsafe minimum can undermine an otherwise sensible trigger. Monitor scaling notifications and application behavior rather than assuming a rule’s existence proves it is effective.

lessons.title: Introduction
points: An App Service plan determines the compute capacity and scaling features available to its web apps.

lessons.title: Implement Azure App Service plans
points: An App Service plan defines the operating system, region, pricing tier, instance size and instance count.
Multiple apps can share a plan and its compute resources, potentially reducing cost.
Check remaining capacity before adding an app; overloading shared resources can affect every app in the plan.
Use a separate plan for a resource-intensive app, independent scaling or a different region.

sections.title: Separate the application from its hosting capacity
paragraphs: An App Service app contains application configuration and deployment content. Its App Service plan defines the compute resources on which it runs: operating system, region, pricing tier, instance size and instance count. This separation matters because creating another app does not necessarily create another independently scaled server farm. Several apps can use the same plan. In dedicated tiers they share that plan’s allocated instances, so you need to consider their combined resource requirements rather than assessing each app in isolation.

sections.title: Share resources deliberately
paragraphs: Hosting a small internal portal and a lightly used API in one plan can reduce the cost of separate compute allocations. The tradeoff is shared capacity: increased CPU or memory use by one app can affect the others. Before adding an app, compare its needs with the capacity already consumed. Standard plan-wide scaling changes apply across the apps using that capacity. Separate the apps when one is resource-intensive, requires independent scaling or must run in another region. A different plan is a compute-design choice, not merely a way to tidy the resource list. Review operating-system compatibility as well as capacity before moving another app into a shared plan.

lessons.title: Determine Azure App Service plan pricing
points: The pricing tier determines available features and how apps run and scale. Compare hardware needs with requirements such as backups and staging slots.
Free and Shared tiers use shared compute, apply CPU quotas and do not scale out; they are intended for development and testing without an SLA.
Basic, Standard and Premium tiers provide dedicated compute shared only by apps in that plan.
Isolated tiers add dedicated network isolation through App Service environments.
Apps in the same plan share instance capacity and generally scale together. Higher tiers provide additional scaling and deployment features.

sections.title: Treat the tier as a feature contract
paragraphs: A plan tier defines more than price. It determines compute isolation, instance choices and features such as scaling and deployment slots. Free and Shared use shared infrastructure, apply CPU quotas and do not support scale-out; they are for development and testing and have no SLA. Basic, Standard and Premium provide dedicated compute for apps in that plan. Selecting dedicated compute does not mean each app receives its own private instance: apps in the same plan still share the allocated capacity.

sections.title: Match capabilities to the workload
paragraphs: For a production website that needs staging slots and rule-based autoscale, compare the supported Standard or Premium offerings instead of choosing the cheapest size first. A larger Basic size does not automatically unlock every Standard feature. Premium generations differ, and current hosting choices include Premium v4, so avoid treating an older training table as a permanent catalogue. IsolatedV2 uses an App Service Environment for dedicated network isolation as well as compute isolation. Region and operating-system support also affect which plans can be selected.

sections.title: Make the decision in two passes
paragraphs: First list required features: deployment slots, backup behavior, scaling method and any network-isolation requirement. Then estimate CPU, memory and instance capacity for the apps that will share the plan. This prevents two common mistakes: buying sufficient hardware in a tier missing a required feature, or paying for advanced features while underestimating the shared workload. Review current plan details before purchase because instance limits and available hardware depend on the actual offering, not a generic label such as Premium.

lessons.title: Scale up and scale out Azure App Service
points: Scale up by changing the plan tier or instance size to obtain more CPU, memory, storage or features.
Scale out by increasing the number of instances; the selected tier limits the available count.
Rule-based autoscale adjusts instance counts according to metrics or schedules.
Plan scaling affects apps sharing the plan, but does not automatically scale dependencies such as Azure SQL or Storage.
Scale down when higher capacity or features are no longer required; confirm the lower tier still supports the app.

sections.title: Scaling up changes what each instance can provide
paragraphs: Scale up when the application needs more CPU, memory or storage per instance, or a feature available in a higher tier. You can select a larger size within a tier or move to a different tier. For example, a small app may first need a tier change to gain staging slots, even if its current CPU use is low. Moving down reverses that choice, so confirm the lower tier still supports both the workload and the features it uses.

sections.title: Scaling out changes how many instances serve the app
paragraphs: Scale out increases the number of instances rather than making each one larger. Manual scaling sets a chosen count; rule-based autoscale adjusts the count according to metrics or schedules within configured limits. The plan’s tier bounds the available choices. Apps sharing the plan generally share its scale changes unless a supported per-app configuration applies. A busy API and a quiet website can therefore compete for the same scaled capacity, which is one reason to consider separate plans for independent requirements.

sections.title: Scale the complete service, not only the frontend
paragraphs: App Service plan changes do not automatically resize an Azure SQL database or another external dependency. If the website’s requests are waiting on a constrained database, adding app instances may not remove that bottleneck. Use application and resource monitoring to decide which component needs capacity. For an event-registration site, choose a safe plan capacity for peak demand, then examine database throughput and storage behavior separately. Scale down after the event when appropriate, taking care that the remaining tier and instance count still meet the application’s needs.

lessons.title: Configure Azure App Service autoscale
points: Configure autoscale profiles with minimum, maximum and safe default instance counts. When metrics are unavailable, autoscale scales out to the default only if current capacity is lower; it does not scale in to the default.
A metric rule combines a trigger with a scale-in or scale-out action. Scheduled profiles apply capacity limits and rules at specified times.
Use both scale-out and scale-in rules so performance can recover under load and unnecessary instances can be removed afterward.
Choose the appropriate metric statistic and leave adequate space between the minimum and maximum capacity.
Configure email or webhook notifications to observe scaling events.
Automatic scaling is a separate HTTP-traffic-driven feature on Premium v2, v3 and v4, configured per app with always-ready instances and no custom scaling rules.
Choose rule-based autoscale for custom metrics or schedules; consider automatic scaling for unpredictable HTTP traffic with less rule management.

sections.title: Build a bounded rule-based profile
paragraphs: Rule-based autoscale uses profiles with capacity limits and metric rules. A rule includes a metric, evaluation window, threshold and a scale action. Pair scale-out and scale-in rules so the application can both recover under sustained demand and remove unnecessary instances later. Minimum capacity supports the required baseline, while maximum capacity limits growth and cost. The default count is a fallback when metrics are unavailable: autoscale can scale out to it if current capacity is lower, but does not automatically reduce a higher count to the default.

sections.title: Use schedules and notifications for predictable operations
paragraphs: A scheduled profile applies settings at specified times, useful when traffic follows a regular pattern. For example, a reservation site might need a higher baseline during a recurring booking period. Choose the aggregation and time window so the metric describes sustained demand rather than a fleeting peak. Configure email or webhook notifications for scaling events. Those notifications report what autoscale is doing; a scheduled profile is not itself a general-purpose scheduler for unrelated application jobs.

sections.title: Distinguish automatic scaling from autoscale rules
paragraphs: App Service automatic scaling is a separate HTTP-traffic-driven feature on supported Premium v2, v3 and v4 plans. It uses per-app settings, always-ready instances and a plan maximum burst instead of custom metric rules. Choose rule-based autoscale when custom metrics or schedules are necessary. Consider automatic scaling when the main requirement is responding to unpredictable incoming HTTP demand with less rule maintenance. Neither choice removes the need to check application state, dependencies and an appropriate maximum capacity.
