lessons.title: Introduction
points: Azure App Service hosts web apps, mobile backends and APIs without managing their underlying servers directly.

lessons.title: Implement Azure App Service
points: App Service supports web apps and APIs on Windows or Linux using supported languages and frameworks.
Deployment integrations connect source repositories and build pipelines to application releases.
Apps can scale vertically or horizontally, subject to the selected App Service plan.
Built-in authentication, IP restrictions and managed identities support application security.

sections.title: Understand what the platform manages
paragraphs: App Service hosts web applications, mobile backends and APIs while managing the underlying hosting infrastructure. You select the application runtime and configuration rather than building a VM solely to run the web stack. Supported languages and frameworks depend on the chosen operating system and deployment approach; a custom container is another option. This is useful when the main task is delivering an HTTP application, but the application still needs compatible dependencies and suitable data services outside its code package.

sections.title: Connect development to repeatable releases
paragraphs: Deployment integrations let repositories and build pipelines publish the application. Continuous integration can compile code and run tests, while staging slots provide a place to validate a release before production. These features support different parts of the release process: a successful build demonstrates that the artifact was produced, whereas a staging check examines how it behaves with its hosting configuration. Choose the App Service plan separately, because available deployment and scale features depend on that plan’s tier.

sections.title: Combine hosting with explicit security choices
paragraphs: Built-in authentication can handle sign-in with supported identity providers; IP restrictions control network-based access; managed identities support access to other Azure resources. They are complementary controls rather than replacements for one another. For an internal research API, decide which users may call it, which network paths are permitted and how its backend resources authorize the app. Then use monitoring to observe failures and performance. Platform hosting reduces server administration, but does not decide the application’s authorization policy or business behavior for you.

lessons.title: Create an app with App Service
points: Choose a unique app name, code or container publishing, runtime stack, operating system, region and App Service plan.
The runtime stack determines the supported language and version; Linux or custom-container apps can provide a startup command.
Always On keeps an app loaded during idle periods and is required for continuous or CRON-triggered WebJobs.
Session affinity routes a client to the same instance during its session. HTTPS Only redirects HTTP requests to HTTPS.

sections.title: Choose a runtime and plan that can actually host the app
paragraphs: The creation form combines an app name, publishing method, runtime stack, operating system, region and App Service plan. Code publishing relies on a supported platform runtime; a custom container includes the chosen application environment. Verify the language and version against the selected OS rather than assuming all combinations are interchangeable. The region determines which plans can host the app. The app’s default hostname is useful for an initial deployment, while custom-domain mapping is a separate configuration step.

sections.title: Understand the post-creation switches
paragraphs: Always On keeps the app loaded during idle periods, avoiding the unload and subsequent warm-up behavior. It is required for continuous or CRON-triggered WebJobs in supported configurations. Session affinity keeps a client on the same instance during its session, which can help an app that stores session state locally; stateless apps may not need it. HTTPS Only redirects HTTP requests to HTTPS. These switches solve different problems, so do not use session affinity or Always On as a substitute for transport security.

sections.title: Keep application configuration explicit
paragraphs: Linux runtime and custom-container configurations can specify a startup command when needed. App settings supply environment-specific values at startup, and changing them can restart the app. For a test API, separate its runtime choice from settings such as a backend URL, then check the deployed startup behavior before assuming it is ready. This makes failures easier to distinguish: an incompatible runtime, an incorrect command and a missing configuration value can all stop an app without indicating a capacity problem.

lessons.title: Explore continuous integration and deployment
points: Configure deployment sources through Deployment Center. Continuous deployment publishes updates through a repeatable pipeline.
GitHub integration can use GitHub Actions or App Service Build Service. Other supported sources include Azure Repos and Bitbucket.
Build and release pipelines can compile code and run tests before deploying.
Manual deployment includes pushing to the app remote Git endpoint.

sections.title: Turn a repository change into a deliberate deployment
paragraphs: Deployment Center connects the app to supported source and build providers. With GitHub, you can use GitHub Actions or App Service Build Service; other supported integrations include Azure Repos and Bitbucket. A pipeline can compile code, run tests and publish an artifact when the configured trigger occurs. Choose the repository and branch deliberately. A deployment source defines where updates come from, while the pipeline defines how they are built and released. Changing either can change what reaches the app.

sections.title: Distinguish continuous deployment from a manual push
paragraphs: A remote Git deployment endpoint lets an administrator push code to the app manually. That is different from a connected repository triggering future deployments automatically. For a small prototype, a manual push may be sufficient. For a team-maintained service, automated builds and tests make repeated releases easier to reproduce. Neither approach alone validates production behavior: combine it with the appropriate staging, application configuration and monitoring for the chosen plan. Avoid treating a successful transfer of files as proof the application started correctly.

sections.title: Use a release path you can explain
paragraphs: Imagine a support portal maintained by several developers. Select the intended source branch, establish the build provider, run the tests and identify the deployment destination. A staging slot can serve as the destination before a controlled production swap when the plan supports slots. Keep deployment credentials and permissions appropriate to the selected provider. The useful outcome is a traceable relationship between source, built artifact and running app, rather than an update process that depends on someone remembering several undocumented clicks.

lessons.title: Create deployment slots
points: Deployment slots are live apps with their own hostnames, available on supported Standard, Premium and Isolated tiers.
Deploy to a staging slot to validate an update before swapping it into production.
A swap moves app content and eligible configuration between slots; the previous production version remains in the other slot for rollback.
Swapping a warmed deployment can reduce interruption compared with replacing production content directly.

sections.title: A slot is a live environment for the same app
paragraphs: A deployment slot is a separately addressable live app with its own hostname, available on supported Standard, Premium and Isolated tiers. You can deploy new content to staging and exercise it before changing production. Slots share the hosting plan’s resources, so staging activity still consumes capacity. A slot therefore provides a release boundary, not an automatically isolated server farm. Decide what testing can run safely alongside production, particularly when both versions use external services.

sections.title: Warm and validate before redirecting production
paragraphs: A swap changes the application content and eligible configuration between slots. The swap process prepares the source deployment before changing traffic to help reduce cold starts and interruption. Validate the staged application and its intended settings, then perform the swap. Afterward, the other slot holds the previous production version, allowing a reverse swap if the release fails. That rollback covers the app content and swapped settings; it does not automatically reverse external database changes made by the application.

sections.title: Choose automation with the correct limits
paragraphs: Auto swap can streamline compatible deployments after the source is warmed, but it is not supported for Linux web apps or Web App for Containers. Use a manual or pipeline-controlled swap when that feature is unavailable or when pre-swap validation is needed. For a booking application, test a new page in staging, check its backend connections and then promote it. Review both the release and rollback path before relying on slots as a replacement for application-level testing.

lessons.title: Add deployment slots
points: Create a slot with empty content or clone configuration from an existing slot.
Some settings follow app content during a swap; slot-specific settings remain attached to the slot.
App settings, connection strings and mounted storage can be marked as slot-specific.
Custom domains, scale settings, managed identities and virtual network integration stay with their slots. Review configuration before swapping.

sections.title: Cloning copies configuration, not deployment content
paragraphs: When adding a slot, you can start with an empty configuration or clone settings from an existing slot. Cloning makes it easier to reuse runtime versions and settings, but you still need to deploy the application content. Review the cloned configuration rather than assuming every property or network resource was duplicated. For example, a staging app may need a different connection string from production even when its runtime is identical. Its separate hostname lets you test those settings directly.

sections.title: Decide which values follow the release
paragraphs: Some configuration follows the content during a swap; other properties remain with the slot. App settings, connection strings and mounted storage can be marked as deployment-slot settings. Mark environment-specific values when they must remain attached to staging or production instead of moving with the code. Custom domains, scale settings, managed identities and virtual network integration normally remain slot-specific. This means an identity available in one slot does not simply move with the application to the other slot.

sections.title: Review the whole configuration before swapping
paragraphs: For a release that uses different test and production databases, keep the intended connection values slot-specific and confirm the staged app’s behavior with its assigned resources. Inspect runtime, startup settings, identities and network access as well as the files being deployed. A swap is a release operation across settings with distinct rules, not an unconditional exchange of every property. Reviewing the current swapped-versus-sticky table is useful whenever the application depends on a setting whose behavior is uncertain.

lessons.title: Secure your App Service app
points: App Service built-in authentication runs separately from application code and can authenticate users, handle tokens and pass identity information in headers.
You can instead use authentication supplied by your application framework.
Allow anonymous requests when the application should decide how to handle unauthenticated visitors.
Requiring authentication for every request can also restrict access to a public home page.
Use authentication logs and failed-request traces to investigate sign-in failures.

sections.title: Put platform authentication in front of application requests
paragraphs: App Service’s authentication module runs separately from the application code and can authenticate through configured providers, handle tokens and add identity information to headers. It reduces the amount of sign-in plumbing the application must implement. You can also choose your framework’s authentication features instead. The platform module is a request-processing facility, not an instruction that every request should be public or every signed-in user should receive the same business permissions.

sections.title: Choose anonymous behavior to match the user flow
paragraphs: Allowing anonymous requests lets the application decide what public visitors can see and when to request sign-in. Requiring authentication protects the app broadly, but can also restrict a public home page. For browser experiences, a redirect to the provider may be appropriate; an API may need an unauthorized response instead of an HTML sign-in flow. Current settings support explicit rejection choices. Decide from the client’s expected behavior, rather than assuming that one default is suitable for browsers, mobile clients and APIs alike.

sections.title: Investigate failures at the correct layer
paragraphs: Use authentication traces and application logs to distinguish a provider or token problem from an application error after sign-in. Failed-request tracing is useful in supported Windows configurations; do not assume the same Windows module trace appears in every Linux or container deployment. For a customer portal with a public welcome page, test both anonymous and authenticated requests, then check which identity information reaches the application. A successful login is only one part of the desired access behavior.

lessons.title: Create custom domain names
points: A custom domain maps a domain you control to the default App Service hostname.
Use an A record to map to an IP address or a CNAME to map to another hostname. A CNAME remains valid when the target IP changes.
Some DNS providers do not allow CNAME records at the domain root, requiring another supported mapping.
Validate and add the domain in App Service, then configure a TLS binding using a suitable certificate.

sections.title: Map a name you control to the running app
paragraphs: The default App Service hostname provides a working address without requiring a custom domain. For a branded address, you must control the domain and configure its DNS records before adding it to the app. DNS mapping and App Service hostname validation are separate steps. A DNS record can direct traffic toward the service, but the app must also recognize the hostname. Keep the default app hostname available while checking the custom mapping so you can distinguish DNS problems from application failures.

sections.title: Choose the right DNS record and verify ownership
paragraphs: An A record maps a name to the app’s IP address; a CNAME maps a subdomain to the app hostname. A CNAME follows changes to that target’s IP, whereas a directly mapped A record may need updating. The normal root-domain mapping uses an A record rather than a root CNAME. App Service supplies domain-verification information, and the recommended TXT record helps protect against subdomain takeover. Follow the actual values shown for your app rather than copying another deployment’s hostname or verification identifier.

sections.title: Add TLS after the domain is recognized
paragraphs: Validate and add the hostname in App Service, then configure a suitable certificate and TLS binding. A correct DNS record alone does not provide the HTTPS certificate for your custom name. App Service Managed Certificates are available for supported configurations on Basic or higher tiers; check eligibility rather than assuming every hostname and deployment supports one. For a company help site, test the custom hostname over HTTPS and confirm it reaches the intended app after mapping and binding are complete.

lessons.title: Back up and restore your App Service app
points: App Service supports restoring app content and configuration from backups; supported tiers and backup types determine available options.
Custom backups use a storage account and container. Review storage access and firewall requirements before configuring the destination.
A backup contains compressed app data and a manifest; backup schedules and retention control when copies are kept.
A full restore replaces existing content; a partial restore leaves excluded files and folders unchanged.
Automatic backups exclude linked databases. Custom backups support only specified linked database types; protect other dependencies separately and verify restore support.

sections.title: Distinguish automatic backups from custom backups
paragraphs: App Service offers automatic and custom backups on supported Basic, Standard, Premium and Isolated plans. Basic covers the production slot. Automatic backups do not require you to configure a destination storage account; custom backups use your chosen storage account and container. Backup content and limits differ between the two types. Identify which type you are relying on before assuming that a backup schedule, destination or database coverage from one applies to the other.

sections.title: Protect external dependencies separately
paragraphs: Automatic backups exclude linked databases. Existing custom backups that already include linked databases continue to protect them until 31 March 2028. New custom backup configurations stopped offering linked MySQL and PostgreSQL databases in November 2025, and linked Azure SQL and SQL Server databases in April 2026. Plan database recovery through the database service’s supported backup mechanism. Custom backups can use firewall-protected storage when the documented virtual-network configuration permits the app to reach its backup storage through that network.

sections.title: Know what a restore will overwrite
paragraphs: A full restore replaces the site content with the selected backup; files absent from that backup can be removed. Partial backups exclude selected files or directories, and excluded locations are left unchanged during the corresponding restore. Custom backup files include compressed content and a manifest, which can be inspected without a restore. For a portal release, identify whether you need app rollback, file recovery or database recovery before choosing an operation. Test the required restore behavior rather than treating the presence of a backup as proof the entire service is recoverable.

lessons.title: Use Azure Application Insights
points: Application Insights is part of Azure Monitor and helps diagnose application performance and usage.
Monitor request rates, response times and failures to identify problems under load.
Track dependency calls to determine whether external services contribute to slow or failed requests.
Use exceptions, trace logs and performance counters to investigate individual failures and resource pressure.
Custom events and metrics can measure application-specific activity.

sections.title: Observe the request path, not only the server
paragraphs: Application Insights is an Azure Monitor capability for application performance and usage. Request rates, duration and failure rates help answer whether the service is receiving more work and whether users are experiencing problems. Compare the signals together: rising response times during increased request volume may indicate a capacity bottleneck, while failures with normal volume can point to a different issue. Instrumentation is necessary for application telemetry; hosting an app is not equivalent to collecting every application-specific event.

sections.title: Follow dependencies and investigate individual failures
paragraphs: Dependency telemetry helps identify calls to databases or external services that contribute to slow or failed requests. Exceptions and diagnostic traces provide detail beyond a summary failure percentage. For an ordering API, a slow response might come from the API’s own processing or from a database call it waits for. Correlating the request with dependency and exception information makes that distinction more useful than repeatedly scaling the web tier without understanding the cause.

sections.title: Measure the outcomes that matter to the app
paragraphs: Page views, user and session measurements can describe usage when the relevant client telemetry is configured. Custom events and metrics let the application record domain-specific activity, such as a completed registration or a processing queue outcome. Performance counters and host diagnostics supply additional resource context where supported. Choose telemetry that answers an operational or product question, then use trends and detailed traces together. A useful dashboard should help you decide what to investigate, not merely display all available numbers.

lessons.title: Exercise: Implement Web Apps
points: This optional lab requires an Azure subscription and migrates a PHP web app to App Service.
Create the web app and a staging slot, configure deployment and deploy code into staging.
Swap the tested staging deployment into production, then configure and test autoscaling.
Follow the full interactive instructions on Microsoft Learn.

sections.title: Translate the migration into distinct tasks
paragraphs: The optional lab migrates a PHP web application to App Service and demonstrates slots, deployment and scaling. It requires an Azure subscription; use the linked current lab for exact files and deployment settings. First identify a supported runtime and App Service plan, including a tier that supports the required staging slot and autoscale behavior. A source application’s previous server OS does not by itself determine the appropriate target runtime. Confirm the target stack rather than assuming every language and OS combination is supported.

sections.title: Release through staging rather than replacing production immediately
paragraphs: Create the web app and staging slot, configure deployment, and send the new code to staging. Test its hostname and configuration before swapping it into production. The slots share plan capacity, while selected environment settings can remain slot-specific, so check both the application and the settings involved in promotion. After the swap, use the previous version retained in the other slot to understand the rollback path. Do not assume this also reverses changes made in an external database.

sections.title: Test scaling as observable behavior
paragraphs: Configure bounded autoscale settings, then follow the lab’s workload and observation steps to see whether the intended condition adds or removes capacity. A rule that exists in the portal has not necessarily been exercised. Check the app’s response and scaling results together. Keep the demonstration within resources you deliberately created, and clean up those lab resources afterward. The useful lesson is the complete release-and-capacity sequence: deploy, validate, promote, observe and then stop paying for a finished experiment.

Configure deployment and deploy the code to staging.
Validate the staged app and its environment settings.

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Containers package applications and dependencies with lighter virtualization than complete virtual machines.

lessons.title: Compare containers to virtual machines
points: Containers virtualize the operating-system environment, while VMs run a complete guest operating system and kernel.
Containers generally use fewer resources and start faster. Typical process-isolated containers share the host kernel and provide a weaker security boundary than a full VM.
Container images make application packaging and deployment consistent across environments.
Use orchestration when many containers require coordinated deployment, scaling and recovery.

sections.title: Virtualize the application environment or the whole machine
paragraphs: A VM runs a complete guest operating system, including its kernel, on virtualized hardware. A typical process-isolated container packages the application and the user-mode environment it needs while sharing the host kernel. That difference helps explain why containers often need fewer resources and start faster. It also explains why ordinary process isolation is a different security boundary from a full VM. Avoid assuming every container technology uses an identical isolation model; platform-managed hosting can provide additional isolation around containers.

sections.title: Use packaging for consistent deployment
paragraphs: A container image includes application code, runtime, libraries and settings needed by that workload. Reusing the image helps make deployments consistent rather than rebuilding each host by hand. The image does not magically make all operating systems, processors or storage interfaces compatible, so select an appropriate host platform. For a small API, a container can carry the required runtime alongside the code. A VM may be more appropriate when the workload needs broad control of the guest OS or machine-level dependencies.

sections.title: Distinguish one container from orchestrated applications
paragraphs: Running a container and coordinating a fleet are separate concerns. An orchestrator manages placement, scaling and recovery of many containers; a VM also needs an explicit availability and recovery design. Persistent data must use an appropriate durable storage service rather than assuming a replaced container or VM retains its local state. Choose the management model from the application: an isolated task may not need a cluster, while a multi-service application may need coordinated deployment and health management.

lessons.title: Review Azure Container Instances
points: Azure Container Instances runs containers without requiring you to manage a VM or Kubernetes cluster.
A container image packages application code, runtime, libraries, tools and settings.
Choose CPU and memory when deploying the container group. Changing its CPU, memory or GPU allocation requires deleting and recreating the group.
Container Instances supports Windows and Linux containers. Azure Files volume mounts for persistent storage are supported only for Linux containers.
A supported publicly exposed group can have an IP address and DNS name. Linux groups deployed into a virtual network use private connectivity without a public IP.

sections.title: Use ACI when an isolated container is enough
paragraphs: Azure Container Instances runs container workloads without requiring you to maintain a VM or operate a Kubernetes cluster. You provide a compatible image and configure the container group. This makes it useful for an isolated processing task or a simple containerized application that does not require a full orchestration platform. An image carries the software environment, but the group still needs suitable CPU, memory, network and storage settings. Fast startup is an advantage, not a guarantee that every application is instantly ready.

sections.title: Understand resource and platform limits
paragraphs: Select CPU and memory when deploying. Changing CPU, memory or GPU allocation requires deleting and recreating the group rather than resizing it in place. ACI supports both Linux and Windows containers, but its features differ by platform: multi-container groups and Azure Files volume mounts are Linux-only. An Azure Files mount supplies persistent shared storage for a supported Linux workload. Do not infer that Windows support includes every feature described in a Linux example.

sections.title: Choose public exposure or private connectivity
paragraphs: A publicly exposed group can have an IP address, DNS label and explicitly exposed ports. A supported Linux group deployed into a virtual network uses private connectivity and does not receive a public IP. Decide which access pattern the task needs before deploying. For an internal document-processing container, private communication with Azure resources may be more suitable than an internet-facing endpoint. For a demonstration web container, an exposed port and application response provide a straightforward way to verify the deployment.

Microsoft Learn: container instances container groups

lessons.title: Implement container groups
points: A container group schedules containers on the same host; they share lifecycle, local networking, storage volumes and group resources. Multi-container groups support Linux only; Windows groups support one container.
Group resource requirements are calculated from the requests of its containers.
Deploy groups using ARM templates, Bicep or YAML according to the surrounding infrastructure.
For external access, expose the port at both the group IP address and the container. Containers share a port namespace, so port mapping is not supported.
Deleting a group releases its IP address and fully qualified domain name.
Separate supporting tasks into containers, such as an app plus logging, monitoring or content-update components.

sections.title: Think of a group as a shared lifecycle boundary
paragraphs: An ACI container group schedules its containers on the same host, sharing lifecycle, resources, local networking and storage volumes. A multi-container group is similar to a Kubernetes pod in purpose, but does not require you to operate Kubernetes. In ACI, multi-container groups support Linux; a Windows group supports a single container. Group resource requirements are calculated from the containers’ requests, so a helper container consumes real capacity rather than being an unlimited add-on to the main app.

sections.title: Use cooperating containers for one functional unit
paragraphs: An original example is a small reporting app paired with a helper that retrieves updated content, or an application paired with a logging component. Separate images let the components have different responsibilities while sharing the group’s local environment. Deploy the definition with an ARM template, Bicep or YAML according to the broader infrastructure workflow. YAML focuses on the container deployment, while infrastructure-as-code approaches are useful when the group is part of a larger set of Azure resources.

sections.title: Expose the ports the group actually uses
paragraphs: Containers in a group share the network and port namespace. For an external client to reach a container, expose its port on both the group IP configuration and the container definition. ACI does not support translating one group port into another container port through port mapping. Plan the applications’ listening ports so they do not conflict. Deleting the group releases its assigned IP address and DNS name; do not treat those values as persistent identifiers independent of the group lifecycle.

lessons.title: Review Azure Container Apps
points: Azure Container Apps provides managed container hosting for APIs, microservices, background jobs and event-driven workloads.
It scales using HTTP traffic, event sources, CPU or memory, and KEDA-supported scalers; supported workloads can scale to zero.
Container Apps supports service discovery, traffic splitting and on-demand, scheduled or event-driven jobs.
It abstracts the underlying Kubernetes platform rather than exposing its Kubernetes APIs directly.
Choose Container Instances for isolated tasks, Container Apps for managed serverless microservices, or AKS when direct Kubernetes control is needed.

sections.title: Choose managed application hosting rather than a cluster
paragraphs: Azure Container Apps provides managed hosting for containerized APIs, microservices, event-driven workloads and jobs. It uses Kubernetes and related technologies internally without exposing the Kubernetes API for direct cluster management. This is useful when the desired outcome is running services with managed deployment and scaling, rather than controlling every Kubernetes resource. Features such as service discovery and traffic splitting help multiple components work together. Supported jobs can run on demand, on a schedule or in response to events.

sections.title: Match scaling to the event that creates work
paragraphs: Container Apps can scale using HTTP traffic, supported event sources and KEDA scalers, including CPU or memory signals. Supported event-driven configurations can scale to zero, but a configuration without ingress or a suitable custom rule can reach zero and have no way to restart. Set a minimum of one or more replicas when the app must keep a running baseline. For a queue-driven worker, queue demand can be the useful trigger; for an HTTP API, incoming requests may be more appropriate. Select the rule from the workload rather than treating all signals as interchangeable.

sections.title: Compare ACI, Container Apps and AKS by control needs
paragraphs: ACI is a direct option for isolated container tasks without cluster management. Container Apps adds a managed application experience for services and event-driven processing. AKS is the option when the design needs direct Kubernetes APIs and more control over orchestration. For example, a single short processing job does not automatically justify a cluster, while a team requiring custom Kubernetes management may need AKS. The choice is about operational features and control, not simply whether the application has already been packaged as a container.

lessons.title: Exercise: Implement Container Instances
points: This optional exercise requires an Azure subscription.
Deploy an Azure Container Instance from a Docker image, then test and verify that the application responds.
Use the linked Microsoft Learn lab for the complete deployment instructions.

sections.title: Prepare a container deployment you can verify
paragraphs: The optional lab deploys an Azure Container Instance from a Docker image and tests the resulting application. You need an Azure subscription and permission to create the lab resources. Follow the linked exercise for its exact image and settings instead of substituting unrelated commands. Before deployment, identify the image’s operating-system requirements, resource allocation and listening port. These choices have separate roles: the image supplies software, CPU and memory supply execution capacity, and networking determines which clients can reach it.

sections.title: Check both provisioning and application behavior
paragraphs: A completed resource deployment confirms that Azure created the group, but you still need to verify that its application responds as intended. For a public web demonstration, inspect the assigned endpoint and exposed application port, then use the lab’s test to confirm the response. A private virtual-network deployment would need a client with the appropriate private connectivity instead. A wrong port or incompatible image is not fixed merely by waiting longer for the deployment notification.

sections.title: Use the lifecycle to understand the service
paragraphs: Inspect the group configuration and relate it to the running container. Note which data is temporary and whether a supported persistent volume is configured; do not assume group recreation preserves local application files. Keep the exercise scoped to the resources you created, and remove them after testing when they are no longer needed. The aim is to connect the image, resource settings and endpoint to an observable application result, rather than memorizing one image name from a walkthrough.

Configure the specified group resources and networking, then deploy.
Verify group deployment and test the application through the expected endpoint.
Inspect the configuration and clean up only the completed lab resources.

paths.title: AZ-104: Monitor and back up Azure resources

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Backup planning defines recovery requirements, backup frequency, retention and access controls for important data.
Azure Backup protects supported Azure workloads and selected on-premises data.

lessons.title: What is Azure Backup?
points: Azure Backup manages backup storage and policies for supported workloads such as VMs, managed disks, file shares and databases.
Central management helps govern and monitor many protected resources.
Recovery time objective is the target time to restore service after an incident. Recovery point objective is the maximum tolerable data loss measured in time.
Use encryption, access controls and deletion protection to secure backups; choose policies that meet recovery and compliance needs.

sections.title: Start with the object you must recover
paragraphs: Azure Backup provides managed protection for supported resources, but the protected object differs by workload. A whole-VM recovery, a particular database recovery and recovery of a deleted file are different operational needs. Choose the relevant backup offering before selecting a schedule. Central management helps administrators govern policies and monitor protected resources across their estate; it does not make every workload share the same recovery options.

sections.title: Translate business requirements into RPO and RTO
paragraphs: Suppose a reporting service can tolerate losing at most four hours of changes and must return within three hours. The first requirement is its recovery point objective: how far back the recovered data may be. The second is its recovery time objective: how long restoring usable service may take. A backup interval alone does not prove the service meets both targets; recovery also needs an available recovery point and a successful restore.

sections.title: Protect the backups themselves
paragraphs: Recovery copies need protection as well as the live workload. Encryption protects data, access controls limit who can manage backup and restore operations, and deletion protection helps retain recoverable backups after an accidental or malicious deletion. Treat these capabilities as parts of a protection design, rather than assuming the existence of a backup makes every ransomware scenario harmless. Pair the policy’s retention and schedule with the workload’s recovery and compliance requirements.

lessons.title: How Azure Backup works
points: Use the MARS agent for supported Windows files, folders and system state; DPM or Azure Backup Server can protect additional on-premises workloads.
Azure VM backup takes disk snapshots. Application- or filesystem-consistent backups use a VM extension; supported agentless backups are crash-consistent. Vaults manage recovery points and policies.
An initial full backup captures the protected data; later incremental backups transfer changed blocks. SQL database protection also supports differential and transaction-log backups.
Snapshot-tier recovery can be faster because data is near the source. Vault-standard stores an isolated copy; supported archive storage targets infrequently accessed long-term recovery points.
Choose locally, zone- or geo-redundant backup storage based on failure-protection requirements.
Backup policies define schedule and retention; enhanced VM policies support more frequent backups and selective disk protection.
Encryption, role-based access control and soft delete reduce exposure to unauthorized access and accidental deletion.

sections.title: Separate collection from management
paragraphs: The method of collecting protected data depends on the workload. MARS can protect supported Windows files, folders and system state; MABS or DPM supports additional on-premises scenarios. Azure VM protection uses snapshots, with extensions for application- or filesystem-consistent backup and supported agentless crash-consistent options. Recovery Services vaults and Backup vaults manage policies and recovery points for their supported workloads, so choose the vault and collection path together.

sections.title: Follow the recovery point through storage
paragraphs: A VM snapshot near the source supports faster operational recovery, while the vault copy provides a separately managed recovery copy and longer retention. Supported archive storage serves infrequently accessed long-term points and has a different retrieval profile. These tiers are not interchangeable promises of instant recovery. The first backup captures protected data, and later incremental VM backups identify changed blocks rather than retransferring every unchanged block.

sections.title: Apply schedule, retention and redundancy independently
paragraphs: Consider a VM with a four-hour backup requirement and a separate need to retain older points. Enhanced policy can schedule multiple VM backups per day, as frequently as every four hours; retention controls how long points remain, not when jobs run. Vault redundancy determines the storage failure protection. Review these three decisions separately so that extending retention is not mistaken for improving backup frequency or adding regional protection.

Microsoft Learn: backup azure vms enhanced policy

lessons.title: When to use Azure Backup
points: Use Azure Backup for operational recovery from accidental deletion or corruption and for long-term compliance retention.
Choose whole-VM backup or workload-aware database backup according to what must be recovered. SQL protection supports full, differential and transaction-log backups.
Do not confuse backing up a workload across regions with restoring to a supported paired secondary region. Check the workload support matrix.
On-demand backups can use their own retention settings rather than the scheduled policy retention.
Monitor job status in vaults; reporting and workbooks help assess a wider backup estate.

sections.title: Choose the right recovery granularity
paragraphs: For a database hosted on a VM, recovering the entire machine and recovering one database to a particular time are different goals. Whole-VM backup protects the VM’s disks and configuration for VM recovery. Workload-aware SQL protection offers full, differential and transaction-log backups, including database-level recovery. Choose the offering around what the application owner needs back, rather than selecting VM backup merely because the database happens to run inside a VM.

sections.title: Design planned and exceptional retention
paragraphs: A compliance requirement to retain annual recovery points is a policy-design question, while an extra backup before a risky change is an on-demand operation. On-demand backup can have its own retention setting instead of inheriting the scheduled policy’s retention. For an original example, an administrator can plan routine retention for daily operations and separately record how long a pre-upgrade recovery point must remain available.

sections.title: Verify placement and operational evidence
paragraphs: Vault placement and restore support are workload-specific. A backup design spanning regions must not assume that support for restoring into a paired secondary region permits protecting any source from any vault region. Review the workload support before selecting a vault. Then inspect job outcomes and reporting: a policy assignment establishes intended protection, whereas completed backups and available points show that the protection has actually produced recovery data.

points: Complete the interactive check on Microsoft Learn.

lessons.title: Summary
points: Match workload support, schedule, retention and security to the required recovery time and acceptable data loss.

modules.title: Protect your virtual machines by using Azure Backup

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Azure Backup protects VM data so that Windows and Linux workloads can be recovered after loss or corruption.
Optional practical exercises use your own Azure subscription.

lessons.title: Azure Backup features and scenarios
points: Azure Backup retains recovery points for returning to an earlier data state. Azure Site Recovery instead replicates workloads and coordinates failover.
Choose protection based on recovery time, acceptable data loss, application criticality and cost.
Azure VM backups are managed through a Recovery Services vault. Supported on-premises scenarios use MARS, Azure Backup Server or DPM.
Backup data is encrypted; role-based access control separates backup responsibilities. Customer-managed keys are available for supported configurations.
Soft delete preserves deleted backup data for recovery; enhanced soft delete can extend retention and enforce always-on protection.
Select LRS, GRS or ZRS to match the required storage failure protection.

sections.title: Distinguish history from failover
paragraphs: Azure Backup keeps earlier recovery points so you can recover from deletion, corruption or an unwanted change. Site Recovery replicates workloads and coordinates failover during an outage. In a simple example, an accidentally deleted business document needs an earlier clean copy; a regional outage needs a plan for running the workload elsewhere. Both concerns can exist in the same system, but copying an unwanted change into a replica does not itself provide the earlier clean state.

sections.title: Treat the vault as a protection boundary
paragraphs: A Recovery Services vault manages Azure VM recovery points and policies and provides a boundary for backup access. Role assignments govern who can perform backup administration or restore operations. Encryption and supported customer-managed-key configurations protect backup data, while soft delete adds recovery opportunity after deletion. These controls address different threats, so assigning a backup policy should be accompanied by a review of permissions and deletion protection.

sections.title: Select resilience for the recovery copies
paragraphs: Locally redundant, zone-redundant and geo-redundant vault storage protect against different storage failure scopes. Match the selection to the continuity plan rather than choosing it solely from the live VM’s location. As a design exercise, identify the incident you need to withstand, the acceptable age of recovered data and the time allowed to restore service. These answers guide both backup protection and whether replication and failover are also needed.

lessons.title: Back up an Azure virtual machine by using Azure Backup
points: A Recovery Services vault manages VM recovery points, policies and access permissions.
Azure Backup takes disk snapshots on the policy schedule, then transfers changed blocks to vault storage.
Application-consistent snapshots use Windows VSS writers; Linux application consistency needs appropriate pre- and post-backup scripts.
File-system-consistent backups preserve filesystem integrity but applications may need cleanup. Crash-consistent backups omit pending memory and input/output state.
Policies set backup frequency and retention; enhanced policies support more frequent protection and selected data disks.
Snapshot recovery can be quicker than vault recovery; transfer to the vault can take time after the snapshot is created.

sections.title: Follow snapshot creation and vault transfer
paragraphs: The policy starts a VM backup job. For supported agent-based backups, the extension coordinates the snapshot; Azure Backup then transfers the changed disk blocks to vault storage. Disks can be backed up in parallel. Snapshot creation and completion of the vault transfer are distinct milestones, so a recently created local recovery point is not proof that its vault copy has already completed.

sections.title: Know what consistency preserves
paragraphs: Application-consistent Windows backups coordinate with VSS writers, while Linux applications need suitable pre- and post-backup scripts. Filesystem consistency protects filesystem integrity but an application may still require recovery or cleanup when it starts. Crash consistency captures data already on disk and omits pending memory or unwritten I/O. VSS coordination does not mean the backup contains a runnable copy of all process memory.

sections.title: Choose policy against the workload
paragraphs: For a service that needs several scheduled backups per day, inspect Enhanced policy instead of assuming every VM policy is daily-only. It supports schedules as frequently as four hours and longer snapshot retention, up to thirty days. Selective disk protection can focus protection on required disks, but excluded data will not appear in that recovery point. Compare the intended recoverable data, schedule and retention before enabling protection.

Create the lab resource group and virtual network, then deploy the two VMs using Cloud Shell.

Start an on-demand backup with az backup protection backup-now, then inspect backup jobs and last-backup status.
Review the current interactive instructions before running commands, and clean up only the lab resources you created afterward.

sections.title: Prepare a controlled backup experiment
paragraphs: Use a lab Windows VM and Linux VM to compare how protection is enabled through the portal and CLI. The purpose is to follow the protection lifecycle, not to treat the exercise’s historical image or size as the only supported choice. Identify the lab resource group, VM names, vault and policy before beginning. The chosen policy must exist and support the VM configuration rather than relying on a policy name being universally present.

sections.title: Distinguish configuration from a backup job
paragraphs: Enabling protection associates the VM with a vault and policy. It does not mean an initial backup has already finished. Start an on-demand backup when you need a point before the next scheduled run, then inspect jobs until you can distinguish ConfigureBackup completion from Backup completion. The read-only command below lists jobs in the selected vault; its placeholders identify your own lab resources.

sections.title: Collect evidence from both views
paragraphs: For a useful practical record, compare the VM’s last-backup status with the vault’s backup-job view. The VM view answers whether that item has a recent backup outcome; the vault view lets you follow operations across protected items. Record the selected policy and the backup outcome together, then inspect the available recovery points. This is stronger evidence for a later restore exercise than a screenshot showing only that protection was enabled.

lessons.title: Restore virtual machine data
points: Create a new VM to recover into another VM, or restore disks when you need to customize the recovered deployment.
Replace existing restores disks into a VM that still exists, taking a snapshot of its current disks first. It cannot replace a deleted VM.
Cross-region restore targets a supported paired secondary region; it supports creating a VM or restoring disks rather than replacing existing disks.

Cross-subscription restore uses vault-tier points for supported managed VMs in the same tenant. Restore to a subscription other than the protected VM or vault subscription requires the vault setting; ADE- and customer-key-encrypted disks are unsupported.
Cross-zonal restore has vault-redundancy and VM-support requirements. Verify the support matrix before planning it.
File recovery can mount supported backup recovery points. For Azure Disk Encryption VMs, file-level recovery and replacing the existing VM are not supported; restore the VM and copy needed files.

sections.title: Choose where recovery will land
paragraphs: Create a new VM is a convenient path to bring up a recovered machine, while Restore disks gives you recovered disks and a template for a customized VM configuration. Replace existing uses a VM that still exists and replaces its disks from the selected point, taking a snapshot of current disks first. A deleted original VM cannot be the target of Replace existing, so its disappearance changes the restore decision.

sections.title: Check regional and subscription conditions
paragraphs: Cross-region restore uses a supported paired secondary region and supports creating a VM or restoring disks rather than replacing existing disks there. Cross-subscription restore has separate managed-VM, vault-tier, tenant and encryption requirements. Do not infer that a point usable for an ordinary local restore automatically qualifies for every cross-region, cross-subscription or cross-zonal path. Check the current support matrix against the actual point and VM configuration.

sections.title: Select the smallest supported recovery
paragraphs: For a misplaced report, file recovery can avoid restoring an entire otherwise healthy VM when the configuration supports it. Azure Disk Encryption VMs have restrictions: file-level recovery and replacing the existing VM are not supported in that workflow. An appropriate alternative is to restore the VM and then copy the needed files. Decide the target and encryption conditions before choosing a recovery action, rather than discovering those boundaries halfway through an incident.

points: This optional exercise restores a VM protected in the preceding backup exercise.
Create a staging storage account and stop the lab VM before performing the demonstrated disk-replacement restore.
Open the VM Backup page, select Restore VM and choose an available recovery point.

sections.title: Prepare for the demonstrated disk replacement
paragraphs: This exercise uses an existing backed-up VM, a staging storage account and a recovery point. Its Stop step applies to the demonstrated replacement workflow; it is not a universal requirement to stop a live source before every kind of backup restore. First verify that the lab VM still exists and the desired recovery point is available. Then choose the staging account and stop the replacement target as directed.

sections.title: Choose a point for a reason
paragraphs: Suppose an unwanted change occurred after yesterday’s successful backup. Select a recovery point from before that change, accepting that later changes will not be present in the restored disks. The point’s timestamp is part of the recovery decision, while its consistency and available tier also matter. Choosing the newest point without considering the incident could recover the same unwanted state you are trying to undo.

sections.title: Follow the job to its outcome
paragraphs: Open the VM’s Backup page, select Restore VM, choose the point, and use Replace existing with the lab staging location. Starting the operation and seeing a restore notification is only submission. Inspect Backup Jobs for the restore status and subtasks, and then verify the recovered VM and the relevant data. This connects the chosen historical point to an observable result instead of assuming that a submitted job completed successfully.

Submit the disk-replacement restore for the stopped lab target.

modules.title: Monitor your Azure virtual machines with Azure Monitor

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Monitor both the Azure VM host and its guest operating system, workloads and applications.
The practical steps require an Azure subscription with suitable permissions; this module specifies Contributor access.

lessons.title: Monitoring for Azure VMs
points: Metrics are numerical measurements over time; logs are timestamped events and structured records. Azure Monitor provides tools for both.
Azure automatically collects VM host metrics and activity logs. Configure Azure Monitor Agent and data collection rules for guest performance counters and event logs.
Use host metrics to track availability, CPU, disks and networking. Recommended or custom alerts notify you when monitored conditions occur.
Boot diagnostics provides screenshots and boot output for troubleshooting startup problems.
A data collection rule specifies what guest data to collect and where to send it; Log Analytics workspaces store log data for querying.

The lesson uses classic logs-based VM insights: Azure Monitor Agent collects common guest performance data into Log Analytics for curated charts and workbooks. Current monitoring also offers OpenTelemetry metrics stored in an Azure Monitor workspace.
Create additional rules for guest event logs and query them with Kusto Query Language.

sections.title: Investigate the correct layer
paragraphs: A VM has host-level signals, a guest operating system, workloads and applications. CPU and network activity visible from the Azure host do not tell you everything happening inside an application. Azure collects host metrics and activity logs automatically, while the guest counters and event logs demonstrated here need additional collection configuration. Boot diagnostics gives a startup screenshot and serial output, which is especially useful when normal guest access is unavailable.

sections.title: Match the data to its store
paragraphs: Metrics describe numerical values over time; logs provide timestamped records that can explain events. A DCR describes the collected guest sources and their destination. Current OpenTelemetry guest metrics use an Azure Monitor workspace, while classic logs-based performance collection uses Log Analytics. Guest event logs also use Log Analytics and KQL. These workspace types serve different data paths, so a visible host chart does not prove guest logs are arriving.

sections.title: Work from symptom to evidence
paragraphs: For an original investigation, imagine a VM has high host CPU and users report slow requests. Use the host graph to identify the time interval, then compare available guest performance data and relevant event records during that interval. An activity-log operation may explain a configuration change, while Syslog may reveal an operating-system event. Correlated timing helps focus the investigation, but a graph by itself does not establish which application caused the symptom.

lessons.title: Monitor VM host data
points: Create the lab Linux VM with recommended alert rules enabled on the Monitoring tab, and configure alert notifications.
Enable boot diagnostics with managed storage. Avoid the deprecated Linux Diagnostics Agent option in this exercise.
After deployment, inspect the default availability, CPU, disk and network graphs on the VM overview. Guest metrics require further configuration.
View Activity log for resource operations and Boot diagnostics for startup screenshots and serial output.

sections.title: Know what the lab enables
paragraphs: Creating the lab Linux VM gives you a chance to inspect monitoring that is available before guest collection is configured. Enable the recommended alert rules and their notifications explicitly, and use boot diagnostics with managed storage. The Linux Diagnostics Agent is deprecated; it is not the required path to collect new guest data. Host charts and recommended alerts can reveal conditions without collecting every guest event or performance counter.

sections.title: Read three different evidence sources
paragraphs: The VM overview’s platform graphs show availability, CPU, disks and networking. The activity log records Azure resource operations, which helps establish whether a management change occurred around the incident. Boot diagnostics shows startup screenshots and serial output. These are complementary surfaces: a restart operation in the activity log and a failed boot message answer different parts of the same investigation, even when the VM is inaccessible through its usual application.

sections.title: Explain a missing guest measurement
paragraphs: If host Percentage CPU is visible but guest available memory is absent, first ask whether guest collection was enabled. Creating the VM and enabling boot diagnostics does not automatically create the DCR needed for the demonstrated guest counters and event logs. In the lab, compare the populated host charts with the unconfigured guest section before moving to enhanced monitoring. This makes the host-versus-guest boundary visible instead of treating every empty chart as a VM failure.
steps: Review the lab VM’s platform metric graphs.
Inspect a relevant resource operation in Activity log.
Open the boot screenshot and serial log, then identify which guest data still needs collection configuration.

lessons.title: Use Metrics Explorer to view detailed host metrics
points: Open Metrics Explorer from the VM Metrics page or Azure Monitor. Choose the resource scope, namespace, metric and aggregation.
Aggregation options include count, average, minimum, maximum and sum; choose one that answers the investigation.
Add more than one metric to correlate trends, and select an appropriate time range and sampling granularity.
The example compares maximum Percentage CPU with average Inbound Flows over the last 30 minutes.

sections.title: Define the question before the chart
paragraphs: Metrics Explorer lets you select the resource scope, metric namespace, metric and aggregation. The namespace matters because it identifies the collection of metrics offered by a resource; storage, for example, exposes service-specific namespaces. Start with a question such as whether brief CPU peaks coincide with increased inbound traffic, then choose the VM scope and the metrics that can actually address it. Adding more charts is useful only when each contributes relevant evidence.

sections.title: Choose the meaning of each plotted value
paragraphs: Maximum CPU shows the highest recorded CPU value within each interval, whereas Average can hide a short peak among lower samples. Sum adds values, Count reports the number of values, and Minimum identifies the lowest value. Not every aggregation is meaningful for every metric. Distinguish the time range shown on the screen from the grain that groups samples into each plotted interval.

sections.title: Build and interpret a comparison
paragraphs: For the lab investigation, plot Percentage CPU using Max and add Inbound Flows using Avg over the same thirty-minute range. Compare when the curves change rather than treating their different units as equivalent quantities. A coincident increase suggests where to investigate next; it does not prove that one signal caused the other. Adjust the selected interval if aggregation obscures the detail you need, while retaining a time range relevant to the incident.
steps: Select the VM scope and Percentage CPU with Maximum aggregation.
Add Inbound Flows with Average aggregation.
Set the common time range and examine whether the recorded peaks occur together.

lessons.title: Collect client performance counters by using VM insights
points: The lesson demonstrates classic logs-based VM insights with a data collection rule and Log Analytics workspace. Current portal onboarding uses Monitor and Configure, with OpenTelemetry metrics selected by default and a logs-based option.
For classic logs-based monitoring, Azure Monitor Agent collects a predefined set of guest performance counters. Allow time for agent installation and data ingestion.
Confirm the agent under Extensions and applications, then inspect guest performance data.
View classic logs-based counters in VM insights performance charts and workbooks. These counters go to Log Analytics; OpenTelemetry monitoring instead stores metrics in an Azure Monitor workspace.
VM insights Map and Dependency Agent are deprecated and retire on 30 June 2028. New portal onboarding ended on 30 September 2025; do not enable them for new deployments.

sections.title: Choose the current guest-metrics experience
paragraphs: The training unit demonstrates classic logs-based VM insights, but current portal onboarding starts from Monitor and Configure. OpenTelemetry metrics are selected by default and are recommended for new deployments; logs-based monitoring remains an alternative. Select deliberately because OpenTelemetry guest metrics go to an Azure Monitor workspace, while classic VM insights performance data goes to Log Analytics. The choice affects both storage and how you later view and query the data.

sections.title: Trace the supported classic collection path
paragraphs: When studying the classic workflow, follow Azure Monitor Agent, its DCR and the selected Log Analytics workspace as separate pieces. The rule defines the guest performance collection, the agent collects it, and the workspace holds the records used by the performance workbooks. Allow time for installation and ingestion, and confirm the agent and DCR association before assuming an empty workbook means the workload is healthy or broken. The classic performance workbook does not display metrics-only OpenTelemetry collection.

sections.title: Avoid the retired onboarding direction
paragraphs: Do not follow the older unit’s suggestion to enable dependency mapping for a new VM. VM insights Map and Dependency Agent are deprecated; new portal onboarding ended on 30 September 2025 and retirement is scheduled for 30 June 2028. For a worked planning example, a newly deployed application server should use the supported guest-monitoring experience appropriate to its telemetry needs, rather than making a new monitoring design depend on the deprecated Map feature.

lessons.title: Collect VM client event logs
points: Create a data collection rule for guest event logs; the default VM insights rule does not collect every event source.
For the Linux example, associate the VM with a Linux rule and select Linux Syslog as the data source.
Send Syslog to a Log Analytics workspace. The lesson creates a data collection endpoint, but ordinary public-endpoint Syslog collection does not require one; Private Link does.
In the VM Logs page or Azure Monitor Logs, select the appropriate scope and run a KQL query against the Syslog table.
Filter by relevant fields such as severity to investigate events associated with a performance problem.

sections.title: Collect events independently of performance counters
paragraphs: The classic VM insights DCR collects a predefined set of performance counters, not every event from the guest. To investigate operating-system events, define a separate Linux Syslog source, choose the relevant facilities and severities, associate the rule with the VM and send the records to Log Analytics. Sharing a DCR across compatible VMs can keep collection settings consistent, while different source requirements may justify additional rules.

sections.title: Decide whether an endpoint is required
paragraphs: The training example creates a data collection endpoint, but that is not a universal prerequisite for public-endpoint Syslog collection. Azure Monitor Agent requires a DCE for Private Link configurations, including agents on networks sharing DNS with an Azure Monitor Private Link Scope. Assess the network design before adding an endpoint. A DCR controls the data collection specification; a DCE addresses the relevant collection endpoint and network-access requirements.

sections.title: Query the records that actually arrived
paragraphs: After configuration, select the correct VM or Log Analytics workspace scope and inspect Syslog records in the relevant time range. The original query below groups last-hour records by their reported severity. It helps establish which severities are being received before you narrow an investigation. An empty result should prompt checks of scope, time range, source filters, agent status and association, rather than an immediate conclusion that no guest events occurred.

code.text:
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| summarize count() by SeverityLevel
| order by count_ desc

points: Use host metrics for platform health, VM insights for guest performance, and data collection rules plus Log Analytics for event investigation.
